tagline: A Radio Station Made of Genes
dek: Pandora played you a free radio station built around one song you loved, then found more music like it.
lede: Pandora's founders broke songs down like a scientist maps DNA. Their Music Genome Project tagged each track by its melody, rhythm, and voice, so the service could play you more music that sounded like the song you chose. By 2011 people were streaming those stations on phones and in cars. Pandora filed to go public as the biggest name in internet radio, carrying heavy royalty bills and a question about whether ads could ever pay them.

sections.heading: From Savage Beast to Radio
sections.body: Will Glaser and Tim Westergren dreamed up the Music Genome Project around 1999. In January 2000 they joined Jon Kraft to found Savage Beast Technologies. The first plan was to license the music analysis to retailers as a recommendation tool. That business struggled. In 2005 the company turned to listeners directly and launched Pandora, a free internet radio service. A user typed in one artist or song, and Pandora built a station around it, learning from thumbs up and thumbs down.

sections.heading: A Pop, Then a Long Fade
sections.body: Pandora priced its IPO at $16 a share in June 2011, almost twice the price it first expected. The stock opened at $20 and climbed to $26 before closing the day at $17.42. Spotify and Apple Music soon pulled listeners toward on-demand streaming, and royalty costs kept squeezing profits. Sirius XM took a stake in 2017. In February 2019 Sirius XM bought the rest of Pandora in an all-stock deal valued at $3.5 billion.

cover.theme: Pandora (the myth behind the name)

fate: Taken private by Hellman & Friedman and Permira, 2022 ($10.2B)
tagline: Calm Help From a Copenhagen Loft
dek: Zendesk gave companies a simple way to answer customer emails, chats, and calls without the chaos of a crowded inbox.
lede: Zendesk started in a Copenhagen loft, where three friends wrote help-desk software while paying their bills with consulting work. Customer service tools of the day were heavy, costly, and hard to set up. Zendesk ran in the browser and took minutes to start. By 2014 the company had moved to San Francisco and signed up businesses across the world. It filed to go public as one of the friendliest names in a crowded field of cloud software.

sections.heading: Three Friends, One Loft
sections.body: Mikkel Svane, Morten Primdahl, and Alexander Aghassipour founded Zendesk in Copenhagen in 2007. They built the first version in Svane's loft and paid for it themselves. Within a few months of launch it had about 1,000 trial customers. The bet was that support software should feel light. Any team could sign up online, pay by the month, and turn every customer email into a ticket it could track. The founders later moved the company to San Francisco to raise money and grow.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars, Then a Buyout
sections.body: Zendesk priced its IPO at $9 a share in May 2014 and raised $100 million. The stock opened at $11.40 on the New York Stock Exchange and closed its first day near $13.50. Zendesk kept growing for years. In 2022 it turned down a $17 billion bid, then faced pressure from the activist investor Jana Partners. That November a group led by Hellman & Friedman and Permira took Zendesk private in a $10.2 billion deal, at $77.50 a share.

cover.theme: a calm Hotei, the laughing Buddha (zen)
cover.artwork: Hotei Smoking his Pipe, from The Picture Book of Realistic Paintings of Hokusai

tagline: Phone Calls in a Few Lines of Code
dek: Twilio let any programmer add calls and text messages to an app with a few lines of code.
lede: Twilio turned the phone network into something a programmer could rent by the minute. Before it, adding a text message or a phone call to an app meant deals with carriers and racks of telecom gear. Twilio hid all of that behind a simple interface. Uber, Airbnb, and thousands of smaller apps used it to text riders and guests. In 2016 Twilio became the first venture-backed tech company to go public in the United States that year.

sections.heading: Selling to Developers First
sections.body: Jeff Lawson, Evan Cooke, and John Wolthuis founded Twilio in 2008. All three had studied at the University of Michigan. Lawson had seen at earlier startups how painful it was to connect software to phones. Twilio's bet was to sell to programmers before their bosses. A developer could sign up with a credit card, write a few lines of code, and send a message that afternoon. Twilio charged for each call and text, so its revenue grew as its customers grew.

sections.heading: A 92 Percent First Day
sections.body: Twilio priced its IPO at $15 a share in June 2016, above its expected range, and raised $150 million. The stock opened near $24 and closed its first day at $28.79, up about 92 percent. Twilio spent heavily on acquisitions in the years after, including the email company SendGrid. Growth slowed after 2021 and the stock fell hard. Lawson stepped down as CEO in January 2024, and Khozema Shipchandler took his place. Twilio still trades on the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.theme: twilight over haystacks (the name)

dek: Dayforce ran payroll, schedules, and HR for big employers in one cloud system that kept pay up to date daily.
lede: Ceridian bought a small Toronto startup in 2012 and then handed that startup's founder the keys to the whole company. The startup was Dayforce, and its founder, David Ossip, became Ceridian's CEO. He rebuilt an old payroll business, with roots in the mainframe maker Control Data, around his cloud software. In April 2018 Ceridian went public in New York and Toronto. It was the largest Canadian tech IPO on record, and Dayforce was its main product.

sections.heading: The Startup That Took Over
sections.body: Ceridian processed paychecks for decades on older systems. Dayforce took a different approach. It kept payroll, time clocks, scheduling, and benefits in one database, and it recalculated pay as hours came in, so employers saw costs every day. After the 2012 deal, Ceridian moved its customers onto Dayforce and let the old products shrink. The bet was that big employers would pay a premium for one system that replaced a pile of separate tools.

sections.heading: Two Listings, One New Name
sections.body: Ceridian priced its IPO at $22 a share in April 2018, listing on both the New York and Toronto stock exchanges. The stock closed its first day up about 42 percent, at roughly $31. The company grew Dayforce for years and in 2024 renamed itself after it. In August 2025 Thoma Bravo agreed to buy Dayforce for $70 a share in cash, about $12.3 billion including debt. The deal closed in February 2026, and Dayforce left both exchanges.

cover.theme: a sunrise (a new day of payroll)

dek: Jumia let shoppers across Africa order online and pay on delivery, in markets few big retailers dared to serve.
lede: Jumia became the first African tech startup to list on the New York Stock Exchange, and its stock jumped 75 percent on day one. Founded in Lagos in 2012, it sold phones, clothes, and groceries online in countries where roads were rough, addresses vague, and few people had credit cards. Investors called it the Amazon of Africa. Within weeks of its April 2019 debut, a short seller accused it of fraud.

sections.heading: Building Roads for Parcels
sections.body: Sacha Poignonnec and Jeremy Hodara started Jumia in Nigeria in 2012 with Nigerian entrepreneurs Tunde Kehinde and Raphael Afaedor, who left in 2015. The company had to build what Western retailers took for granted. It ran its own delivery network, set up pickup points, and let customers pay cash when parcels arrived. It added a payments service, JumiaPay, and food delivery. The bet was that whoever built the rails first would own online shopping across a continent of more than a billion people.

sections.heading: A Short Seller Arrives
sections.body: Jumia priced its IPO at $14.50 a share in April 2019. The stock opened at $18.95 and closed its first day near $25.46. In May, Citron Research accused Jumia of inflating its numbers. Jumia later found that some sales agents in Nigeria had placed improper orders. By August 2019 the stock had fallen below its IPO price. Jumia pulled out of several countries to cut losses. It still trades on the New York Stock Exchange, far below its $14.50 offer price.

cover.theme: a camel caravan (trade across Africa)
cover.artwork: Camel Caravan Crossing Plane Above Waterfall

fate: Delisted from Nasdaq, 2026; trades over the counter (CMBMF)
dek: Cambium sold radios that beam internet across fields and rooftops to places cables never reach.
lede: Cambium Networks began as two wireless businesses that Motorola Solutions no longer wanted. The private equity firm Vector Capital bought them in 2011 and gave them a new name. The products were radios that send broadband through the air, from tower to tower and tower to home. Small rural internet providers, cities, and factories used them where laying cable cost too much. When Cambium went public in June 2019, Vector still owned about 75 percent of the company.

sections.heading: Orthogon and Canopy
sections.body: Motorola launched its Canopy radios in 1999 to bring broadband to rural areas. In 2006 it bought Orthogon Systems, a maker of long point-to-point links. Five years later neither business fit Motorola's plans, and Vector Capital bought both. The new company took the name Cambium, a word for the growing layer inside a tree. Its bet was that small operators all over the world would keep building wireless networks, and that they would buy their radios, Wi-Fi, and software from one place.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to the Expert Market
sections.body: Cambium priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 2019 and listed on Nasdaq as CMBM. It raised about $66 million after fees. Later it fell behind on its financial reports to the SEC. After several extensions, Nasdaq suspended trading in March 2026. Cambium's shares moved to the over-the-counter Expert Market as CMBMF, where most investors cannot trade them easily. The last reported sale there on March 30, 2026 was 13 cents a share.

cover.theme: trees (cambium, the growing layer of a tree)

dek: SiTime made tiny silicon timing chips that keep electronics in sync, built to outlast the quartz crystals they replace.
lede: Almost every electronic device needs a clock, and for decades that clock was a sliver of quartz crystal. SiTime bet it could do the job with a tiny vibrating structure carved from silicon. Its MEMS timing chips were smaller, tougher, and easier to make in volume. By the time it went public in November 2019, SiTime belonged to a Japanese chip company, MegaChips, which still kept about two-thirds of the shares after the offering.

sections.heading: Replacing a Quartz Crystal
sections.body: Markus Lutz and Aaron Partridge founded SiTime in Santa Clara in 2005. Quartz had ruled timing for a century, and suppliers had little reason to change. SiTime's devices used microelectromechanical systems, called MEMS, built on ordinary silicon. They resisted shock and heat, and they could be programmed to many frequencies. The bet was slow and patient. SiTime had to win designers one product at a time. In 2014 MegaChips bought the company for $200 million in cash.

sections.heading: Bottom of the Range
sections.body: SiTime priced its IPO at $13 a share in November 2019, the low end of its range. The stock closed its first day at $18.65. Demand for its chips grew with 5G networks, data centers, and cars, and the stock climbed far above its offer price in the years after. MegaChips sold down its stake over time. SiTime still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker SITM.

cover.theme: a pocket watch (timing)

tagline: A Teenager's Card Business, Grown Up
dek: Shift4 processed card payments for restaurants, hotels, and stadiums, tied into the software they already ran.
lede: Jared Isaacman started a card-processing business at 16, and twenty years later he took it public in the middle of a pandemic. The company, first called United Bank Card and later Shift4, moved money for restaurants and hotels. Those were the businesses COVID-19 had just shut down. Shift4 went public in June 2020 anyway, and investors bid it up. Its founder later flew to orbit and went on to lead NASA.

sections.heading: Payments Inside the Software
sections.body: Isaacman founded the company in 1999 as United Bank Card. It grew by selling card processing to small merchants, then focused on businesses with complex checkouts. Restaurants, hotels, and stadiums ran their own point-of-sale software. Shift4 built its payments into those systems, so a merchant could take cards without changing how it worked. The bet was that payments sold through the software a merchant already trusted would be hard to replace.

sections.heading: Thirty-Three Dollars in a Pandemic
sections.body: Shift4 priced its IPO at $23 a share in June 2020, above its expected range of $19 to $21. Isaacman bought $100 million more stock in a private placement alongside the offering. The shares closed their first day at $33.54, up about 46 percent. In 2021 Isaacman commanded Inspiration4, a private SpaceX flight to orbit. In December 2025 he was sworn in as NASA's 15th administrator. Shift4 still trades on the New York Stock Exchange as FOUR.

cover.theme: a busy shop (point of sale)

dek: JFrog gave software teams one place to store, secure, and ship the finished builds they release to the world.
lede: JFrog sold software that most people never see, and its stock jumped 47 percent on day one. Programmers write code, but companies ship compiled packages, containers, and libraries. Those files have to live somewhere safe before they reach servers and phones. JFrog's Artifactory became that warehouse for thousands of companies. The Israeli company went public in September 2020, as the pandemic pushed every business to ship software faster.

sections.heading: Artifactory Before DevOps
sections.body: Shlomi Ben Haim, Yoav Landman, and Fred Simon founded JFrog in Israel in 2008. Landman had built Artifactory as an open-source tool for storing Java build files. The founders turned it into a business that handled every kind of package. They sold it to developers first and let usage spread inside companies. JFrog later added tools for scanning packages for security flaws and pushing updates to devices. The bet was that every company would turn into a software company and need a place for its builds.

sections.heading: Forty-Four Dollars, Then More
sections.body: JFrog priced its IPO at $44 a share in September 2020, above its expected range, and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker FROG. The stock closed its first day at $64.79, up 47 percent, valuing the company at more than $5.7 billion. JFrog kept selling to large companies and moving customers to its cloud service. It still trades on Nasdaq as FROG.

cover.theme: a toad in the path (the frog)
cover.artwork: A Toad in the Path: Early Spring in Norfolk

tagline: Backups for the Corner Office IT Shop
dek: Datto gave small businesses big-company backup and recovery, sold through the local IT firms that ran their computers.
lede: Datto never sold to the businesses that used it. A dentist's office or a small law firm rarely had its own IT staff, so it hired a local managed service provider to run its computers. Datto sold backup and recovery tools to those providers, and they resold Datto to thousands of small clients. By its October 2020 IPO, Datto was owned mostly by Vista Equity Partners, and remote work had made small business IT more urgent than ever.

sections.heading: Finding the MSP Channel
sections.body: Austin McChord founded Datto in 2007 in Connecticut. His idea was to give small and midsize businesses the kind of backup and recovery that only big companies could afford. Datto's boxes copied a client's servers and could run them from the backup if the originals failed. The key move was the sales channel. Datto sold only through managed service providers, the small IT firms that look after offices on contract, and it added software to help them run their whole businesses.

sections.heading: Twenty-Seven Dollars, Then Kaseya
sections.body: Datto priced its IPO at $27 a share in October 2020 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as MSP. It sold 22 million shares and used much of the money to pay down debt. After the offering, Vista still owned about 72 percent of the company. Less than two years later, in April 2022, Kaseya agreed to buy Datto. The deal closed in June 2022 at $35.50 a share in cash, and Datto left the exchange.

cover.theme: pairs of animals entering the ark (two copies of everything)
cover.artwork: The Pairs of Animals Entering the Ark

fate: Sold Wish to a Qoo10 affiliate, 2024 (~$161M); shell trades OTC as LOGC
dek: Wish sold rock-bottom-priced goods from overseas merchants to shoppers on their phones, if they were willing to wait.
lede: Wish raised about $1.1 billion when it went public in December 2020, then sold its whole business three and a half years later for about $161 million. In between, it ran one of the largest shopping apps in the world. Wish connected more than 100 million monthly users in over 100 countries to some 500,000 merchants, most selling cheap goods that took weeks to arrive. Investors bet the pandemic shopping boom would last.

sections.heading: Cheap Goods, Long Waits
sections.body: Peter Szulczewski and Danny Zhang started the company, ContextLogic, in 2010. Its Wish app showed shoppers an endless scroll of low-priced items, from phone cases to garden tools, with deep discounts. The bet was on shoppers that big retailers ignored, people who cared more about price than speed. Wish spent heavily on ads to find them. Revenue grew from $1.1 billion in 2017 to $1.9 billion in 2019. Szulczewski, as founder and CEO, controlled most of the votes.

sections.heading: From Wish to LOGC
sections.body: Wish priced its IPO at $24 a share in December 2020 and sold 46 million shares on Nasdaq under the ticker WISH. The stock soon fell far below its offer price. In April 2024 ContextLogic sold almost all its assets, including Wish, to an affiliate of Qoo10 for about $161 million in cash. It kept its tax losses, left Nasdaq in 2025, and now trades over the counter as LOGC.

cover.theme: Wishes, from Klinger's dreamlike print series
cover.artwork: Wishes, plate three from A Glove

dek: Bumble built a dating app where women send the first message, then stretched the idea to friendship and work.
lede: On Bumble, only women can send the first message, and by 2020 they had done it more than 1.7 billion times. Whitney Wolfe Herd launched the app in 2014 with a simple rule meant to make online dating feel safer and more polite. It grew into one of the biggest dating apps in the world. When Bumble went public in February 2021, it also owned Badoo, and Blackstone held a large stake.

sections.heading: One Rule, Built In
sections.body: Wolfe Herd launched Bumble in Austin in 2014. Other apps let anyone message anyone. Bumble gave women the first move. The bet was that a better experience for women would bring more of them, and men would follow. Bumble later added modes for making friends and for business networking. In January 2020 Blackstone bought a majority stake in the company that owned Bumble and Badoo.

sections.heading: A CEO Who Came Back
sections.body: Bumble priced its IPO at $43 a share in February 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as BMBL. It sold 50 million shares and raised about $2.2 billion. The stock fell well below that price in the years after. In January 2024 Wolfe Herd handed the CEO job to Lidiane Jones and became executive chair. In 2025 she returned as CEO. Bumble still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: bees (Bumble)
cover.artwork: A Moth, Butterflies, and Bees, from Diversae Insectorum Volatilium Icones

fate: Still public (NYSE: COUR); merged with Udemy, 2026
tagline: A Stanford Lecture Hall for Everyone
dek: Coursera put courses from top universities online so anyone, anywhere, could learn from them, often for free.
lede: Coursera grew out of a single Stanford class on machine learning that Andrew Ng put online in 2011. Ng and fellow professor Daphne Koller turned the idea into a company that brought university courses to anyone with an internet connection. By the end of 2020 it had 77 million registered learners and more than 150 university partners. It went public in March 2021, a year into a pandemic that had pushed school online.

sections.heading: Two Professors, One Platform
sections.body: Ng and Koller founded Coursera in 2011 and launched its first open online course in 2012. Universities supplied the teaching, and Coursera supplied the platform. Most courses were free to watch. Coursera made money from certificates, then from degree programs, and from 2016 from an Enterprise product that let companies train their staff. The bet was that a credential from a famous school would be worth paying for, even when the lectures were free.

sections.heading: Thirty-Three Dollars and Udemy
sections.body: Coursera priced its IPO at $33 a share in March 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as COUR. It went public as a public benefit corporation, with its education mission written into its charter. In December 2025 Coursera agreed to combine with its rival Udemy. The all-stock deal closed in May 2026, and Coursera still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: an old man teaching a boy to read (learning)
cover.artwork: Old Man with a Boy Reading

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2023 ($24.90 a share)
tagline: Teaching Staff Not to Take the Bait
dek: KnowBe4 trained employees to spot phishing emails by sending them fake ones and teaching them when they clicked.
lede: KnowBe4 sold a security product built around a former hacker's name. Its main course was Kevin Mitnick Security Awareness Training, named for the hacker turned security consultant. KnowBe4's idea was that attackers walked past firewalls by fooling people. So it sent workers fake phishing emails and taught the ones who clicked. By the time it went public in April 2021, its founder had spent more than two decades in the security business.

sections.heading: Fixing the Human Layer
sections.body: Stu Sjouwerman had worked in cybersecurity for 15 years when he started KnowBe4 in Clearwater, Florida, in 2010. He saw companies spend billions on security products and still get breached through a single click. KnowBe4 sold training and simulated attacks by subscription. A company could send its own staff a fake phishing email, see who fell for it, and assign short lessons. KnowBe4 later added PhishER, a tool for sorting the suspicious emails employees reported.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars to Vista
sections.body: KnowBe4 priced its IPO at $16 a share in April 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as KNBE. The company sold 9 million new shares, and early holders sold more alongside them. In October 2022 Vista Equity Partners agreed to buy the company. The deal closed on February 1, 2023, at $24.90 a share in cash, and KnowBe4 left Nasdaq less than two years after its debut.

cover.theme: a bass striking a lure (phishing)

dek: Marqeta let fintech apps and delivery companies issue their own payment cards, with rules written in code.
lede: Marqeta started at a San Francisco sushi bar in December 2009, when a friend pulled out a handful of Groupon coupons. He told Jason Gardner, a payments veteran, to find a way to put them on a card. That idea grew into a platform that let companies like Square create and control their own debit cards through software. By its June 2021 IPO, Square alone brought in 70 percent of Marqeta's revenue.

sections.heading: Cards You Can Program
sections.body: Gardner had co-founded a company that MoneyGram bought. He started Marqeta in 2010. Legacy card issuing technology was rigid and slow to change. Marqeta offered a modern cloud platform with open APIs. A company could decide in code where a card worked, how much it could spend, and when to approve each swipe. Square became a customer in 2016 and launched its Square Card on Marqeta in 2018. DoorDash used it to pay for orders, and Affirm and Klarna used it for installment cards.

sections.heading: Square-Sized Risk
sections.body: Marqeta priced its IPO at $27 a share in June 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as MQ. Its biggest strength was also its biggest risk, since one customer drove most of its sales. The stock fell well below its offer price. Gardner handed the CEO job to Simon Khalaf in January 2023 and became executive chairman. Khalaf stepped down in February 2025, and the board named finance chief Mike Milotich CEO that September. Marqeta still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: card players (a card company)

dek: Confluent turned Kafka, free software that streams data between apps instantly, into a service companies could rent.
lede: Confluent's founders built the core of their product before the company existed. As engineers at LinkedIn in 2011, Jay Kreps, Jun Rao, and Neha Narkhede created Apache Kafka, open-source software for moving streams of data between systems the moment they happen. In 2014 the three left to sell Kafka as a business. When Confluent went public in June 2021, it pitched data in motion as the central nervous system of every company.

sections.heading: Selling Free Software
sections.body: Kafka was free, so Confluent had to sell something more. It started with Confluent Platform, which added tools for running Kafka inside big companies. The bigger bet was Confluent Cloud, a managed service that ran Kafka for customers so they did not need their own experts. Its pitch was that most databases handled data at rest, and modern apps needed to act on data the instant it arrived.

sections.heading: Thirty-Six Dollars to IBM
sections.body: Confluent priced its IPO at $36 a share in June 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as CFLT. It went public with two classes of stock, and insiders held the Class B shares with extra votes. In December 2025 IBM agreed to buy Confluent for cash. The deal closed on March 17, 2026, at $31 a share, five dollars below the IPO price. Confluent left Nasdaq and became part of IBM.

cover.theme: a stream rushing through a gorge (data in motion)

tagline: Software for Plumbers, Doctors, and Trainers
dek: EverCommerce sold booking, billing, and payment software to small service businesses like contractors, clinics, and gyms.
lede: EverCommerce served more than 500,000 small businesses, and almost none of their customers ever heard its name. Its software ran the back offices of home contractors, physical therapists, personal trainers, and salon owners. Each industry got tools built for its own work, plus payments to tie them together. When the Denver company went public in July 2021, its private equity backers, Silver Lake and Providence Strategic Growth, still controlled it.

sections.heading: A Roll-Up With a Plan
sections.body: Eric Remer co-founded PaySimple, a payments company for small businesses, in 2006 and ran it for a decade. In October 2016 he founded EverCommerce and folded PaySimple into it. The company grew by buying software makers in three areas: home services, health services, and fitness and wellness. The bet was that service businesses would pay for software made for their trade, and that payments, marketing, and customer tools could be sold on top.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars on Nasdaq
sections.body: EverCommerce priced its IPO at $17 a share in July 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as EVCM. EverCommerce sold its shares to the public while Remer stayed on as CEO. Alongside the offering, Silver Lake agreed to buy $75 million more stock at the same price. The shares soon traded below their offer price. EverCommerce kept reorganizing around its three businesses, including its EverHealth and EverPro units. It still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: an evergreen pine (EverCommerce)

tagline: Language Lessons Built Like a Game
dek: Duolingo made learning a language free, bite-sized, and as habit-forming as a phone game.
lede: By 2021 more people in the United States were learning languages on Duolingo than in all American high schools combined. The app came from a Carnegie Mellon professor and his Ph.D. student. It taught 40 languages to about 40 million monthly users in short, game-like lessons, nudged along by a green owl. Duolingo was free, and only about 5 percent of users paid. It went public in July 2021 from its home in Pittsburgh.

sections.heading: A Professor and His Student
sections.body: Luis von Ahn grew up in Guatemala and became a computer science professor at Carnegie Mellon and a MacArthur Fellow. He founded Duolingo in 2011 with Severin Hacker, his Ph.D. student, and launched it in 2012. The bet was that free education could reach far more people than paid classes, if the product was fun enough to open every day. The team ran constant A/B tests. They lifted the share of learners who came back the next day from 12 percent to over 40 percent.

sections.heading: Paid Users, Then Profits
sections.body: Duolingo added a paid tier, Duolingo Plus, in 2017. Paying subscribers grew from 0.9 million at the end of 2019 to 1.6 million a year later. The company priced its IPO at $102 a share in July 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as DUOL. It kept adding subjects, including math and music, and grew its paying base. Duolingo still trades on Nasdaq, with its headquarters in Pittsburgh.

cover.theme: an owl (Duo, the mascot)
cover.artwork: Ornament with Owl Mocked by Day Birds

dek: Toast gave restaurants one system to take orders, run the kitchen, pay staff, and process every card payment.
lede: Toast was built for one industry only, and by mid-2021 it ran about 48,000 restaurant locations. Its tablets and software took orders at the table, sent tickets to the kitchen, handled delivery, and processed payments. Those restaurants ran over $38 billion of card payments through Toast in a year. The Boston company went public in September 2021, as diners returned to restaurants after the first waves of COVID-19.

sections.heading: One Industry, Every Workflow
sections.body: Aman Narang, Steve Fredette, and Jonathan Grimm started Toast in 2011 and launched operations in 2013. They believed restaurants were poorly served by general tools built for every kind of shop. Toast built its point-of-sale software on Android and added kitchen displays, online ordering, payroll, and loans through Toast Capital. Most of its revenue came from processing card payments. Each new product gave a restaurant one more reason to stay.

sections.heading: Forty Dollars and a Founder CEO
sections.body: Toast priced its IPO at $40 a share in September 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as TOST. Its 48,000 locations belonged to about 29,000 customers. Chris Comparato, who had run Toast for years, stepped down as CEO at the start of 2024. Co-founder Aman Narang, who had been co-president and operating chief, took over. Toast still trades on the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.theme: a toast with raised glasses

dek: Arteris licensed the on-chip networks that move data between the many parts of a modern processor.
lede: A modern chip holds dozens of separate blocks, from processor cores to memory controllers, and they all need to talk. Arteris sells the roads between them. Its FlexNoC technology turns signals inside a chip into small packets of data, like a tiny computer network. Chipmakers license it rather than build their own, and it had gone into hundreds of designs by the time Arteris went public in October 2021.

sections.heading: A Network on a Chip
sections.body: Arteris was founded in 2003 and built its business on network-on-chip interconnect, known as NoC. Older chips wired each block to the others directly, which grew messy as designs got bigger. Arteris packetized the traffic so the connections could scale. It sells this as intellectual property, so chip designers pay license fees and royalties instead of buying parts. Arteris licenses part of its FlexNoC technology from Qualcomm. It bet on demand from cars, AI, 5G, and data centers.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars on Nasdaq
sections.body: Arteris priced its IPO at $14 a share in October 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as AIP. Its chief executive, K. Charles Janac, and the venture firm Ventech held large stakes going in. The company was small next to the chipmakers it served, with offices in California, Texas, France, China, South Korea, and Japan. Arteris still trades on Nasdaq, from its headquarters in Campbell, California.

cover.theme: a railway yard (routing traffic)

dek: HashiCorp gave engineers tools to build, secure, and run cloud servers by writing code instead of clicking through consoles.
lede: HashiCorp's best-known product, Terraform, let an engineer describe a whole data center in a text file and then build it with one command. That idea, infrastructure as code, spread through companies moving to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. HashiCorp gave much of its software away as open source and sold the enterprise versions. It went public in December 2021 at $80 a share, late in a boom year for software stocks.

sections.heading: Terraform, Vault, Consul, Nomad
sections.body: Mitchell Hashimoto and Armon Dadgar founded HashiCorp, and Dadgar became its chief technology officer in 2013. The company built a family of tools for the cloud. Terraform set up servers and networks. Vault guarded passwords and keys. Consul connected services, and Nomad ran workloads. Its lineup also included Vagrant and Packer. The bet was that companies would run across several clouds at once and want one neutral set of tools for all of them.

sections.heading: Eighty Dollars to IBM
sections.body: HashiCorp priced its IPO at $80 a share in December 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as HCP. David McJannet was CEO, and Hashimoto had left the board that July but stayed on as an employee. The stock fell sharply as software valuations dropped in 2022. In April 2024 IBM agreed to buy HashiCorp. The deal closed on February 27, 2025, at $35 a share in cash, less than half the IPO price.

cover.theme: oxen plowing a field (terraforming the land)

tagline: Wiring for the AI Data Center
dek: Astera Labs made the connectivity chips that keep data moving between processors, memory, and networks in AI servers.
lede: Astera Labs' founders bet in 2017 that AI would hit a wall, and that the wall would be wiring. Processors were getting faster, but moving data between them, their memory, and the network was falling behind. Astera built chips to fix that, starting with Aries retimers that clean up PCIe signals inside servers. When it went public in March 2024, every major cloud company was racing to build AI data centers.

sections.heading: Betting on the Bottleneck
sections.body: Jitendra Mohan, Sanjay Gajendra, and Casey Morrison founded Astera Labs in 2017. They believed AI models would grow so large that they would only run at cloud scale. The limit, they argued, would be connectivity. Their Aries retimers became the main product, joined by Taurus Ethernet cable modules and Leo memory controllers. Astera worked with NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel, and it sold to the hyperscalers. Revenue grew 45 percent in 2023 on higher Aries shipments.

sections.heading: Thirty-Six Dollars and AI Demand
sections.body: Astera Labs priced its IPO at $36 a share in March 2024 and listed on Nasdaq as ALAB. Its revenue for 2023 was $115.8 million. By then its products had shipped in millions of devices across all the major hyperscalers, all managed by its COSMOS software. Mohan remained CEO and Gajendra president. Astera Labs still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Ad Astra, to the stars (Astera)

tagline: The Founder Who Bought It Back
dek: StubHub let fans resell tickets to concerts, games, and shows on a marketplace that stood behind every seat.
lede: Eric Baker co-founded StubHub as a Stanford business student in 2000, left, and then bought it back twenty years later. Before StubHub, reselling tickets meant scalpers outside the stadium or classified ads. StubHub built the first online marketplace for secondary tickets and sold to eBay. Baker went on to start viagogo, which bought StubHub from eBay in 2020. In September 2025 the combined company went public, with Baker as CEO.

sections.heading: Scalpers Move Online
sections.body: Baker started StubHub at Stanford Business School with the goal of making tickets easy to resell safely. The company handled search, payment, delivery, and support, so buyers did not have to trust a stranger. It made money from fees on each sale. Baker later launched viagogo in 2006. In February 2020 viagogo bought StubHub from eBay, just before the pandemic closed every arena. In 2021 the company renamed itself StubHub Holdings.

sections.heading: Twenty-Three Fifty on the NYSE
sections.body: StubHub priced its IPO at $23.50 a share in September 2025 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as STUB. It planned to use most of the money to repay debt. The listing came five and a half years after viagogo closed its StubHub purchase. The offering raised about $735 million for the company after fees. Baker kept running the business as founder and CEO. StubHub still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a theatre audience (live events)
cover.artwork: Audience at a Parisian Theatre II

dek: NIQ tracked what consumers buy in stores and online, and sold that data to the brands and retailers making them.
lede: NIQ traces its roots to Arthur C. Nielsen, the man who invented market share. For a century his company measured what people bought, aisle by aisle and brand by brand. By 2025 NIQ covered more than 90 countries and about 85 percent of the world's population. It went public in July 2025 as a data company with deep roots, four years after private equity pulled it out of Nielsen.

sections.heading: Spun Out of Nielsen
sections.body: Nielsen ran two businesses for decades, one measuring TV audiences and one measuring shopping. The shopping side, called Connect, had fallen behind newer rivals. In March 2021 Advent International and the executive Jim Peck bought it from Nielsen. They invested in data and software and built an omnichannel view of shopping. In July 2023 NIQ combined with GfK, the German market research firm. The bet was that brands would pay for one global view of every channel where shoppers spend.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Dollars in Chicago
sections.body: NIQ priced its IPO at $21 a share in July 2025 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as NIQ. The company is registered in Ireland and run from Chicago. After the offering, Advent still held a majority of the votes, which made NIQ a controlled company under NYSE rules. NIQ still trades on the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.theme: shoppers lined up at a butcher shop (consumer behavior)
cover.artwork: Line in Front of the Butcher Shop

dek: BitGo kept digital assets safe for exchanges, funds, and governments, and let them trade and settle from the same vault.
lede: BitGo protected bitcoin with a simple trick: three keys, any two of which could move the money. That 2-of-3 multi-signature design, introduced in 2013, became a standard way to secure crypto. BitGo grew into a custodian for exchanges, funds, and even the governments of El Salvador and Bhutan. By September 2025 it held about $104 billion in assets on its platform. It went public in January 2026, after a planned sale to Galaxy fell apart.

sections.heading: Securing Bitcoin First
sections.body: Mike Belshe co-founded BitGo in 2013 with the idea that digital assets needed secure storage. A single lost or stolen key could wipe out a fortune. Multi-signature wallets spread that risk across several keys held in different places. By 2014 BitGo had built wallet systems for institutions. It later added a trust company, trading, settlement, and tools for launching stablecoins. BitGo served clients in more than 100 countries and supported over 1,550 digital assets.

sections.heading: Galaxy Walks, BitGo Lists
sections.body: Galaxy Digital agreed to buy BitGo for $1.2 billion, then terminated the deal in 2022. BitGo sued, saying Galaxy wrongfully walked away. Instead of a sale, BitGo chose the public markets. It priced its IPO at $18 a share in January 2026 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as BTGO. Belshe, its CEO, held Class B shares that gave him about 55 percent of the votes. BitGo still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: ornate keys and locks (custody)

dek: Red Hat made free Linux software safe for big companies to bet on, and charged for the support.
lede: Red Hat took its name from a red Cornell lacrosse cap that co-founder Marc Ewing wore, a cap that belonged to his grandfather. The company sold Linux, an operating system anyone could download for free. Its customers paid for a tested version, manuals, and someone to call when things broke. When Red Hat filed to go public in June 1999, Linux was the rebel of the server room and Microsoft ruled the desktop.

sections.heading: A Cap and a Catalog
sections.body: Ewing packaged Linux in North Carolina. Bob Young ran a business that sold Linux and Unix software by catalog. Young bought Ewing's company in 1995 and the two built Red Hat together. The code was open, so any rival could copy it. Red Hat bet that companies would pay for a brand they trusted, plus updates, training, and support. It sold boxed copies of Red Hat Linux in stores and signed service deals with businesses that ran Linux on their servers.

sections.heading: Shares for the Hackers
sections.body: Red Hat priced its IPO at $14 a share on August 10, 1999. The next day the stock closed near $52, one of the biggest first-day gains Wall Street had seen. The company set aside shares for the open-source programmers whose work it sold, so some of them could buy in at the offer price. Red Hat survived the dot-com crash and became the first open-source company to pass $1 billion in yearly revenue. IBM bought it for $34 billion in July 2019.

cover.theme: a man in a red cap (the red hat)
cover.artwork: Portrait of a Man in a Red Cap

dek: Workday moved the payroll, hiring, and staff records of big companies off their own servers and into the cloud.
lede: Workday began as a comeback. Dave Duffield had built PeopleSoft into a giant of business software, and Oracle took it from him in a hostile takeover in 2005. Within months he and Aneel Bhusri started over. Their new company ran human-resources software over the internet, so customers never had to install it. When Workday went public in October 2012, it was the largest tech IPO since Facebook that spring.

sections.heading: Starting Over From Scratch
sections.body: Duffield and Bhusri founded Workday in 2005 in Pleasanton, California, close to the old PeopleSoft campus. They brought many former PeopleSoft people with them. The bet was that large employers would trust their most sensitive data, such as salaries and staff records, to software that lived in the cloud. Workday wrote every line new. It sold one version to every customer and updated it for all of them at once. Finance and accounting software came next.

sections.heading: Seventy-Four Percent in a Day
sections.body: Workday priced its shares at $28 on October 11, 2012, above its target range, and raised $637 million. The next day the stock closed at $48.69 on the New York Stock Exchange, a gain of about 74 percent. In 2017 the company moved its listing to Nasdaq and kept the ticker WDAY. Today Workday runs payroll and HR systems for many of the world's largest employers. It trades on Nasdaq under WDAY.

cover.theme: a rooster at dawn (the start of the work day)

dek: Arista built fast network switches for the giant data centers behind the cloud, and took on Cisco to sell them.
lede: Two of Arista's founders had already sold a company to Cisco, and then they built the company Cisco would sue. Andy Bechtolsheim, a co-founder of Sun Microsystems, teamed up with Stanford professor David Cheriton and engineer Ken Duda. Their switches moved data between servers in the huge data centers that cloud companies were building. When Arista filed to go public in March 2014, those data centers were growing faster than the old network gear could keep up.

sections.heading: Software on Cheap Chips
sections.body: The company started in 2004 under the name Arastra and became Arista in 2008. That year Jayshree Ullal, a longtime Cisco executive, joined as chief executive. Arista's bet was software. It wrote one operating system, EOS, that ran across all its switches and let customers program the network themselves. It built on chips that other firms sold, so it could move fast. Its first big buyers were trading firms and cloud companies that wanted speed above everything else.

sections.heading: Cisco in the Courtroom
sections.body: Arista priced its IPO at $43 a share on June 5, 2014, above its target range. The stock jumped by roughly 30 percent when it opened on the New York Stock Exchange the next day. Six months later Cisco sued, claiming Arista had copied its patents and command language. The fight ran for years. In 2018 Arista agreed to pay Cisco $400 million to settle it. Arista still trades on the NYSE under ANET and sells to the largest cloud companies.

cover.theme: a wheat field (arista, the bristle on an ear of grain)

tagline: The Data Center in One Box
dek: Nutanix let companies run their own data centers like a cloud, with storage and computing folded into one simple system.
lede: Nutanix filed to go public in December 2015 and then waited nine months for the market to want it. The wait paid off. Its software let companies stop buying separate storage arrays and servers. Instead they stacked identical boxes, and Nutanix software pooled them into one system that grew as they added more. In 2016, cloud computing from Amazon was drawing work away from corporate data centers, and Nutanix offered those data centers a way to compete.

sections.heading: Three Engineers From Google's Era
sections.body: Dheeraj Pandey, Mohit Aron, and Ajeet Singh founded Nutanix in 2009. Aron had worked on Google's file system, which spread data across thousands of cheap machines. The founders bet that ordinary companies wanted the same design. They called it hyperconverged infrastructure: computing, storage, and networking in one appliance managed by software. Nutanix first sold its own boxes. Over time it shifted to selling the software alone, running on hardware from Dell, Lenovo, and others.

sections.heading: The Year's Biggest Pop
sections.body: Nutanix priced at $16 a share on September 29, 2016, above a range it had already raised. The next day the stock closed at $37 on Nasdaq, up 131 percent, the best debut of the year. Losses stayed large for years. In 2020 Bain Capital invested $750 million in the company, and Pandey handed the chief executive job to Rajiv Ramaswami. Nutanix still trades on Nasdaq under NTNX.

cover.theme: a squirrel (nuts, stored up)

tagline: Small Loans From a Security Giant
dek: 360 Finance matched Chinese borrowers with banks through a lending app, using data to judge who would pay back.
lede: 360 Finance grew out of Qihoo 360, the Chinese antivirus company, and used that company's huge base of users to find borrowers. Its app offered small personal loans. Banks and other lenders put up most of the money, and 360 Finance used data to decide who could borrow. When it listed in New York in December 2018, Chinese regulators had just cracked down on online lending, and investors had soured on the whole sector.

sections.heading: Credit Scored by Data
sections.body: 360 Finance started in 2016 in Shanghai, backed by the Qihoo 360 group. Many people in China had no credit history at banks. The company bet it could judge them from other data and offer them loans through an app. It earned fees for finding and screening borrowers. Over time it moved more of the lending risk onto its bank partners and sold its technology to them as a service.

sections.heading: Four Names, One Ticker
sections.body: The company priced its American depositary shares at $16.50 on December 13, 2018, the low end of its range, and raised about $51 million. They began trading on Nasdaq the next day under QFIN. The company renamed itself 360 DigiTech in 2020 and Qifu Technology in 2023. It added a listing in Hong Kong under the code 3660. In 2025 shareholders approved a new English name, Qfin Holdings. The Nasdaq ticker has stayed QFIN.

cover.theme: a carp (a Chinese symbol of wealth)

dek: Pinterest let people save pictures of what they wanted to cook, wear, build, or buy, and plan around them.
lede: Pinterest grew out of a habit Ben Silbermann had as a boy: he collected insects and stamps. His website let people collect pictures instead, pinned to boards for a kitchen, a wedding, or a trip. It launched in March 2010 as an invite-only site. By the time Pinterest filed to go public in March 2019, about 250 million people used it each month, and advertisers prized it because users came there to plan what to buy.

sections.heading: Boards Full of Wants
sections.body: Silbermann left a job at Google to start a company. With Paul Sciarra and Evan Sharp, an architecture student, he built Pinterest. Other social sites asked users to share their lives with friends. Pinterest asked them to save ideas for themselves. That made it calmer than Facebook or Twitter, and it drew many women in the American Midwest early on. The bet was that a board full of wants would one day make an ideal place to sell ads.

sections.heading: Above the Range
sections.body: Pinterest priced its shares at $19 on April 17, 2019, above its planned range. The stock opened at $23.75 on the New York Stock Exchange the next day and closed at $24.40, up 28 percent. Lyft and Zoom were going public in the same weeks. Growth slowed after the pandemic, and in 2022 Silbermann handed the chief executive job to Bill Ready, a former Google commerce executive. Pinterest still trades on the NYSE under PINS.

cover.theme: a rack picture of cards pinned to a board

dek: Change Healthcare ran the hidden network that carried medical bills and insurance claims between doctors, hospitals, and insurers.
lede: Few patients knew its name, yet Change Healthcare handled a huge share of American medical bills. When a doctor sent a claim to an insurer, it often passed through Change's network on the way. The Nashville company was formed in 2017 when McKesson merged its health IT business with Change Healthcare, a company backed by Blackstone. It filed to go public in 2019, carrying heavy debt and a promise that software and data could take cost out of health care.

sections.heading: A Clearinghouse for Claims
sections.body: Change Healthcare traced its roots to Emdeon, a claims business that once sat inside WebMD. Its core job was dull and vital. It checked insurance claims, sent them on, and moved payments back. On top of that network it sold software and analytics to hospitals and insurers. The 2017 deal with McKesson made it larger. The bet was that a company sitting between every party in the system could sell them tools to waste less money.

sections.heading: Bought, Then Breached
sections.body: Change cut its IPO price to $13 a share on June 26, 2019, below its target range, and used the money to pay down debt. The stock rose about 15 percent on Nasdaq the next day. In 2021 UnitedHealth Group agreed to buy it for about $13 billion, including debt. The Justice Department sued to block the deal and lost. The purchase closed in October 2022. In February 2024 a ransomware attack shut down Change's systems and exposed data on about 190 million people.

cover.theme: a crowded post office window (a clearinghouse for messages)
cover.artwork: "Any Thing for Me, If You Please?"—Post-Office of the Brooklyn Fair in Aid of the Sanitary Commission

dek: Canaan designed the chips and machines that bitcoin miners run around the clock to earn new coins.
lede: Canaan shipped the world's first bitcoin mining machines built on custom chips, under the name Avalon, in 2013. Those chips did one thing: the math that secures the bitcoin network and pays out new coins. Mining had moved from home computers to warehouses full of special machines, and most of them came from China. When Canaan went public in New York in November 2019, bitcoin had crashed from its 2017 peak and the larger rival Bitmain had shelved its own IPO plans.

sections.heading: One Chip, One Job
sections.body: Nangeng Zhang founded Canaan in 2013 and led it as chief executive. The company designs its chips and pays other firms to make them. Its bet was that bitcoin mining would reward whoever built the most efficient hardware, since miners compete on the cost of electricity per coin. Canaan sold its AvalonMiner machines to mining farms around the world. Its sales rose and fell with the price of bitcoin.

sections.heading: A Penny Below
sections.body: Canaan priced its American depositary shares at $9 on November 20, 2019, the low end of its range, and raised $90 million. The stock jumped almost 40 percent in early trading on Nasdaq the next day, then closed at $8.99. Later Canaan began mining bitcoin itself and added a quiet miner for homes. In January 2026 Nasdaq warned that its shares had traded below $1. Canaan moved to the Nasdaq Capital Market in July 2026 and still trades under CAN.

cover.theme: a miner (bitcoin mining)

hq: Shanghai, China and Santa Clara, CA
tagline: Live Voice for Other People's Apps
dek: Agora let app makers add live voice and video with a few lines of code, without building the hard parts.
lede: Agora went public under the ticker API, which is exactly what it sold. Its software interface let any app add live voice and video, from online classrooms to dating apps to games. Founder Tony Zhao had been chief technology officer at YY, a Chinese live-streaming company. Agora filed to go public in June 2020, three months into the pandemic, when the whole world had moved its classes, meetings, and parties onto video calls.

sections.heading: The Hard Part of Real Time
sections.body: Zhao founded Agora in 2014 with offices in Shanghai and Silicon Valley. Live video is hard to get right over shaky networks. Agora built its own global network to carry audio and video with little delay, and charged developers by the minute. The bet was that most apps would want live features but few would want to build the plumbing. Early customers included Chinese education and social apps. In 2021 the audio chat app Clubhouse ran on Agora's technology.

sections.heading: More Than Double on Day One
sections.body: Agora priced its American depositary shares at $20 on June 25, 2020, above its range, and raised $350 million. They opened at $45 on Nasdaq the next day, more than double the offer price. The stock climbed further during the Clubhouse craze, then fell as Chinese regulators cracked down on online tutoring, a key market. Agora now runs two divisions: Agora for global customers and Shengwang for China. It still trades on Nasdaq under API.

cover.theme: the Acropolis above the Athenian agora

dek: Sumo Logic gathered the logs that servers and apps write and turned them into alerts and answers.
lede: Sumo Logic went public the day after Snowflake, the biggest software IPO in history, and caught some of the same wind. Its product read the endless text that machines write about themselves, called logs, and found the problems hiding in them. Engineers used it to spot outages and security teams used it to spot attackers. In September 2020, with the pandemic pushing companies onto cloud software, Sumo Logic was a ten-year-old company still losing money.

sections.heading: Logs as a Service
sections.body: Christian Beedgen and Kumar Saurabh founded Sumo Logic in 2010 after working together at ArcSight, a security software company. Older log tools ran on a customer's own servers and grew costly as data piled up. Sumo Logic ran its tool in the cloud from the first day, so customers sent their logs and paid for what they used. The bet was that as companies moved to the cloud, they would want their monitoring to live there too.

sections.heading: Snowflake's Shadow
sections.body: Sumo Logic priced at $22 a share on September 16, 2020, above its range, and raised about $326 million. The next day it closed at $26.88 on Nasdaq, up 22 percent. The gain faded. Larger rivals such as Datadog and Splunk grew faster, and Sumo's shares sank below the IPO price. In February 2023 Francisco Partners agreed to buy the company for $12.05 a share in cash. The $1.7 billion deal closed that May, and Sumo Logic left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a sumo wrestler
cover.artwork: Portrait of the Sumo Wrestler Ikezuki Geitazaemon

fate: Taken private by an Advent International-led group, 2022
dek: McAfee sold antivirus and online safety software that guarded hundreds of millions of home computers and phones.
lede: When McAfee went public in October 2020, it was the second time. John McAfee founded the antivirus company in 1987 and first listed it in the early 1990s. Intel bought it in 2011 for $7.68 billion, then sold control to the buyout firm TPG in 2017. By 2020 the founder had long since left and become famous for other reasons. The company that kept his name mostly sold security software to families who bought new laptops.

sections.heading: From Intel and Back
sections.body: McAfee Associates began in 1987, as the first computer viruses spread on floppy disks. It became one of the best-known names in antivirus software. Intel paid $48 a share for the company in 2011, betting that security belonged inside its chips. The plan never quite worked. In 2017 Intel sold a majority stake to TPG, and McAfee became independent again, with Intel keeping 49 percent. The new owners leaned on consumer subscriptions, often bundled with new PCs.

sections.heading: A Slip on Day One
sections.body: McAfee priced its shares at $20 on October 21, 2020, and raised $740 million. The stock opened at $18.60 on Nasdaq the next day and closed at $18.70, below the offer price. In 2021 the company sold its business for corporations to Symphony Technology Group and kept only consumer products. Later that year an investor group led by Advent International agreed to buy the rest. The deal closed on March 1, 2022, and McAfee left the public market a second time.

cover.theme: a suit of field armor (protection)

dek: Poshmark let people sell the clothes in their closets from their phones, to shoppers who followed them like friends.
lede: Poshmark's stock more than doubled on its first day of trading, in the middle of a pandemic that had closed most of America's clothing stores. The app turned closets into small shops. Sellers snapped photos of a dress or a pair of sneakers, set a price, and shipped with a prepaid label. Buyers followed sellers, shared listings, and joined live online shopping events. By January 2021, used clothing was selling online like never before.

sections.heading: Selling Like Socializing
sections.body: Manish Chandra founded Poshmark in 2011 with Tracy Sun, Gautam Golwala, and Chetan Pungaliya. Chandra had already built and sold an earlier startup. The bet was that the iPhone would make selling clothes as easy as posting a photo, and that shopping would feel social. Poshmark kept the rules simple. It took a flat fee on small sales and 20 percent on larger ones. It held themed online events called Posh Parties, where sellers shared listings with each other.

sections.heading: A 140 Percent Pop
sections.body: Poshmark priced its shares at $42 on January 13, 2021. They opened at $97.50 on Nasdaq the next day, and the stock closed up more than 140 percent. The gains did not last. As stores reopened and growth slowed, the shares slid far below the offer price. In October 2022 the South Korean internet company Naver agreed to buy Poshmark for $17.90 a share in cash, about $1.2 billion. The deal closed in January 2023.

cover.theme: a fitting at the dressmaker (clothes changing hands)

tagline: A Game Made of Other Games
dek: Roblox gave kids millions of games built by other players, and the tools to build and sell their own.
lede: By 2020 more than half of American children under 16 played Roblox, according to the company's own filing. Roblox was a giant platform for games. Players built worlds with its free tools, and other players visited them, spending a virtual currency called Robux. Some young creators earned real money. When Roblox listed its shares in March 2021, a year of lockdowns had turned it into the place where many kids met their friends.

sections.heading: A Physics Lab for Kids
sections.body: David Baszucki and Erik Cassel founded Roblox in 2004. They had earlier built software that let students run physics experiments on a computer. Roblox grew from that idea: a world where things fell, rolled, and crashed, and where anyone could build. It launched in 2006. The bet was that players would build more games than any studio could. Roblox earned money when players bought Robux and shared a cut with the creators whose games they played.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing
sections.body: Roblox skipped a traditional IPO and chose a direct listing on the New York Stock Exchange. The exchange set a reference price of $45 a share on March 9, 2021. The next day the stock opened at $64.50 and closed at $69.50. Roblox raised no new money in the listing, and existing holders could sell right away. The company has kept growing its audience and adding older players. It still trades on the NYSE under RBLX.

cover.theme: a toy seller (a world of toys)
cover.artwork: The Toy Seller, illustration for The Fresh-Water Clam (Shijimi-gai)

dek: Compass gave real estate agents software and a sleek brand, and signed thousands of them away from older brokerages.
lede: Compass called itself a technology company, yet nearly all its revenue came from the commissions of real estate agents. Founders Robert Reffkin and Ori Allon started it in New York in 2012. With hundreds of millions of dollars from SoftBank, Compass recruited top agents from older brokerages and gave them software to run their business. When it filed to go public in March 2021, low interest rates and a pandemic rush for space had made the housing market roar.

sections.heading: Recruit the Best Agents
sections.body: Reffkin had worked at Goldman Sachs and in the White House. Allon was an engineer who had sold a search startup to Google. They began as Urban Compass, a rental search site, then turned into a brokerage. The bet was that agents, not buyers, were the customers that mattered. Compass offered them a shared platform for listings, marketing, and client records. It grew fast by moving into city after city and buying local firms.

sections.heading: Bigger Than the Old Guard
sections.body: Compass priced its shares at $18 on March 31, 2021, at the low end of a reduced range. The stock opened at $21.25 on the New York Stock Exchange the next day. Higher mortgage rates soon cooled the housing market, and Compass cut staff and costs. In January 2026 it completed an all-stock purchase of Anywhere Real Estate, owner of Coldwell Banker and Century 21. Compass still trades on the NYSE under COMP.

cover.theme: the New York skyline (a city of homes)

dek: monday.com gave teams colorful boards to see who was doing what, and let them build their own work tools.
lede: monday.com started life under a different name, daPulse, and only took its current one in 2017. The Tel Aviv company sold boards of colored rows and columns that showed who owned each task and when it was due. Marketing teams, builders, and schools bent them into whatever they needed. When monday.com went public in June 2021, the pandemic had scattered office workers, and companies were buying any tool that kept remote teams in step.

sections.heading: From daPulse to Monday
sections.body: Roy Mann and Eran Zinman founded the company in Tel Aviv in 2012 and later ran it as co-chief executives. Their first product was daPulse, a tool to keep a team's work visible in one place. In 2017 they renamed it monday.com. The bet was that anyone, without writing code, could shape their own workflow from simple blocks: items, columns, views, and automations. The company called its product a Work OS and sold it to teams of every size.

sections.heading: A Pop, Then the AI Scare
sections.body: monday.com priced its shares at $155 on June 9, 2021, and listed on Nasdaq under MNDY. The stock rose about 15 percent on its first day. In February 2026 its shares fell 21 percent on fears that AI agents could replace work-management software. In July 2026 monday.com cut about 20 percent of its staff. It still trades on Nasdaq under MNDY.

cover.theme: children setting off on a Monday morning
cover.artwork: Black Monday, or the Departure for School

dek: SentinelOne used AI on laptops and servers to spot attacks and stop them without waiting for a human.
lede: SentinelOne listed on the New York Stock Exchange under a one-letter ticker, S, and raised $1.2 billion doing it. Its software sat on laptops, servers, and cloud machines, watching how programs behaved. When something acted like an attack, it could stop it and roll back the damage on its own. In June 2021, ransomware had just shut down a major American fuel pipeline, and companies were rushing to replace old antivirus tools.

sections.heading: Fight Machine With Machine
sections.body: Tomer Weingarten, Almog Cohen, and Ehud Shamir founded the company in Israel in 2013 as Sentinel Labs, and later moved its headquarters to Mountain View, California. Older antivirus software looked for known bad files. SentinelOne bet that AI could judge behavior instead, and catch new attacks no one had seen before. It sold one platform, called Singularity, that covered endpoints, cloud workloads, and identity. It went after the same customers as CrowdStrike, its larger rival.

sections.heading: A One-Letter Ticker
sections.body: SentinelOne priced its shares at $35 on June 29, 2021, above its range. The stock rose about 21 percent on its first day of trading. The company kept buying smaller firms. It paid $616.5 million for Attivo Networks in 2022 and in 2025 agreed to buy Prompt Security, which guards AI tools. Its losses narrowed as revenue grew, though the stock spent long stretches below the offer price. SentinelOne still trades on the NYSE under S.

cover.theme: a soldier on guard (the sentinel)

tagline: A Mortgage Without the Paper Pile
dek: Blend gave banks software that let people apply for a mortgage online in minutes, without stacks of paper.
lede: Getting a mortgage used to mean faxing pay stubs and signing a thick stack of paper. Blend turned that into an online form that pulled in a borrower's bank and tax records on its own. Banks, credit unions, and lenders put their names on it and gave it to their customers. When Blend went public in July 2021, mortgage rates sat near record lows and Americans were buying and refinancing homes at a furious pace.

sections.heading: Engineers From Palantir
sections.body: Nima Ghamsari and his co-founders started Blend in San Francisco in 2012, after working together at Palantir, the data analysis company. They saw how much of lending still ran on paper and old systems. Blend's bet was to sell its software to lenders and leave the lending to them. Its software handled the part a borrower sees, from the first application to the final signature. Later it added tools for car loans, credit cards, and new bank accounts.

sections.heading: Caught by Rising Rates
sections.body: Blend priced its shares at $18 on July 15, 2021, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under BLND. The stock rose about 16 percent on its first day. In 2022 mortgage rates climbed fast, home loan volume collapsed, and Blend's revenue fell with it. The company cut staff several times to slow its losses, and the stock sank far below the offer price. Blend still trades on the NYSE under BLND.

cover.theme: a cottage by the road (a home to buy)
cover.artwork: The Cottage by the Roadside, Stormy Sky

dek: MeridianLink sold the software that credit unions and community banks used to take loan applications and decide who got approved.
lede: MeridianLink's most loyal customers were credit unions. By its own count, it served 63 of the top 100. Its cloud software let a member apply for a car loan or a credit card, pulled a credit report, and let the lender decide in minutes. The Costa Mesa company had been around since 1998. When it went public in July 2021, it was owned by the buyout firm Thoma Bravo.

sections.heading: A Quiet Lender's Toolkit
sections.body: MeridianLink began in Southern California in 1998, as lenders first moved loan applications onto the web. It built software to take an application, check a borrower's credit, and route the file for a decision. Over time it added mortgage tools, account opening, and data analytics. The bet was steady and unglamorous: smaller lenders would rent their technology rather than build it. By its IPO it had about 1,900 customers, including credit-reporting agencies.

sections.heading: Down on Day One
sections.body: MeridianLink priced an upsized IPO at $26 a share on July 27, 2021, the top of its range, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under MLNK. The stock fell about 5 percent on its first day. It drifted lower for years as lending slowed. In August 2025 the company agreed to sell itself to Centerbridge Partners for $20 a share in cash, below the IPO price. The deal closed on October 24, 2025.

cover.theme: noon, when the sun crosses the meridian
cover.artwork: Noon, plate two from The Four Times of the Day

tagline: Sending Wages Home From a Phone
dek: Remitly let immigrants send money home from a phone, faster and cheaper than a wire office counter.
lede: Remitly began in Kenya, where co-founder Matt Oppenheimer saw how much families depended on money sent by relatives working abroad. Sending it was slow, confusing, and expensive, and usually meant standing in line at a money-transfer counter. Remitly moved the whole thing onto a phone. By the time it went public in September 2021, it reached customers in more than 135 countries, and the pandemic had pushed many immigrants to send money online for the first time.

sections.heading: A Lesson in Kenya
sections.body: Oppenheimer, Josh Hug, and Shivaas Gulati started the company in Seattle in 2011. It began as BeamIt Mobile, a search engine for remittance services, and took the name Remitly in 2012. The founders soon decided to move the money themselves. The bet was that immigrants would trust an app if it showed the fee and the exchange rate up front and delivered on time. Remitly built partnerships with banks, mobile wallets, and cash pickup points in each country.

sections.heading: Above the Range
sections.body: Remitly priced its shares at $43 on September 22, 2021, above its range, and listed on Nasdaq under RELY. The stock rose about 13 percent on its first day. Growth continued as more customers moved from counters to phones, and in 2025 Remitly reported revenue of about $1.6 billion and a full-year profit. It also faced a short seller's report that year. Remitly still trades on Nasdaq under RELY.

cover.theme: emigrants reading news from home

tagline: The Chip Factory That Left AMD
dek: GlobalFoundries makes chips that other companies design, in factories in New York, Germany, Singapore, and Vermont.
lede: GlobalFoundries began as the factories AMD no longer wanted to own. In 2009 AMD spun off its chip plants, and an investment arm of the Abu Dhabi government, Mubadala, took control. The new company made chips for anyone who designed them. When it went public in October 2021, a global chip shortage had idled car plants, and governments wanted factories outside China and Taiwan. GlobalFoundries called itself the only large contract chipmaker with a global footprint that was not based in China or Taiwan.

sections.heading: Stepping Off the Treadmill
sections.body: Mubadala poured money into the company. It bought Chartered Semiconductor of Singapore in 2010 and IBM's chipmaking business in 2015. For years it raced Taiwan's TSMC to make the smallest, fastest chips. In August 2018 GlobalFoundries quit that race and halted work on its 7-nanometer process, citing the cost. The new bet was on specialized chips for cars, phones, radios, and power systems. Those chips did not need the newest, costliest factories.

sections.heading: Owned by Abu Dhabi
sections.body: GlobalFoundries priced its shares at $47 on October 27, 2021, the top of its range, and raised about $2.6 billion. The stock slipped about 1 percent on its first day on Nasdaq. Mubadala kept about 82 percent of the company. In February 2024 the U.S. government announced a $1.5 billion CHIPS Act award for its plants. GlobalFoundries bought chip designer MIPS in 2025 and still trades on Nasdaq under GFS.

cover.theme: an iron forge (a foundry)

dek: Samsara put cameras and sensors in trucks and factories, so fleet and plant managers could see their operations live.
lede: Samsara's founders had done this once before. Sanjit Biswas and John Bicket started Meraki, which ran office Wi-Fi from the cloud, and sold it to Cisco in 2012. Then they turned to trucks, forklifts, and pipelines. Samsara's devices sat in vehicles and machines and sent data to a cloud dashboard: where a truck was, how it was driven, when a motor ran hot. When Samsara went public in December 2021, supply chains were snarled and every fleet wanted to know where its goods were.

sections.heading: Meraki for the Physical World
sections.body: Biswas and Bicket founded Samsara in San Francisco in 2015. The industries that move and make things, such as trucking, construction, and utilities, still ran on paper logs and old radios. Samsara's bet was that cheap sensors and cloud software could give those companies the same live view that office IT already had. It sold the hardware and charged a yearly subscription for the software. Its products included dash cameras, vehicle trackers, and sensors for industrial machines.

sections.heading: Ticker IOT
sections.body: Samsara priced its shares at $23 on December 14, 2021, and raised $805 million. It listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker IOT, short for Internet of Things. The stock rose about 7 percent on its first day. Growth stayed strong as more fleets signed up. Samsara passed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue in December 2023. It still trades on the NYSE under IOT.

cover.theme: travelers on a highway (fleets on the road)

dek: Rubrik kept a clean copy of company data that hackers could not lock, so businesses could recover from attacks.
lede: Rubrik started out selling backups, the dullest corner of corporate IT, and turned them into security. Ransomware gangs had learned to lock up a company's backups before they demanded payment. Rubrik built backups the attackers could not change or delete, then added tools to find where sensitive data lived and to restore systems fast. When it went public in April 2024, ransomware had become one of the costliest threats a company faced.

sections.heading: From Backup to Security
sections.body: Bipul Sinha, Arvind Jain, Soham Mazumdar, and Arvind Nithrakashyap founded Rubrik in Palo Alto in January 2014. Its first product was a backup appliance that was simpler to run than the old tools. Customers could keep copies on site or in the cloud. Over time Rubrik rebuilt itself as a cloud software company and called its approach Zero Trust Data Security. The bet was that, after an attack, the company that could recover fastest would lose the least.

sections.heading: Tripling Its Price
sections.body: Rubrik priced its shares at $32 on April 24, 2024, above its range, and raised $752 million. It listed on the New York Stock Exchange under RBRK, and the stock rose about 16 percent on its first day. Rubrik was still losing money, but its subscription revenue kept growing. By October 2026 the stock traded at more than four times its offer price. Rubrik still trades on the NYSE under RBRK.

cover.theme: a fortress on a hill (data that holds)
cover.artwork: Landscape with a Fortress on a Hill

dek: Gemini gave people and institutions a regulated place in the United States to buy, sell, and store crypto.
lede: The crypto exchange Gemini went public under the legal name Gemini Space Station, Inc. Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss were already famous for their fight with Mark Zuckerberg over the idea for Facebook. They put money into bitcoin early and built an exchange that courted regulators from the start. When Gemini went public in September 2025, Washington had turned friendly toward crypto, and Circle and Bullish had just gone public to strong demand.

sections.heading: Twins Who Bet on Bitcoin
sections.body: The Winklevoss twins founded Gemini in 2014 in New York and opened the exchange in October 2015. They pitched it as the safe choice. Gemini ran a custody business as a New York trust company and sought licenses state by state. The bet was that big money would enter crypto only through firms that looked like banks. The model had cracks. A lending program called Gemini Earn froze in 2022, and in 2024 Gemini agreed to return at least $1.1 billion to its users.

sections.heading: Up the Range, Then Down
sections.body: Gemini raised its target range and then priced its shares above it, at $28, on September 11, 2025. It raised $425 million and listed on Nasdaq under GEMI. The stock rose about 14 percent on its first day. Crypto prices fell in the months that followed, and Gemini's shares slid with them. By October 2026 the shares had lost about 90 percent of their offer price. Gemini still trades on Nasdaq under GEMI.

cover.theme: two sisters side by side (Gemini, the twins; founded by twin brothers)

dek: Figma let designers, engineers, and product teams draw and edit the same screen together, live, in a web browser.
lede: Figma's stock opened at $85 on its first day, more than two and a half times its offer price. Two years earlier, Adobe had agreed to buy the company for $20 billion, and regulators had killed the deal. Figma ran in a web browser, so a whole team could work on one design at once, the way people edit a Google Doc. By 2025 it had more than 13 million monthly users, and two-thirds of them were not designers.

sections.heading: Two Students From Brown
sections.body: Dylan Field and Evan Wallace met as computer science students at Brown University. Field left school as a Thiel Fellow, and they founded Figma in 2012. They tried ideas such as drone software and a meme maker before they settled on a graphics editor that lived in the browser. The bet was that design should be shared work. Wallace built the fast graphics engine that made it possible. Teams at companies like Uber, Netflix, and Airbnb came to build their apps in it.

sections.heading: A Billion-Dollar Breakup
sections.body: Adobe agreed in September 2022 to buy Figma for about $20 billion. European and British regulators objected, and in December 2023 the two companies called it off. Adobe paid Figma a $1 billion breakup fee. Figma then went public on its own. It priced at $33 on July 30, 2025, and closed its first day on the New York Stock Exchange up 250 percent. By June 2026 the shares had fallen below $20. Figma still trades on the NYSE under FIG.

cover.theme: a figure study in colors

tagline: Japan Learns to Pay by QR Code
