dek: PayPay let shoppers across Japan pay by scanning a QR code with their phone, in a country that loved cash.
lede: Japan was one of the most cash-loving rich countries in the world when PayPay launched in October 2018. The app let shoppers pay by scanning a QR code at the counter, and it built its system with help from Paytm, the Indian payments company. SoftBank and Yahoo Japan set it up as a joint venture. By the time PayPay listed in New York in March 2026, it had tens of millions of users and millions of merchants.

sections.heading: A SoftBank Joint Venture
sections.body: PayPay was founded in Tokyo in June 2018. Its parents were SoftBank and Yahoo Japan, and it is now part of LY Corporation, which SoftBank controls. The bet was that phones could replace cash at the shop counter, from big chains to corner stores. A merchant needed little more than a printed QR code at the register. PayPay then added credit cards, banking, and other financial services, so that everyday payments became the front door to everything else.

sections.heading: Below the Range
sections.body: PayPay priced its American depositary shares at $16 on March 11, 2026, below its range of $17 to $20. It raised $880 million at a value of about $10.7 billion and listed on Nasdaq under PAYP. The stock rose about 13 percent on its first day. By October 2026 it traded about 10 percent below its offer price. PayPay still trades on Nasdaq under PAYP.

cover.theme: Nihonbashi, the merchant heart of old Tokyo
cover.artwork: Nihonbashi, from the series "Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido Road (Tokaido gojusan tsugi)"

fate: Renamed Booking Holdings, 2018; still public (NASDAQ: BKNG)
dek: Priceline let travelers say what they would pay for a seat and let empty planes say yes.
lede: Priceline sold its stock at $16 a share and watched it close its first day at $69. The idea behind it was simple. A traveler named a price for a plane ticket, and an airline with empty seats could take the offer or leave it. The Connecticut company came from Jay Walker's invention lab. It went public in March 1999, at the height of the dot-com rush, as one of the hottest stocks of the year.

sections.heading: An Invention Lab's Big Idea
sections.body: Jay Walker founded Priceline in 1997. He ran Walker Digital, a lab that patented new ways of doing business online. Priceline flipped the usual deal. The buyer set the price, and the seller decided. Airlines had seats that flew empty every day, and they did not want to cut fares in public. A hidden bid let them fill those seats quietly. Priceline took the plan to hotels, cars, and mortgages next.

sections.heading: From $69 to Booking.com
sections.body: Priceline priced its offering at $16 a share on March 29, 1999. The stock closed its first day at $69 on Nasdaq under PCLN. When the bubble burst, the shares lost most of their value. The company survived and in 2005 bought Booking.com, a small Dutch hotel site. Booking.com grew into the main business. In 2018 the company renamed itself Booking Holdings, and it trades on Nasdaq as BKNG.

cover.theme: an auctioneer (name your own price)

dek: Palo Alto Networks built firewalls that could tell which app was talking, so companies could block the risky ones.
lede: Nir Zuk had already built firewalls at Check Point and NetScreen when he decided they were looking at the wrong thing. Old firewalls checked ports and addresses. By the mid-2000s, apps slipped through any open door. Zuk founded Palo Alto Networks to build a firewall that knew which app was behind the traffic. When it filed to go public in 2012, it was the fastest-growing name in network security.

sections.heading: Three Firewalls In
sections.body: Zuk founded Palo Alto Networks in 2005. He had worked as an engineer at Check Point in the 1990s. He then co-founded OneSecure, which NetScreen bought in 2002, and served as NetScreen's chief technology officer. His bet was that a firewall should see apps, users, and content. That let a company allow one app and block another on the same port. Big companies began to swap out their old boxes.

sections.heading: A Watchtower on Wall Street
sections.body: Palo Alto Networks priced its offering at $42 a share on July 19, 2012. The stock rose 26.5 percent on its first day on the New York Stock Exchange and closed at $53.13. The company then spread from firewalls into cloud security and security operations. It moved its listing to Nasdaq in 2021. Palo Alto Networks still trades there as PANW.

cover.theme: a lone watchtower (guarding the network)

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: GPRO); merger with Starman Optical pending, 2026
tagline: A Camera Strapped to a Surfer
dek: GoPro gave surfers, skiers, and bikers a tiny tough camera to film themselves in the middle of the action.
lede: Nick Woodman wanted pictures of himself on a wave, and no camera could ride along. So he built one. GoPro started as a wrist strap for a cheap camera and grew into the little box on helmets, surfboards, and handlebars all over the world. When it filed to go public in 2014, YouTube was full of GoPro clips. Woodman and his family owned about half the company.

sections.heading: A Surf Trip, a Strap
sections.body: Woodman started the company in 2002 as Woodman Labs. Surfers then had no good way to film themselves. His first product was a strap that held a camera to the wrist. Later models became small, waterproof digital cameras with wide lenses. Athletes filmed stunts and posted them online. Each clip worked as an ad, and each ad sold more cameras. The company built its brand on that loop.

sections.heading: From $24 to a Rescue
sections.body: GoPro priced its offering at $24 a share on June 25, 2014. The stock closed its first day on Nasdaq at $31.34, up about 31 percent. Smartphones then got better cameras, and GoPro's sales slowed. A drone recall and years of losses followed. In 2026 Woodman lent the company $20 million. That September, GoPro agreed to merge with Starman Optical in a $285 million cash deal, set to close by year end.

cover.theme: a breaking wave (surf and action)

dek: MongoDB gave developers a database that stored data the way their code already thought about it.
lede: MongoDB takes its name from "humongous," and it began as a side part of a bigger plan. Three veterans of DoubleClick, the ad company, set out in 2007 to build a full cloud platform. The database inside it turned out to be the product. Developers liked storing flexible documents instead of rigid tables. By the time MongoDB went public in October 2017, its free version had spread to millions of downloads.

sections.heading: The Part That Won
sections.body: Dwight Merriman, Eliot Horowitz, and Kevin Ryan founded the company as 10gen in New York in 2007. They first tried to build a platform where developers could run whole apps. About a year in, Google launched App Engine, and the plan looked crowded. The team dropped the platform and kept the database. It released MongoDB as open source in February 2009. In 2013 the company took the database's name.

sections.heading: Ten Years to the Day
sections.body: MongoDB priced its offering at $24 a share on October 18, 2017, above its planned range. The stock opened at $33 and closed its first day on Nasdaq at $32.07, up about 34 percent. It sold 8 million shares and raised $192 million before the underwriters' extra shares. The IPO landed close to the company's tenth birthday. Its cloud service, Atlas, then grew into its largest business. MongoDB still trades on Nasdaq as MDB.

cover.theme: the fall of the giants (humongous)

dek: Peloton put a live spin class on a screen bolted to a bike in your living room.
lede: Peloton raised early money on Kickstarter, about $300,000 from fewer than 300 backers, to build a bike most people had never seen. The bike had a screen. The screen streamed live cycling classes from a New York studio. Riders could see where they ranked against everyone else on the ride. When Peloton filed to go public in 2019, it was selling a lifestyle as much as a machine.

sections.heading: A Barnes & Noble Pitch
sections.body: John Foley was an executive at Barnes & Noble when he pitched a colleague, Tom Cortese, on an idea. Studio cycling classes were hard to book and easy to skip. Technology could bring the class home. Foley, Cortese, Hisao Kushi, Graham Stanton, and Yony Feng founded Peloton in January 2012. They ran a Kickstarter campaign in 2013. The first bikes shipped in 2014, along with a monthly subscription for the classes.

sections.heading: A Rough First Ride
sections.body: Peloton priced its offering at $29 a share on September 25, 2019, and raised about $1.3 billion. The stock fell about 11 percent on its first day on Nasdaq. Then the pandemic shut gyms, and sales soared. When gyms reopened, demand fell hard. A treadmill recall and layoffs followed, and Foley stepped down in 2022. Peloton still trades on Nasdaq as PTON.

cover.theme: a motion study of a cyclist (the ride)

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: ZM); renamed Zoom Communications, 2024
tagline: The Meeting Link That Just Worked
dek: Zoom made video meetings start with one click, so nobody spent the first ten minutes fixing the call.
lede: Zoom was a profitable software company when it went public, which almost nobody else in its class could say. It earned $7.6 million on $330.5 million in sales in the year before its IPO. Its founder, Eric Yuan, had built video calls at WebEx and Cisco and thought they were still too painful. When Zoom listed in April 2019, it was a business tool. A year later it was how the world went to school and work.

sections.heading: The Pitch Cisco Passed On
sections.body: Yuan was refused a U.S. visa eight times before he got one on the ninth try. He joined WebEx as an engineer, and Cisco bought WebEx for $3.2 billion. Yuan rose to vice president of engineering. He proposed a new video system built for phones and the cloud, and Cisco said no. He left and founded Zoom in 2011. The bet was that a call should simply connect, every time, on any device.

sections.heading: Seventy-Two Percent, Then the World
sections.body: Zoom priced its offering at $36 a share on April 17, 2019. The stock jumped more than 72 percent on its first day on Nasdaq and closed at $62. Eleven months later, the pandemic sent offices and classrooms home, and Zoom became a verb. Growth slowed once offices reopened. The company added phone, chat, and AI tools, and in 2024 it renamed itself Zoom Communications. It still trades on Nasdaq as ZM.

cover.theme: an old camera and its lens (zoom)
cover.artwork: A Foreign Camera (Gaikoku shashinkyo no zu)

dek: DouYu let Chinese gamers watch their favorite players stream live and pay them in virtual gifts.
lede: DouYu means "fighting fish" in Chinese, and it fought for every viewer in a crowded pool. The Wuhan company streamed live video games to millions of Chinese fans. Viewers sent streamers virtual gifts that cost real money, and DouYu took a share. Tencent was its biggest backer. When DouYu went public in July 2019, it raised about $775 million, the largest U.S. listing by a Chinese company that year to that point.

sections.heading: Esports in a Chat Window
sections.body: Chen Shaojie became DouYu's chief executive in May 2014, when the platform launched. He had earlier built online platforms for esports games such as Warcraft. DouYu's bet was that Chinese gamers would watch other people play the way sports fans watch games. Star streamers drew huge audiences, and fans paid them through gifts. A close rival, Huya, chased the same fans. Tencent invested in both.

sections.heading: Flat Debut, Hard Years
sections.body: DouYu priced its offering at $11.50 a share on July 16, 2019. The stock dipped in early trading on Nasdaq and closed its first day right at $11.50. In 2020 Tencent arranged a merger of DouYu and Huya. China's market regulator blocked it in July 2021. In November 2023, police detained Chen on gambling charges, and in 2026 he resigned as chief executive. DouYu still trades on Nasdaq as DOYU.

cover.theme: a carp leaping up a waterfall (Douyu, the fighting fish)

tagline: A Coach Inside the Glucose Meter
dek: Livongo let people with diabetes share their blood sugar readings and get advice the moment one looked wrong.
lede: Glen Tullman's youngest son was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age 8, and Tullman promised to keep people healthy until a cure came. Livongo was that promise as a business. Members shared their blood sugar readings, and the company answered with data and coaching. Employers paid for it to cut the cost of chronic illness. Livongo went public in July 2019 as one of the first digital health companies on Wall Street.

sections.heading: A Father's Promise
sections.body: Tullman had run Allscripts, a large health records company. He founded Livongo in 2014 to manage chronic conditions with data. Members used a connected device to share their blood sugar records. When a number looked dangerous, the system could reach out. The company sold to large employers and health plans, which paid for the service. Diabetes made up about 90 percent of revenue when Livongo went public, and it was adding high blood pressure and weight programs.

sections.heading: Eighteen Billion in a Year
sections.body: Livongo priced its offering at $28 a share on July 24, 2019, and raised about $355 million. The stock rose as much as 62 percent on its first day on Nasdaq and closed up 36 percent at $38.10. In August 2020, Teladoc Health agreed to buy Livongo in a cash and stock deal valued at $18.5 billion. The merger closed that October, and Tullman took a seat on Teladoc's board.

cover.theme: a wanderer and his dog (a companion on the road)

tagline: A Guide Through the Health Maze
dek: Accolade gave employees a person to call who could untangle their health benefits, bills, and doctors.
lede: Accolade's product was a person who picked up the phone. American health care is a maze of plans, bills, and referrals. Accolade sold employers a team of health assistants and nurses who could guide workers through it. The company bet that a good guide would save money and make people healthier. When it went public in July 2020, the pandemic had made health care the only topic in town.

sections.heading: A Human on the Line
sections.body: Tom Spann left Accenture in 2007 to become Accolade's founding chief executive, and he started the company with Michael Cline in the Philadelphia suburbs. Employers paid Accolade to support their workers. Each member got a guide who could find a doctor, explain a bill, or plan care after a diagnosis. Rajeev Singh became chief executive in 2015. By its IPO, the company said its service supported 1.7 million people.

sections.heading: From $22 to Transcarent
sections.body: Accolade priced its offering at $22 a share on July 1, 2020, above its planned range. The stock jumped more than 40 percent in early trading on Nasdaq and closed its first day at $29.70. The company later added virtual doctor visits and expert medical opinions. Its shares slid after 2021. In April 2025 Transcarent, a digital health startup, took Accolade private for $7.03 a share, about $621 million.

cover.theme: a laurel wreath (an accolade)
cover.artwork: Portrait of a Man Wearing a Laurel Wreath

tagline: The Engine Behind a Million Games
dek: Unity gave small studios the same kind of game engine that big studios built for themselves.
lede: Unity began as a failed game called GooBall. Three young developers in Copenhagen made it for the Mac in 2005, and almost nobody bought it. The tools they built to make it were the real product. Unity turned them into an engine any developer could afford. By the time it filed to go public in 2020, Unity powered a large share of the world's mobile games, from tiny indie projects to hits.

sections.heading: GooBall's Lucky Failure
sections.body: David Helgason, Joachim Ante, and Nicholas Francis founded the company in Copenhagen in 2004. They called it Over the Edge. GooBall flopped, but the three saw value in their tools. They renamed the company Unity Technologies in 2007. The bet was that game making should not need a big studio's budget. Unity offered a cheap or free engine and earned money as its users grew.

sections.heading: A Week of Big IPOs
sections.body: Unity priced its offering at $52 a share on September 17, 2020, above its range, and raised about $1.3 billion. The stock closed its first day on the New York Stock Exchange at $68.35, up 31 percent. In 2022 it merged with ironSource, an ad tech company. In 2023 a new per-install fee angered developers, and chief executive John Riccitiello stepped down. Unity still trades on the NYSE as U.

cover.theme: a puppeteer (the engine behind the game)

dek: Allegro made the tiny magnetic sensors and power chips that tell a car's motors where they are.
lede: Allegro MicroSystems first filed to go public in 2007, then pulled the deal a year later. It took thirteen more years to try again. The company makes chips that sense magnetic fields, which lets a car know the angle of a steering shaft or the speed of a wheel. It shipped more than a billion units a year to over 10,000 customers. When it finally listed in October 2020, electric cars were making those chips more valuable.

sections.heading: Born From Sprague
sections.body: Allegro was formed in 1990 when Sanken Electric, a Japanese power electronics company, bought the semiconductor division of Sprague Electric. It became a specialist in magnetic sensor chips and in power chips that drive small motors. Cars became its biggest market. A modern vehicle uses sensors to track pedals, seats, wipers, and motors. The bet was that every new electric motor in a car would need an Allegro part.

sections.heading: The Second Attempt Works
sections.body: Allegro filed an S-1 in August 2007 and withdrew it in August 2008, as the financial crisis closed the IPO window. Its second offering priced at $14 a share in October 2020, and Allegro raised $350 million. Its shares listed on Nasdaq under ALGM. Sanken remained a major shareholder after the deal. Electric cars and factory automation then lifted demand for its parts. Allegro still trades on Nasdaq as ALGM.

cover.theme: a village violinist (allegro, the quick tempo)

tagline: Pay Over Time, No Hidden Fees
dek: Affirm let shoppers split a purchase into fixed payments and see the full cost before they clicked buy.
lede: When Affirm filed to go public, its biggest merchant was Peloton. The bike maker made up about 28 percent of Affirm's revenue, because shoppers split the price of a bike into monthly payments. Max Levchin, a PayPal co-founder, built Affirm as an honest alternative to the credit card. It showed the total cost up front and charged no hidden fees. Affirm listed in January 2021, as pandemic shopping moved online.

sections.heading: A PayPal Founder's Second Act
sections.body: Levchin co-founded PayPal and later sold his photo-sharing company, Slide, to Google. In 2011 he started HVF, a lab for data-heavy companies, and Affirm spun out of it in 2012. The bet was that a lender could judge each purchase on its own, with better data than a credit score. Merchants paid Affirm to offer the loans, because shoppers bought more. By September 2020 it had 3.9 million active consumers.

sections.heading: Nearly Double on Day One
sections.body: Affirm priced its offering at $49 a share in January 2021 and sold 24.6 million shares. The stock nearly doubled on its first day on Nasdaq, as investors bet that online shoppers would keep paying in installments. Buy now, pay later became a crowded field. Affirm signed deals with Amazon and Shopify, and the stock swung hard as interest rates rose. Levchin remained chief executive. Affirm still trades on Nasdaq as AFRM.

cover.theme: a shopper at the market (buy now, pay over time)

tagline: Ordered at Midnight, Here by Seven
dek: Coupang delivered almost anything in South Korea by the next morning, often before people woke up.
lede: A Coupang customer in Seoul could order groceries at midnight and find them at the door before 7 a.m. The company called it Rocket Delivery. Bom Kim built Coupang in South Korea, a dense country where fast delivery could reach almost everyone. By the time it filed to go public in 2021, Coupang employed more than 50,000 people and was one of Korea's three largest private employers.

sections.heading: Building the Whole Road
sections.body: Kim founded Coupang in 2010. It started as a daily deals site and turned into an online store that owned its own logistics. Coupang built warehouses, hired its own drivers, and wrote the software that tied them together. The bet was that controlling every step would make next-day delivery cheap enough to offer on nearly every order. It added fresh groceries with Rocket Fresh and food delivery with Coupang Eats.

sections.heading: A Korean Giant in New York
sections.body: Coupang priced its offering at $35 a share in March 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as CPNG. The stock rose about 41 percent on its first day. Kim held Class B shares with 29 votes each, which gave him about 77 percent of the voting power. Coupang later expanded into Taiwan and bought the luxury retailer Farfetch. It still trades on the NYSE as CPNG.

cover.theme: a man lighting a rocket (Rocket Delivery)
cover.artwork: Man Lighting a Rocket, also called Peace is Better than a Victory, from Communia Gaudia (The Wide-Spread Rejoicing at the Siege of Namur)

tagline: From Car Thieves to Fleet Data
dek: Karooooo's Cartrack tracked cars and trucks and turned that data into software that helps fleets run cheaper.
lede: Cartrack began in South Africa by finding stolen cars. Its trackers sat in vehicles, and when one went missing, a recovery team went after it. Over two decades those trackers became a data business. Fleets used Cartrack's software to watch fuel, drivers, and routes in real time. When its parent, Karooooo, listed on Nasdaq in April 2021, Cartrack served more than 1.3 million subscribers in 23 countries.

sections.heading: Stolen Vehicle Recovery
sections.body: Zak Calisto founded Cartrack in South Africa in 2001 and has run it ever since. Before that, he worked in vehicle tracking services. The trackers fed a constant stream of location data. Calisto's bet was that the data was worth more than the recovery. Cartrack built its own devices and software and sold subscriptions to businesses and drivers. It ran its own design, software, sales, and customer service teams instead of relying on outside vendors.

sections.heading: A Small Float, a Big Owner
sections.body: Karooooo sold 1,050,000 shares at $28 each in April 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as KARO. The company had moved its headquarters to Singapore in 2020. Cartrack left the Johannesburg exchange, and Karooooo took a secondary listing there as KRO. The offering was small, about $29 million, for a company with more than a million subscribers. After the IPO, Calisto held about 66 percent of the voting power. Karooooo still trades on Nasdaq as KARO.

cover.theme: a stagecoach holdup (stolen vehicle recovery)

dek: Similarweb showed businesses how much traffic their competitors' websites and apps were getting, and where it came from.
lede: Every company knows its own web traffic. Similarweb sold a look at everyone else's. Its software estimated visits to millions of websites and apps, then showed where the visitors came from and where they went next. Marketers, salespeople, and investors used it to size up rivals. When the Tel Aviv company went public in May 2021, the pandemic had pushed more of life onto screens than ever.

sections.heading: Reading the Whole Web
sections.body: Or Offer founded the company in 2009 and has run it since. Benjamin Seror joined as a co-founder and chief product officer. Similarweb launched its platform in 2013. The bet was that public digital signals, gathered at huge scale, could estimate any site's traffic. Businesses usually saw only their own numbers. Similarweb sold them a view of the market, priced as a subscription.

sections.heading: A Flat First Day
sections.body: Similarweb priced its offering at $22 a share on May 11, 2021, above its planned range, and raised $176 million. Offer sold 500,000 of his own shares in the deal. The stock finished its first day on the New York Stock Exchange about where it started. Similarweb kept adding tools for sales teams and investors. It still trades on the NYSE as SMWB.

cover.theme: a spider's web (the web, studied)
cover.artwork: Two Chinese Women Examining Thread and a Spider’s Web in a Box, from the series "Diptych for the Drum Group"

dek: Kanzhun's BOSS Zhipin app let Chinese job seekers skip the resume pile and message hiring managers directly.
lede: Kanzhun's app put the boss in the chat. On BOSS Zhipin, a job seeker in China could message the hiring manager directly instead of mailing a resume into silence. The app matched both sides with its own algorithms. It arrived late to a crowded market and still became China's largest online recruitment platform by monthly users in 2020. Kanzhun went public in June 2021, weeks before Beijing turned on its tech giants.

sections.heading: Bosses in the Chat
sections.body: Zhao Peng founded the company and launched BOSS Zhipin in 2014. He already had more than two decades in Chinese recruiting and internet work. Old job sites made employers dig through resumes. Zhao's bet was that two-way chat and smart matching would serve both sides better. Job seekers controlled who saw their resumes. Companies paid to reach more candidates. The company lost money every year through its IPO.

sections.heading: A Review, Then a Return
sections.body: Kanzhun priced its offering at $19 per American depositary share in June 2021 and raised $912 million on Nasdaq under BZ. Weeks later, China's cyberspace regulator opened a security review and stopped the app from signing up new users. Kanzhun added a listing in Hong Kong in December 2022. The ban on new users lifted in 2023. Kanzhun still trades on Nasdaq as BZ.

cover.theme: a job interview (hiring, directly)

tagline: Form Your Company Without a Lawyer
dek: LegalZoom let small business owners form a company, write a will, or file a trademark online for a flat fee.
lede: LegalZoom tried to go public in 2012 and gave up. It filed an S-1, waited, and withdrew it in January 2014. Seven years later it tried again. The company sells the legal paperwork most people dread: forming an LLC, writing a will, filing a trademark. It does this online, at a set price, and brings in a lawyer only when needed. When it listed in June 2021, a pandemic boom in new small businesses was filling its pipeline.

sections.heading: Legal Forms, Flat Fees
sections.body: LegalZoom started as a California company in 1999. Its founders included the lawyers Brian Liu, Brian Lee, and Edward Hartman, and the well-known trial lawyer Robert Shapiro. The bet was that most legal tasks for small businesses follow a pattern. Software and trained staff could handle the routine part, and an independent attorney could step in when the law required one. Customers paid less, and they knew the price up front.

sections.heading: Second Time Lucky
sections.body: After the first IPO stalled, LegalZoom stayed private for seven more years. Its second offering priced at $28 a share in June 2021, and the stock listed on Nasdaq under LZ. LegalZoom kept its executive offices in Glendale, California, and ran operations from Austin, Texas. It added subscriptions for ongoing legal and tax help. LegalZoom still trades on Nasdaq as LZ.

cover.theme: two lawyers (law without the lawyer bill)

dek: Kaltura gave companies and universities the software to host, stream, and manage their own video.
lede: Kaltura gave away a version of its video software under an open-source license and still built a business on it. Companies, universities, and media firms used Kaltura to upload, manage, and stream their own video, from lectures to town halls. The pandemic turned that into daily life. When Kaltura went public in July 2021, classes and meetings had moved onto screens, and it had to price its shares well below its hopes.

sections.heading: Four Founders, One Player
sections.body: Ron Yekutiel, Shay David, Eran Etam, and Michal Tsur started Kaltura in late 2006, the year Amazon launched its cloud and just before the iPhone. The company launched its video management system in 2008. The bet was that every organization would need video, and that an open, flexible platform would win over closed ones. Its research and development team worked mostly in Israel, while the company was based in New York.

sections.heading: A Ten-Dollar Debut
sections.body: Kaltura priced its offering at $10 a share in July 2021, below its planned range, and listed on Nasdaq under KLTR. Yekutiel remained chairman and chief executive. As offices and campuses reopened, growth in video slowed, and the shares traded below the offer price for years. Kaltura added virtual event and AI video tools. It still trades on Nasdaq as KLTR.

cover.theme: a kabuki actor mid-performance (video on stage)
cover.artwork: The actor Bando Mitsugoro II as Ishii Genzo

dek: PowerSchool ran the grades, attendance, and records software used by most K-12 schools in the U.S. and Canada.
lede: If you went to school in the U.S. or Canada in the last twenty years, PowerSchool probably held your grades. By its IPO, its software served schools with over 45 million students, more than 70 percent of all K-12 students in the two countries. Teachers took attendance in it. Parents checked report cards in it. When PowerSchool went public in July 2021, two private equity firms controlled almost 79 percent of the vote.

sections.heading: Every Student's Record
sections.body: PowerSchool started in 1997 as a student information system, the database that tracks who is enrolled, what they take, and how they do. Schools rarely switch those systems once they pick one. That made PowerSchool sticky. The company added tools for special education, hiring, finance, and learning. The bet was that schools would buy one connected platform instead of a dozen separate products. Vista Equity Partners and Onex owned most of it by the IPO.

sections.heading: Back to Private Hands
sections.body: PowerSchool priced its offering at $18 a share in July 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as PWSC. Revenue kept growing, but the stock stayed modest. In 2024 Bain Capital agreed to buy the company, and PowerSchool left the NYSE that October. A few months later it disclosed a data breach that exposed records of students and teachers. It now operates as a private company.

cover.theme: the schoolmaster (the classroom record)

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2024
dek: EngageSmart made software that let therapists run their practices and let towns and utilities take bill payments online.
lede: EngageSmart began with a founder who was annoyed by paying a utility bill. Bob Bennett thought it "shouldn't be that hard," and the phrase became his company's creed. He launched InvoiceCloud to let towns, utilities, and insurers take payments online. EngageSmart later added SimplePractice, software that therapists and other clinicians used to book, bill, and see clients. When it went public in September 2021, telehealth had made SimplePractice a pandemic necessity.

sections.heading: From MicroFridge to InvoiceCloud
sections.body: Bennett's first company, MicroFridge, made small fridge and microwave units. He later ran Sage Payment Solutions. In 2009 he became chief executive of InvoiceCloud, which he started with co-founders. In 2018 and 2019, the growth investor General Atlantic built EngageSmart around InvoiceCloud and SimplePractice. The bet was that small, overlooked industries were still paying on paper. Each product earned subscription fees and a share of payments.

sections.heading: Two Years on the NYSE
sections.body: EngageSmart priced its offering at $26 a share on September 22, 2021, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ESMT. General Atlantic kept control after the deal. SimplePractice also ran Monarch, a marketplace that connected clinicians with people seeking therapy. In 2023 Vista Equity Partners agreed to take it private, and EngageSmart left the NYSE in January 2024. It now operates as a private company.

cover.theme: reading a letter (the bill that shouldn't be hard)

dek: NerdWallet compared credit cards, loans, and insurance in plain language, and got paid when readers signed up.
lede: NerdWallet reached about $44 million in revenue by 2014 without taking any outside equity money. Tim Chen started it in 2009 to answer the money questions people actually search for: which credit card, which mortgage, which savings account. Its articles ranked well on Google, and banks paid NerdWallet when readers signed up. When it went public in November 2021, it had grown from a side project into a household name in personal finance.

sections.heading: Built Without Venture Money
sections.body: Tim Chen and Jacob Gibson co-founded NerdWallet in 2009. The bet was that clear, free advice would win trust, and that trust would turn into sign-ups. Banks and card issuers paid for those sign-ups. NerdWallet grew for years on its own revenue before it raised outside equity. It later added loans, insurance, and small business lending, and bought Fundera, a New York lending marketplace.

sections.heading: Ten Votes a Share
sections.body: NerdWallet priced its offering at $18 a share in November 2021 and listed on Nasdaq under NRDS. Chen held Class B shares with ten votes each and stayed chief executive. Rising interest rates soon shrank demand for credit cards and loans, which hit NerdWallet's partners and its sales. The company kept investing in its app and its brand. NerdWallet still trades on Nasdaq as NRDS.

cover.theme: a scholar in his study (the nerd)

tagline: The Wires Inside the AI Data Center
dek: Credo made chips and cables that move data quickly between servers while using less power.
lede: Credo went public at $10 a share selling something few investors thought about: the links between servers. Its chips push data down copper and optical connections at high speed with less power. One product, the Active Electrical Cable, put a Credo chip inside the cable itself. When it listed in January 2022, data centers were racing from 100-gigabit links to 400 and 800. AI soon made that race much faster.

sections.heading: Four Years of Design
sections.body: Credo was founded in 2008. From 2008 to 2012, its engineers built a low-power design for SerDes, the circuits that turn data into fast serial signals and back. It began selling in 2013. Bill Brennan, a semiconductor veteran, became chief executive in 2013. Credo sold chips, licensed its designs, and built complete cables. The bet was that bandwidth would keep doubling and power would become the limit.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars, Then AI
sections.body: Credo priced its offering at $10 a share in January 2022 and listed on Nasdaq under CRDO. The parent is a Cayman Islands holding company, with offices in North America and Asia. Big cloud companies then built huge AI clusters, wired together with fast cables. Demand for Credo's cables climbed, and its shares rose far above the offer price. Credo still trades on Nasdaq as CRDO.

cover.theme: a suspension bridge (cables that carry the load)
cover.artwork: Suspension Bridge at Minneapolis, No. 1519 from the series "Among the Bluff Scenery of the Upper Mississippi"

dek: Silvaco sold software that lets engineers simulate how a chip will behave before anyone builds it.
lede: Silvaco waited forty years to go public. Founded in 1984, it makes software that simulates semiconductors at the level of the physics, so engineers can test a transistor before a factory makes one. The company calls this "the technology behind the chip." When it listed in May 2024, governments were spending billions to build chip factories at home, and the Pesic family still controlled the company.

sections.heading: Simulating the Physics
sections.body: Katherine Ngai-Pesic co-founded Silvaco in 1984 and remained its controlling shareholder. Its core product was TCAD, software that models how materials and voltages behave inside a device. It added EDA tools for circuit design and licensed semiconductor IP. The bet was that chipmakers would rather simulate a device on a computer than pay to build test wafers again and again. Its customers were semiconductor and photonics companies.

sections.heading: Forty Years to the Bell
sections.body: Silvaco priced its offering at $19 a share in May 2024 and listed on Nasdaq under SVCO. The Pesic family kept special approval rights over any sale or merger while it held at least a quarter of the vote. That gave the founding family a veto over the company's future. The company kept selling to chipmakers and photonics makers around the world. It still trades on Nasdaq as SVCO.

cover.theme: a dense forest drawn line by line (silva, and a chip's maze)

dek: SailPoint told big companies exactly who could open which systems and files, and took access away when it was risky.
lede: SailPoint went public twice under the same ticker. It first listed on the New York Stock Exchange as SAIL in 2017. Thoma Bravo took it private in 2022, and in February 2025 it came back on Nasdaq, again as SAIL. Its question never changed: who has access to what. SailPoint helps large companies track every employee, contractor, and machine that can log in, and shut doors that should be closed.

sections.heading: The Access Question
sections.body: Mark McClain founded SailPoint in Austin in 2005. Its first products focused on governance, meaning the audit of who had which permissions. Customers kept asking how to manage that question across thousands of apps. The bet was that identity would become the center of security as companies moved to the cloud. SailPoint later rebuilt its products as a cloud service and expanded from people to machine accounts.

sections.heading: Same Ticker, Second Time
sections.body: SailPoint traded on the NYSE from November 2017 until Thoma Bravo bought it in August 2022. It returned with an offering priced at $23 a share in February 2025, a $1.38 billion offering on Nasdaq. Thoma Bravo still owned about 86 percent of the stock after the deal. McClain stayed on as chief executive. SailPoint trades on Nasdaq as SAIL.

cover.theme: two sailboats (two trips to the market)
cover.artwork: The Two Sailboats, from Cahier de six eaux-fortes, vues de Hollande

dek: Ambiq made chips that run on so little power that watches and sensors can go much longer between charges.
lede: Ambiq's chips run below the voltage most chips need to switch on. That trick, which it calls SPOT, cuts power use two to five times. That lets a watch, a hearing device, or a sensor run much longer on one charge. By its IPO, Ambiq chips sat in over 270 million devices. When it listed in July 2025, the industry wanted AI on small battery devices, and power was the bottleneck.

sections.heading: Below the Threshold
sections.body: Scott Hanson earned three electrical engineering degrees, including a Ph.D., at the University of Michigan. He founded the company in January 2010 as Cubiq Microchip and renamed it Ambiq Micro in 2012. Ordinary chips waste energy by running at higher voltages than they need. Ambiq's bet was that subthreshold design could work in mass-market products. It shipped more than 42 million units in 2024.

sections.heading: Edge AI on a Battery
sections.body: Ambiq priced its offering at $24 a share in July 2025 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under AMBQ. Hanson served as chief technology officer, and Fumihide Esaka led the company as chief executive. Ambiq estimated that over 40 percent of its 2024 units ran AI algorithms. It aimed its chips at personal devices, medical devices, factories, and smart homes and buildings. It still trades on the NYSE as AMBQ.

cover.theme: a boy blowing on a firebrand (a tiny spark of power)
cover.artwork: A Boy Blowing on a Firebrand

dek: HawkEye 360 used small satellites to locate radio signals on Earth and sold that intelligence to defense agencies.
lede: HawkEye 360 maps the world by its radio noise. Its satellites fly in small clusters and pick up signals from ships, radars, and radios, then work out where each one came from. A ship that turns off its tracking beacon still gives itself away. By its IPO, HawkEye 360 had more than 30 satellites in orbit. It listed in May 2026, when defense budgets were growing and space companies were back in favor.

sections.heading: Signals Intelligence, Commercial
sections.body: A team of military veterans, engineers, and national security technologists founded HawkEye 360 in 2015. Signals intelligence had long been a government-only job, done with large, costly satellites. The bet was that clusters of small satellites could find radio emitters from orbit for far less. HawkEye 360 built a database of signals and AI tools to sort through them. The U.S. government became a key customer.

sections.heading: A Hawk Goes Public
sections.body: HawkEye 360 priced its offering at $26 a share in May 2026 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under HAWK. Its headquarters in Herndon, Virginia, also runs its satellite operations. The company said it was adding clusters to improve how often it could revisit a spot on Earth. It also bought Innovative Signal Analysis, a Texas signal-processing firm. HawkEye 360 trades on the NYSE as HAWK.

cover.theme: a hawk watching from a cliff (eyes in orbit)
cover.artwork: A Hawk on a Cliff near a Kiri Tree

dek: NVIDIA made the chips that drew 3D worlds for gamers, then the chips that train today's AI.
lede: NVIDIA took its name from invidia, the Latin word for envy, and it wanted rival chipmakers to feel it. Three engineers founded it in 1993 to build graphics chips for personal computers. By the time it went public in January 1999, PC gamers wanted fast 3D graphics, and dozens of chip companies fought to supply them. NVIDIA filed its S-1 in March 1998 and waited ten months to sell a share.

sections.heading: Three Engineers and a Graphics Chip
sections.body: Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem started NVIDIA in 1993. Their bet was that the PC would need its own chip for graphics, separate from the main processor. Games were the first market. Drawing a 3D scene takes millions of small sums done at once, and a graphics chip does that work in parallel. That same trick later made NVIDIA's chips useful for science, crypto mining and AI.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars a Share
sections.body: NVIDIA priced its IPO at $12 a share on January 21, 1999, and sold 3.5 million shares on Nasdaq. The offering raised about $42 million. Later that year it launched the GeForce 256, which it called the first GPU. Two decades later, researchers trained neural networks on its chips, and demand for AI turned the company into a giant. In July 2025 NVIDIA became the first company worth $4 trillion.

cover.theme: Envy personified (invidia, the root of the name)
cover.artwork: Invidia, plate 4 from The Seven Vices

dek: Splunk let engineers search the logs their machines spit out, so they could find what broke and why.
lede: Splunk named itself after spelunking, because digging through machine logs felt like crawling through a cave with a flashlight. Every server, app and network device writes a running diary of what it does. Most companies ignored those files until something broke. Splunk made them searchable like a web page. When it filed to go public in early 2012, investors were hungry for anything labeled big data.

sections.heading: A Search Box for Logs
sections.body: Michael Baum, Rob Das and Erik Swan founded Splunk in San Francisco in 2003. Their bet was that the plain text pouring out of machines held answers no one was reading. Splunk's software pulled in that text from any source and indexed it. An engineer could then type a search and find the error behind an outage in minutes. Security teams soon used the same tool to hunt for attackers.

sections.heading: A Double on Day One
sections.body: Splunk priced its IPO at $17 a share on April 18, 2012, well above its first range of $11 to $13. The stock more than doubled on its first day of trading on Nasdaq. It was the best debut for a tech IPO since LinkedIn a year earlier. Splunk grew into a security and observability business sold to large companies. In March 2024 Cisco completed its purchase of Splunk for about $28 billion.

cover.theme: a cave (spelunking, the root of the name)

fate: Taken private by Francisco Partners and TPG, 2023 ($6.5B)
tagline: An Anagram That Watched Your App
dek: New Relic showed software teams how fast their apps ran and where they slowed down.
lede: New Relic is an anagram of its founder's name, Lew Cirne. Cirne had already built and sold one company that watched how software performed. He started New Relic to do the same job as a web service any developer could switch on. When it filed to go public in late 2014, apps had moved to the cloud, and teams needed to see inside code they no longer ran on their own servers.

sections.heading: Lew Cirne's Second Act
sections.body: Lew Cirne founded Wily Technology, which CA bought in 2006. He started New Relic in 2008. The bet was that small teams would pay a monthly fee to see how their apps behaved in real time, with no big install. A developer added a few lines of code, and a dashboard showed slow pages, failed requests and database delays. New Relic sold to startups first and to large companies later.

sections.heading: From NEWR to Private
sections.body: New Relic priced its IPO at $23 a share on December 11, 2014, above a raised range. The shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange the next day under NEWR and rose about 31 percent in early trading. Newer rivals such as Datadog grew faster in the years that followed. In November 2023 Francisco Partners and TPG completed a $6.5 billion deal to take New Relic private.

cover.theme: an observatory (watching what runs)

dek: Okta gave workers one login for all their work apps, and gave IT one place to control it.
lede: Okta is named for the unit weather forecasters use to measure how much of the sky is covered by cloud. The name fit. By 2017 the average company ran dozens of cloud apps, and each one wanted its own password. Okta sat in front of all of them. A worker signed in once, and IT could add or cut off access from one screen. That spring, Okta filed to go public.

sections.heading: Two Salesforce Veterans
sections.body: Todd McKinnon and Frederic Kerrest both worked at Salesforce before they founded Okta in 2009. They had watched companies move their software to the cloud. Their bet was that identity would become the new security perimeter. If a company's apps lived on the internet, the login was the front door. Okta built a neutral service that worked with Microsoft, Google, Salesforce and thousands of smaller apps.

sections.heading: Thirty-Eight Percent Up
sections.body: Okta priced its IPO at $17 a share on April 6, 2017, at the top of its range. It began trading on Nasdaq the next day and closed at $23.51, up about 38 percent. The company kept growing through the cloud boom. In 2021 it bought Auth0, a login service for developers, for about $6.5 billion. Okta still trades on Nasdaq as OKTA.

cover.theme: a cloudy sky (okta, the unit of cloud cover)

tagline: The Chat Room From a Failed Game
dek: Slack moved office talk out of email and into channels anyone on the team could search and join.
lede: Slack began as the chat tool a small game studio built for itself while it made a game that failed. The studio was Tiny Speck, run by Stewart Butterfield, who had co-founded Flickr. When the game shut down, the team kept the chat tool and sold it. By 2019 offices ran on Slack channels, emoji reactions and endless notifications. Slack skipped the usual IPO and listed its shares directly.

sections.heading: What Was Left of Glitch
sections.body: Butterfield and his co-founders started Tiny Speck in 2009 to build Glitch, an online game. Glitch closed in 2012. The team had built an internal messaging tool along the way, and they bet that other teams would want it too. Slack launched to the public in 2014. It organized talk into channels by topic, kept every message searchable, and plugged into other work apps.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing on WORK
sections.body: Slack went public through a direct listing on the New York Stock Exchange on June 20, 2019, under the ticker WORK. It sold no new shares. The exchange set a reference price of $26. The stock opened at $38.50 and closed at $38.62. Microsoft Teams then grew fast by bundling chat with Office. In July 2021 Salesforce completed its purchase of Slack for about $27.7 billion.

cover.theme: office gossip (workplace chat)

fate: Bought out by Light & Wonder, 2023 ($22.95 a share)
dek: SciPlay put casino slot machines on phones for free, then sold players more coins to keep spinning.
lede: SciPlay's players could spin Las Vegas slot machines all day and never win a cent. That was the business. Its games, such as Jackpot Party Casino and Quick Hit Slots, were free to download, and players bought virtual coins to keep playing. The slot designs came from its parent, Scientific Games, which built real machines for casino floors. In 2019 the parent spun SciPlay out as a public company.

sections.heading: Casino Floor to Phone Screen
sections.body: SciPlay began as the social games arm of Scientific Games, and it was called SG Social Games until March 2019. The bet was that famous slot titles would draw players on phones and Facebook the same way they drew gamblers in casinos. SciPlay could use a library of more than 1,500 real slot and table games from its parent. No one could cash out, so the games did not count as gambling.

sections.heading: A Spin-Off, Then a Buyback
sections.body: SciPlay priced its IPO at $16 a share on May 2, 2019, at the top of its range, and raised about $352 million. It began trading on Nasdaq the next day as SCPL and opened at $18. Scientific Games kept control and later renamed itself Light & Wonder. On October 23, 2023, Light & Wonder bought the roughly 17 percent of SciPlay it did not own, for $22.95 a share.

cover.theme: a gambler (free-to-play slots)

dek: Phreesia let patients check in at the doctor's office on a tablet instead of a clipboard.
lede: Phreesia went after one of the most hated objects in American medicine: the clipboard in the waiting room. Patients filled in the same forms at every visit, and front-desk staff typed them up by hand. Phreesia handed patients a tablet instead. The answers went straight into the practice's records, and the device could collect a copay on the spot. In July 2019 Phreesia took that idea to the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: Paperwork, Then Payments
sections.body: Chaim Indig and Evan Roberts founded Phreesia in 2005. Their bet was that check-in was the moment to fix a doctor's office. A patient waiting for an appointment had time to update insurance, answer health questions and pay. Phreesia charged practices for the software. It also earned money from drug makers, which paid to show health messages to patients during check-in.

sections.heading: Up 40 Percent on PHR
sections.body: Phreesia priced an upsized IPO at $18 a share on July 17, 2019, above its range. It began trading on the New York Stock Exchange the next day as PHR, opened at $26.75, and closed about 40 percent above the offer price. The company grew for years at a loss. In 2025 it reported its first quarterly profit and agreed to buy AccessOne, a patient payments company, for $160 million. Phreesia still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a doctor's waiting room

tagline: Paying the Bills, Minus the Checks
dek: Bill.com let small businesses pay and get paid online, so owners stopped writing paper checks.
lede: Small American businesses still mailed paper checks to pay most of their bills when Bill.com started. An invoice came in the mail. Someone typed it into the books, walked it to the owner for a signature, and stuffed an envelope. Bill.com moved all of that online. It sold mostly through accounting firms, which ran the books for thousands of small clients. It went public in December 2019, a few months before the pandemic emptied offices.

sections.heading: A Founder Who Knew Payments
sections.body: René Lacerte founded Bill.com in Palo Alto in 2006. His bet was that the back office of a small business was a payments problem. Bill.com read incoming invoices, routed them for approval, and paid them by bank transfer. It also sent invoices and collected money. Each payment that passed through earned the company a small fee. Accountants could run the bills for many clients from one screen.

sections.heading: Sixty-One Percent Up
sections.body: Bill.com priced its IPO at $22 a share on December 11, 2019, above its range. It began trading on the New York Stock Exchange the next day as BILL and closed at $35.50, up 61 percent. Remote work made it more useful. It bought Divvy and Invoice2go in 2021 and renamed itself BILL. After activist investors pushed for a sale in 2025, it stayed public and still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: paper money (payments)

dek: nCino gave banks one cloud system for opening accounts and making loans, in place of stacks of paper.
lede: nCino began inside a bank. Live Oak Bank, a small-business lender in Wilmington, North Carolina, built its own loan software on Salesforce to cut through its paperwork. The tool worked well enough that other banks wanted it. Most lenders still ran loans on paper, spreadsheets and old systems that did not talk to each other. nCino offered one cloud platform for the whole job, and in July 2020 it went public during the pandemic.

sections.heading: Spun Out of Live Oak
sections.body: nCino spun out of Live Oak Bank as its own company in late 2011. Live Oak leaders Chip Mahan and Neil Underwood helped start it, and Pierre Naudé became its CEO. The bet was that every bank had the same slow, paper-heavy lending process. nCino built a Bank Operating System on Salesforce's cloud. A loan officer could take a customer from application to closing in one place, with every document and approval tracked.

sections.heading: Nearly Tripled on Day One
sections.body: nCino priced its IPO at $31 a share on July 13, 2020, and began trading on Nasdaq the next day as NCNO. The stock rose about 195 percent on its first day. In 2022 nCino bought SimpleNexus, a maker of mortgage software. By 2026 more than 1,100 financial institutions used nCino. Sean Desmond replaced Naudé as CEO in 2025, and the company still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: an oak tree (Live Oak Bank, where nCino began)

tagline: Two Doctors Build a House Call
dek: Amwell let patients see a doctor by video, and sold the system to hospitals and health insurers.
lede: Amwell was founded by two brothers who were both doctors, and it spent fourteen years waiting for the world to want video visits. Ido and Roy Schoenberg started it in Boston in 2006. For most of that time, patients and insurers saw telehealth as a curiosity. Then the pandemic closed doctors' offices, and video visits became normal in a few weeks. Amwell went public in September 2020, at the height of that rush.

sections.heading: Selling to the Hospitals
sections.body: Ido and Roy Schoenberg founded American Well in 2006. Their bet was that hospitals and insurers, more than patients, would pay for telehealth. Amwell sold them the software to run video visits under their own names. It also ran its own network of doctors for urgent care. That made Amwell the plumbing behind many health systems' virtual care, while rival Teladoc built a bigger consumer brand.

sections.heading: A $742 Million Debut
sections.body: Amwell priced an upsized IPO at $18 a share on September 16, 2020, and raised $742 million. Google invested another $100 million at the same price. The stock began trading on the NYSE as AMWL the next day and closed at $23.07, up 28 percent. Demand for video visits fell after the pandemic, and the shares slid. In 2026 the Defense Health Agency moved to give Amwell a sole-source contract, and Amwell still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a well (Amwell, "I am well")

fate: Still public (NYSE: LU), majority-owned by Ping An
dek: Lufax used data and the internet to lend money to China's small-business owners and to sell wealth products to savers.
lede: Lufax raised $2.36 billion in New York in October 2020, just as Beijing began to crack down on online finance. The company was born inside Ping An, the giant Chinese insurer. It had started as a marketplace where savers lent to strangers online, then dropped that business and moved into loans for small-business owners. Investors valued it at more than $30 billion.

sections.heading: Born Inside an Insurer
sections.body: Ping An founded Lufax in Shanghai in 2011. The bet was that the internet could match China's savers with borrowers faster and cheaper than banks did. Lufax began with peer-to-peer lending, then left it as regulators shut that industry down. It rebuilt itself around two businesses. One made loans to small-business owners, often with banks and trusts putting up the money. The other sold wealth management products to the middle class.

sections.heading: Thirteen Fifty an ADS
sections.body: Lufax priced its IPO at $13.50 per American depositary share in late October 2020 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as LU. It sold 175 million ADSs. Tighter Chinese rules on lending and a weak economy then cut into its business, and the stock fell far below its offer price. Ping An raised its stake to about 73 percent. Hong Kong trading in Lufax shares resumed on September 24, 2026, after a suspension of more than 600 days, and the stock fell 41 percent that day.

cover.theme: a Chinese pagoda (a Shanghai lender)

dek: Playtika made free mobile games, led by Slotomania, that earn money when players buy coins and boosts.
lede: Playtika had already been sold twice before it ever went public. Robert Antokol and Uri Shahak founded the Israeli game studio in 2010. Caesars Entertainment bought it a year later. In 2016 Caesars sold it to a Chinese consortium led by Giant Network for $4.4 billion. Its games, such as Slotomania, were free to play and earned money when players paid for coins. In January 2021, with people stuck at home and gaming on phones, Playtika went public.

sections.heading: A Casino Company's Side Bet
sections.body: Antokol and Shahak started Playtika in 2010 with Slotomania, a social slots game on Facebook. Caesars bought the company in May 2011 and let it run on its own. The bet was that a small share of players would spend real money on virtual coins, and that careful data work could keep them playing for years. Playtika bought other studios and their hit games, and ran them all with the same playbook.

sections.heading: Nearly $1.9 Billion Raised
sections.body: Playtika priced its IPO at $27 a share in January 2021 and raised about $1.88 billion. Its shares began trading on Nasdaq as PLTK on January 15 and jumped in their debut. Growth slowed as the pandemic faded. Playtika bought SuperPlay in 2024 and cut about 20 percent of its staff in late 2025. In 2026 a special committee of its board began a review of strategic options, and Playtika still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a cat at play (Playtika)
cover.artwork: Cat Playing with a Toy Butterfly

dek: Olo ran the online ordering behind restaurant chains' own apps and websites, so customers could skip the line.
lede: Olo started in 2005 as a way to order coffee by text message, two years before the iPhone. Founder Noah Glass bet that people would order food from their phones long before most of them could. When phones caught up, Olo became the engine behind the apps and websites of large restaurant chains. It also routed delivery orders into restaurant kitchens. In March 2021, with dining rooms still half empty from the pandemic, Olo went public.

sections.heading: Before the Smartphone
sections.body: Noah Glass founded the company in New York in 2005, first as Mobo Systems. Its first product took orders by text message. The bet was that restaurants would want to own their digital orders, under their own brand, instead of handing customers to a middleman. Olo sold software to chains and charged them for each order. It plugged into each restaurant's point-of-sale system, so online orders went straight to the kitchen.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Dollars, Then Ten
sections.body: Olo priced its IPO at $25 a share on March 16, 2021, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange the next day as OLO. Orders slowed once diners went back to restaurants, and the stock fell well below its offer price. Olo added payments to grow. In September 2025 Thoma Bravo completed its purchase of Olo for $10.25 a share in cash, about $2.0 billion in equity value.

cover.theme: a café (restaurant orders)

dek: Coinbase let ordinary people buy, sell and store bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies through a simple app.
lede: Coinbase went public on the same day bitcoin hit a new record, and the stock opened at $381. Buying bitcoin had once meant strange websites and real risk of losing everything to a hack. Coinbase made it look like a bank app. By April 2021 crypto prices were soaring, and the company was making money fast. It skipped a traditional IPO and listed its shares directly on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: A Bank App for Crypto
sections.body: Brian Armstrong, a former Airbnb engineer, founded Coinbase in 2012, and Fred Ehrsam, a former Goldman Sachs trader, joined him as co-founder. The company went through Y Combinator. The bet was that crypto would only reach normal people if someone made it safe and simple, and followed the rules. Coinbase linked to bank accounts, held customers' coins for them, and earned a fee on every trade.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing at $250
sections.body: Coinbase listed directly on Nasdaq on April 14, 2021, as COIN, with a reference price of $250. It sold no new shares. The stock opened at $381 and closed at $328.28, valuing the company at about $86 billion on a fully diluted basis. A long crypto slump followed in 2022. Coinbase survived it, fought the SEC in court, and joined the S&P 500 in 2025. It still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a gold miner (the crypto rush)

dek: Global-e let online stores sell to shoppers in other countries, handling local prices, payments, duties and shipping.
lede: A shopper in Germany buying from an American website used to face prices in dollars, surprise customs fees, and a checkout that did not take local payment methods. Global-e fixed all of that from behind the scenes. The Israeli company handled currency, taxes, duties and shipping, so a brand's store felt local in each country. In May 2021, with online shopping booming, it listed on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Three Founders, One Checkout
sections.body: Amir Schlachet, Shahar Tamari and Nir Debbi founded Global-e in 2013. Their bet was that cross-border sales were growing fast and that most brands were losing those sales at checkout. Global-e acted as the merchant of record for foreign orders. It showed prices in local currency, collected duties up front, and offered local payment options. Brands paid Global-e a share of each sale it handled.

sections.heading: A $375 Million Offering
sections.body: Global-e priced its IPO at $25 a share in May 2021 and raised $375 million. Its shares began trading on Nasdaq as GLBE on May 12, valuing the company at about $3.6 billion. Later that year Global-e signed a deal with Shopify to power cross-border selling for Shopify merchants. That partnership became its main source of new business. Global-e still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a world map (cross-border commerce)

dek: TaskUs staffed the support desks, content review teams and AI data work behind fast-growing tech companies.
lede: Behind many of the apps people use every day sit thousands of people answering support tickets and reviewing posts. TaskUs supplies them. Bryce Maddock and Jaspar Weir started it in 2008 by hiring help in the Philippines for small online tasks. By 2021 it worked for some of the biggest names in tech, moderating content, labeling data for AI, and handling customer support. That June it went public.

sections.heading: Outsourcing for the Startups
sections.body: Maddock and Weir founded TaskUs in 2008 and built it around fast-growing tech clients. The bet was that startups would need large teams for support and trust and safety work, and would pay to rent them. TaskUs ran big offices in the Philippines and later in India and other countries. Its teams answered customer emails, reviewed flagged posts and labeled data for AI models. Blackstone bought a majority stake in 2018.

sections.heading: A Buyout Voted Down
sections.body: TaskUs priced its IPO at $23 a share in June 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as TASK. The stock later fell as tech clients cut spending. In 2025 Blackstone and the two founders agreed to take TaskUs private. In October 2025 the deal failed to win the required approval from public shareholders, and the merger agreement ended. TaskUs paid a special dividend in 2026 and still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a swarm of bees (many hands on many tasks)
cover.artwork: The Capture of a Swarm of Bees in a Farmyard

tagline: Groceries at the Door in Thirty Minutes
dek: Dingdong delivered fresh vegetables, meat and fish to Chinese city homes within about half an hour of an order.
lede: Dingdong promised Shanghai families fresh vegetables, meat and fish at the door in about thirty minutes. To do it, the company ran small warehouses tucked into city neighborhoods, close to its customers. Shoppers ordered on an app, and riders on scooters carried the food. The pandemic turned it into a daily habit for millions. In June 2021 Dingdong listed in New York, just as Beijing grew wary of Chinese tech companies selling shares abroad.

sections.heading: A Warehouse on Every Block
sections.body: Changlin Liang founded Dingdong Maicai in Shanghai in 2017. The bet was that busy city families would pay for fresh groceries delivered fast, and that speed depended on location. Dingdong built front-line warehouses a short ride from homes, and sourced much of its food straight from farms. Fresh food spoils fast, so the company leaned on data to guess what each neighborhood would buy each day.

sections.heading: A Small Offering, Then a Retreat
sections.body: Dingdong priced its IPO at $23.50 per American depositary share in June 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as DDL. It sold only 4,072,000 ADSs, a small offering for a company of its size. The stock fell hard over the next year. Dingdong pulled back from weaker cities to focus on the Shanghai region and on cost control. It still trades on the NYSE, with founder Changlin Liang in control.

cover.theme: a man carrying a basket of fresh produce (grocery delivery)
cover.artwork: Old Man with a Basket of Fruit and Vegetables

dek: Paycor ran payroll and HR software for American businesses with a few dozen to a few thousand workers.
lede: Paycor started in Cincinnati in 1990 as a payroll service for local businesses, long before anyone called software a cloud. Over three decades it moved its customers from paper checks to online payroll, and then to full HR software. It aimed at the middle of the market: companies too big for a bookkeeper and too small for a giant HR system. In July 2021, after a private equity buyout, Paycor went public.

sections.heading: Payroll First, Then Everything
sections.body: Bob Coughlin founded Paycor in Cincinnati in 1990. The bet was that small and mid-sized employers would hand payroll to a local partner they trusted. Paycor later rebuilt itself as a cloud software company. It added hiring, time tracking, benefits and HR tools on top of payroll, and sold them as one system. Apax Partners bought a majority stake in 2018 to speed that shift.

sections.heading: From PYCR to Paychex
sections.body: Paycor priced its IPO at $23 a share in July 2021 and began trading on Nasdaq as PYCR. It sold 18.5 million shares. The stock drifted for the next few years as larger rivals competed for the same customers. In January 2025 Paychex agreed to buy Paycor for $22.50 a share in cash, or about $4.1 billion. The deal closed in April 2025, and Paycor's stock left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: payday (payroll)
cover.artwork: Pay Day in the Army of the Potomac

tagline: Free Trades for the Merry Men
dek: Robinhood let anyone buy stocks and crypto from a phone app with no trading commissions.
lede: Robinhood saved some of its own IPO shares for the people who used its app, a rare move on Wall Street. That fit the brand. The company had made stock trades free and turned investing into a phone habit for millions of young people. In January 2021 it limited trading in GameStop during a frenzy, and many of those same users turned on it. Six months later, in July 2021, Robinhood went public.

sections.heading: Two Physics Grads, Zero Fees
sections.body: Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt met as students at Stanford and founded Robinhood in 2013. The bet was that if trades were free and the app was simple, a new generation would invest. Robinhood made money in other ways, including payment from the trading firms that handled its customers' orders. It added options, crypto and cash accounts. Its free trades pushed big brokers such as Schwab to drop their own fees in 2019.

sections.heading: A Slow Start, Then a Surge
sections.body: Robinhood priced its IPO at $38 a share on July 28, 2021, at the bottom of its range. It began trading on Nasdaq as HOOD the next day and closed at $34.82, down about 8 percent. The stock sank far lower in 2022. Robinhood then added retirement accounts, futures and a credit card, and trading boomed again. In September 2025 it joined the S&P 500. Robinhood still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a bowcase and quiver (Robin Hood's arrows)

fate: Taken private by a Permira-led group, 2026 ($24.55 a share)
dek: Clearwater gave insurers, companies and asset managers one clear daily view of every investment they held.
lede: One of the most important tools for big investment portfolios was built in Boise, Idaho. Clearwater Analytics did the accounting for trillions of dollars of investments held by insurers, corporate treasuries and asset managers. Before it, many of those firms pulled data from banks and custodians into spreadsheets by hand. Clearwater gathered it every night and checked it, so clients woke up to a clean set of books. It went public in September 2021.

sections.heading: One Clean Set of Books
sections.body: Clearwater was founded in Boise in 2004. The bet was that investment accounting, a dull and error-prone job, could run as a single web service shared by every client. Clearwater pulled holdings and trades from many custodians, matched them, and produced reports for accountants, regulators and boards. Insurance companies became a core market. Clients paid fees based on the assets the software tracked.

sections.heading: Eighteen Dollars to $24.55
sections.body: Clearwater priced its IPO at $18 a share in September 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as CWAN. In 2025 it bought Enfusion, a maker of software for hedge funds and asset managers. In December 2025 it agreed to be acquired by a group led by Permira with Warburg Pincus, Francisco Partners and Temasek. The deal closed on June 25, 2026, at $24.55 a share, about $7.4 billion in cash to shareholders.

cover.theme: a clear brook (Clearwater)

dek: Cian was where Russians went online to find an apartment to buy or rent, starting in Moscow.
lede: Cian sold shares in New York in November 2021, and less than four months later the NYSE stopped trading them. The company ran Russia's leading real estate classifieds site, where Muscovites hunted for apartments to buy or rent. It listed on both the New York Stock Exchange and the Moscow Exchange. Then Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and Western markets froze trading in Russian stocks.

sections.heading: Listings Before the Boom
sections.body: Cian was founded in Moscow in 2001 as an online real estate classifieds site. Russian agents and developers then spent most of their ad money on print and other offline formats. The bet was that home listings would move online, and that the site with the most of them would win. Cian charged agents, developers and private sellers to post and promote listings. It later added N1.ru to expand beyond Moscow and St. Petersburg.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then a Halt
sections.body: Cian priced its IPO at $16 per American depositary share in November 2021 and sold 18,213,400 ADSs. They began trading as CIAN on the NYSE and the Moscow Exchange. After the invasion of Ukraine, the NYSE halted trading in Russian companies. In March 2023 it moved to delist Cian. A NYSE committee upheld that decision on July 21, 2023, and Cian's American shares left the exchange.

cover.theme: a view of Moscow (Russian real estate)
cover.artwork: View of a Part of Moscow and its Surrounding Areas, from Views of Moscow

tagline: From Bitcoin Barns to AI Factories
dek: Applied Digital built power-hungry data centers on the North Dakota prairie, first for bitcoin miners and then for AI.
lede: Applied Digital raised just $40 million when it listed on Nasdaq in April 2022, selling shares at $5. It was then called Applied Blockchain, and it hosted bitcoin mining machines in North Dakota, where power was cheap and the cold air kept computers cool. The public company behind it had gone by several names since 2001. The crypto market was about to crash. Within three years the same playbook was building data centers for AI.

sections.heading: Cheap Power, Cold Air
sections.body: The company took the name Applied Blockchain in 2021, became Applied Digital in 2023, and is run from Dallas by CEO Wes Cummins. The bet was that computing would move to wherever power was cheapest and land was open. Its first sites hosted crypto miners for a fee. It then designed denser buildings for the graphics chips that train and run AI models, at a campus it calls Polaris Forge in Ellendale, North Dakota.

sections.heading: Five Dollars and 400 Megawatts
sections.body: Applied Digital priced its uplisting offering at $5 a share in April 2022 and sold 8 million shares on Nasdaq as APLD. Before that, its stock had traded over the counter. In 2025 it signed leases with CoreWeave for 400 megawatts of capacity at Polaris Forge 1. The first 100-megawatt building there came online in October 2025. Applied Digital still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a snowy northern field (cold-climate data centers)

dek: Waystar's software helped hospitals and clinics file insurance claims correctly and collect what they were owed.
lede: American hospitals lose real money every year to insurance claims that are filed wrong, denied, or never paid. Waystar sells the software that fights that loss. It checks a patient's coverage, cleans up claims before they go out, and chases payments when they stall. The company was built by private equity from two older firms, Navicure and ZirMed. In June 2024, after years of buyouts and mergers, it went public on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Navicure Meets ZirMed
sections.body: Navicure was co-founded in January 2001 to handle medical billing over the internet. ZirMed, a Louisville company, did similar work for hospitals. Private equity owners brought the two together in 2017 under the Waystar name. The bet was that health care payments were so messy that one large platform could take a small cut of billions of transactions. Waystar runs from offices in Lehi, Utah, and Louisville, Kentucky.

sections.heading: A $967 Million Offering
sections.body: Waystar priced its IPO at $21.50 a share on June 6, 2024, and sold 45 million shares, raising about $967 million. It began trading on Nasdaq as WAY the next day. Its owners, EQT, CPP Investments and Bain Capital, kept large stakes. In 2025 Waystar bought Iodine Software, which uses AI to review clinical documentation. Waystar still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a guiding star (Waystar)
cover.artwork: The Star of the Kings: A Night Piece

tagline: From Ether Mining to AI Clouds
dek: CoreWeave rented out huge clusters of NVIDIA chips to AI labs and tech giants that needed computing power fast.
lede: CoreWeave started as a group of commodity traders mining Ethereum with graphics cards in New Jersey. When crypto prices fell, they found a better use for the chips: renting them to anyone who needed heavy computing. Then ChatGPT arrived, and every AI lab wanted NVIDIA GPUs at once. CoreWeave had them. By March 2025 Microsoft was its biggest customer, and the company went public in the biggest U.S. tech IPO since 2021.

sections.heading: Atlantic Crypto Changes Course
sections.body: Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo, Brannin McBee and Peter Salanki founded the company in 2017 as Atlantic Crypto. It mined Ethereum with GPUs. In 2019 it renamed itself CoreWeave and began offering cloud computing on those chips. The bet was that a cloud built only for GPU work could beat the giant clouds on speed and price. CoreWeave borrowed heavily against its chips and contracts to build data centers fast.

sections.heading: A Cut-Down IPO, Then a Run
sections.body: CoreWeave priced its IPO at $40 a share on March 27, 2025, below its planned range, and raised $1.5 billion instead of the $2.7 billion it first sought. It began trading on Nasdaq as CRWV the next day. The stock then soared. CoreWeave signed a contract with OpenAI worth about $12 billion and expanded deals with Meta. Its revenue backlog reached nearly $100 billion in 2026. CoreWeave still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a woman at a loom (CoreWeave)

tagline: A Crypto Exchange Run by Wall Street
dek: Bullish ran a crypto exchange for big institutions and owned CoinDesk, the crypto news and price index business.
lede: Bullish is run by Tom Farley, a former president of the New York Stock Exchange, and in August 2025 he listed his crypto company there. Bullish built a crypto trading venue for banks, funds and other big players. It also owned CoinDesk, whose crypto price indexes serve as benchmarks for more than $30 billion in assets. Its first try at going public, through a SPAC, had fallen apart in 2022.

sections.heading: Exchange First, News Second
sections.body: Bullish set out to be a regulated crypto exchange with deep, steady markets for large traders. Spot trading in bitcoin and other major coins was its core business, and it added perpetual futures in late 2023. In 2023 it also bought CoinDesk, the crypto news site, along with its indexes and data business. The bet was that institutions would only trade crypto at scale on a venue that looked and acted like a traditional exchange.

sections.heading: Thirty-Seven Dollars on BLSH
sections.body: Bullish priced its IPO at $37 a share in August 2025, above its range, and sold 30 million shares, raising about $1.1 billion. BlackRock and ARK funds had signaled interest in buying up to $200 million of the stock. The shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as BLSH on August 13 and jumped in their debut. Bullish still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a bull (Bullish)

tagline: One Chip the Size of a Plate
