dek: Cerebras built AI chips as big as a whole silicon wafer to run AI models faster than racks of GPUs.
lede: Cerebras makes the largest computer chip ever sold, a single square of silicon about 8.5 inches across. Every other chipmaker cuts a wafer into hundreds of small chips. Cerebras keeps the wafer whole, so data never has to leave the chip. Its first IPO filing, in 2024, stalled while U.S. officials reviewed an investment from G42, its big customer in Abu Dhabi. In May 2026 it finally went public, at the height of the AI boom.

sections.heading: Keeping the Wafer Whole
sections.body: Andrew Feldman, Gary Lauterbach, Michael James, Sean Lie and Jean-Philippe Fricker founded Cerebras in 2015. Feldman and Lauterbach had built SeaMicro, a server maker sold to AMD. The bet was that AI needed a new kind of chip, and that the fastest design was the biggest one. Cerebras built its Wafer Scale Engine and the CS systems around it. It later sold AI computing as a cloud service and built its own data centers.

sections.heading: Opened at $350
sections.body: Cerebras first filed its S-1 in September 2024, then pulled it and raised money privately. It came back in 2026, priced its IPO at $185 a share, and sold 30 million shares for $5.55 billion. The stock began trading on Nasdaq as CBRS on May 14, 2026, opened at $350, and ended the day up about 68 percent. In August 2026 it introduced the CS-4 system. Cerebras trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a thinker (the brain, cerebrum)

fate: Acquired by eBay, 2002 ($1.5B); spun off, 2015 (NASDAQ: PYPL)
tagline: Money by Email, After the Crash
dek: PayPal let anyone with an email address send money online, and made it safe to pay strangers on eBay.
lede: PayPal filed to go public 17 days after the September 11 attacks, and its stock jumped 55 percent on day one. The dot-com bubble had burst. Investors had stopped buying internet stories. PayPal had something rarer: millions of people who used it every day to pay for things they won on eBay. It let anyone with an email address send money, and it became the first internet IPO since Loudcloud in March 2001.

sections.heading: Two Startups, One Wallet
sections.body: PayPal began as Confinity, founded in 1998 by Max Levchin, Peter Thiel, Luke Nosek, and Ken Howery. Its first idea was to beam money between Palm Pilots. Email payments worked better. In March 2000 Confinity merged with X.com, the online bank started by Elon Musk. The combined company took the PayPal name. Its growth came from eBay sellers, who put PayPal buttons on their auctions because buyers already had accounts.

sections.heading: Sold Before the Ink Dried
sections.body: PayPal priced its offering at $13 a share in February 2002 and closed its first day at $20.09. It stayed public for only a few months. In October 2002 eBay bought PayPal for about $1.5 billion in stock. For thirteen years PayPal ran inside eBay as its payments arm. In July 2015 eBay spun it off as its own company again, and PayPal still trades on Nasdaq under PYPL.

cover.theme: a lady reading her letters (money sent like a note between pals)
cover.artwork: Lady Reading the Letters of Heloise and Abelard

dek: Trulia let home buyers search listings on a map, and see the neighborhood before they called an agent.
lede: Trulia went public as the housing market was still digging out of the worst crash since the Depression. Home buyers wanted information, and they wanted it on their phones. Trulia gave them listings on a map, plus crime, schools, and commute data for the streets around each house. Agents paid to appear next to those listings. When the San Francisco company priced its offering in September 2012, its stock rose 41 percent in a day.

sections.heading: Two Founders and a Map
sections.body: Pete Flint and Sami Inkinen started Trulia in San Francisco in 2005. Both had come out of Stanford's business school. Their bet was that buyers would start the hunt for a home online, long before they met an agent. Trulia built search around maps and local data. It made money from agents, who paid to put their names beside the listings that buyers were already reading.

sections.heading: The Rival Next Door
sections.body: Trulia priced at $17 a share on September 19, 2012, and closed its first day at $24 on the New York Stock Exchange. Its biggest rival was Zillow, which went public a year earlier. In July 2014 Zillow agreed to buy Trulia. The deal closed on February 17, 2015, valued at about $2.5 billion in stock. Trulia still runs as a brand inside Zillow Group.

cover.theme: a house among the trees (home search)

tagline: The Card Reader in the Headphone Jack
dek: Square let a coffee cart or a craft-fair seller take credit cards with a phone and a small plastic reader.
lede: Square started because a glassblower in St. Louis lost a $2,000 sale when he could not take a credit card. That glassblower was Jim McKelvey. His friend Jack Dorsey, a cofounder of Twitter, built a small white reader that plugged into a phone's headphone jack. Suddenly any small seller could take cards. Square filed to go public in October 2015, with Dorsey running both Square and Twitter at once.

sections.heading: A Lost Sale in St. Louis
sections.body: Dorsey and McKelvey founded Square in 2009. The bet was that millions of small sellers had been shut out of card payments by contracts, fees, and bulky terminals. Square offered one flat rate and no long contract. The free reader came in the mail. Square then added software for small shops: point of sale, payroll, and loans. In 2013 it launched Square Cash, the app that grew into Cash App.

sections.heading: Priced Low, Rose Fast
sections.body: Square priced at $9 a share on November 18, 2015, below its expected range of $11 to $13. Its stock rose 45 percent the next day to close at $13.07 on the New York Stock Exchange. Cash App became as large as the seller business. In December 2021 the company renamed itself Block. In 2025 its ticker changed from SQ to XYZ, and Block still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a street seller with his basket (small merchants)

tagline: The Pack Animal of Enterprise Data
dek: MuleSoft let big companies connect their old systems and new apps, so data could move between them.
lede: MuleSoft took its name from donkey work. Its founder, Ross Mason, was tired of the grinding job of wiring one business system to another, and he wrote open-source software to carry that load. Large companies ran hundreds of apps that could not talk to each other. MuleSoft sold them a way to connect everything through APIs. It went public in March 2017, as cloud software companies were selling for record prices.

sections.heading: Named for the Grunt Work
sections.body: Ross Mason started the Mule open-source project and founded the company in 2006. It was first called MuleSource. The bet was that every company would end up with a tangle of old databases and new cloud apps. MuleSoft's Anypoint Platform let developers build reusable connections, or APIs, between them. Banks, retailers, and governments bought it. The free open-source version brought in developers, and the paid platform brought in revenue.

sections.heading: A Year on the NYSE
sections.body: MuleSoft priced at $17 a share on March 16, 2017, raising $221 million. It closed its first day on the New York Stock Exchange at $24.75, up 46 percent. Salesforce wanted the plumbing behind its own products. In March 2018 it agreed to buy MuleSoft for about $6.5 billion, and the deal closed that May. MuleSoft now runs as a Salesforce product line.

cover.theme: a mule driver (the beast that carries data)

dek: Pinduoduo let shoppers in China team up with friends to buy fruit, tissues, and clothes at group prices.
lede: Pinduoduo reached the Nasdaq less than three years after its founding, with more than 340 million active buyers. Its trick was the group deal. Shoppers shared a product with friends on WeChat, and if enough joined, everyone paid less. The app found its users in China's smaller cities, far from the shoppers that Alibaba and JD.com chased. When it went public in July 2018, it raised $1.6 billion.

sections.heading: A Google Engineer Goes Home
sections.body: Colin Huang worked as an engineer at Google before he returned to China and started several companies. He founded Pinduoduo in Shanghai in 2015. The bet was that shopping could feel like a game played with friends. Farmers sold fruit straight to groups of buyers. Factories sold cheap goods in bulk. Each deal shared on WeChat pulled in new shoppers.

sections.heading: From Shanghai to Temu
sections.body: Pinduoduo priced its American depositary shares at $19 each, the top of its range, in July 2018. They closed their first day at $26.70, up 40 percent. In 2022 the company launched Temu, a shopping app for buyers in the United States and Europe. In 2023 it renamed itself PDD Holdings and moved its headquarters to Dublin, Ireland. It still trades on Nasdaq under PDD.

cover.theme: fruit sellers at market (group-bought produce)

tagline: Push a Button, Get a Ride
dek: Uber let anyone summon a car with a phone, then grew into food delivery and freight.
lede: Uber raised $8.1 billion when it went public, and its shares still fell 7.6 percent on day one. It was one of the largest American IPOs ever, and one of the most awkward. The company had turned a phone into a taxi stand in hundreds of cities. It had also lost billions of dollars a year, fought regulators everywhere, and replaced its founding CEO after a run of scandals. Investors had to decide what all of that was worth.

sections.heading: A Cab Shortage in Paris
sections.body: Garrett Camp and Travis Kalanick founded the company in San Francisco in 2009, first as UberCab. The idea grew from a night in Paris when the two could not find a ride. The bet was that a phone with GPS could match riders and drivers faster than any dispatcher. Uber spent heavily to win city after city. In 2017 Kalanick stepped down as CEO, and Dara Khosrowshahi took over.

sections.heading: Below the Offer Price
sections.body: Uber priced at $45 a share on May 9, 2019, at the low end of its range. It opened on the New York Stock Exchange at $42 and closed at $41.57. Under Khosrowshahi the company cut costs and leaned on Uber Eats, which grew fast during the pandemic. In 2023 Uber posted its first full year of operating profit. It still trades on the NYSE under UBER.

cover.theme: an omnibus (a shared ride through the city)

tagline: Every Hotel Guest Has Something to Say
dek: Medallia let big companies hear what their customers thought, and act on it before they lost them.
lede: Medallia's stock rose 76 percent on its first day, one of the best debuts of 2019. The company sold software that listened. It collected surveys, reviews, and comments from customers of hotels, banks, and airlines, then sorted them so managers could fix problems fast. Its founders, a married couple, had spent eighteen years building it before the offering. By then cloud software was the hottest corner of the stock market.

sections.heading: Feedback Nobody Read
sections.body: Borge Hald and Amy Pressman founded Medallia in 2001. The bet was that companies collected customer feedback and then did nothing with it. Medallia made the comments arrive in real time, routed to the person who could act. Luxury hotels were among the first buyers. Banks, retailers, and telecom companies followed. The company stayed private for nearly two decades and grew to serve some of the largest brands in the world.

sections.heading: A Short Run in Public
sections.body: Medallia priced at $21 a share, above its range, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on July 19, 2019. The stock closed the day up about 76 percent. Its public life lasted just over two years. In 2021 Thoma Bravo agreed to buy the company for $34 a share in cash, about $6.4 billion. The deal closed that October, and Medallia went private again.

cover.theme: a portrait medallion (the name and the face of the customer)
cover.artwork: Medallion Portrait of Mlle de Fontanges

tagline: One Inbox for Every Brand Account
dek: Sprout Social let brands answer, schedule, and measure their social media from one screen.
lede: Sprout Social went public from Chicago, far from the Silicon Valley money that usually funds software companies. It sold one inbox for every brand account on Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn. Marketers used it to schedule posts, answer customers, and prove their work was paying off. By December 2019 social media had become a customer service desk for most companies. Even so, Sprout's stock slipped below its offer price on its first day.

sections.heading: Four Founders, One Dashboard
sections.body: Justyn Howard, Aaron Rankin, Gilbert Lara, and Peter Soung founded Sprout Social in Chicago in 2010. The bet was that small businesses and big brands alike would need a tool to manage a flood of social messages. Sprout sold it as a subscription with a free trial. It grew by adding listening, analytics, and tools for teams. Howard ran the company as CEO for more than a decade.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to NewsWhip
sections.body: Sprout Social priced at $17 a share on December 12, 2019, the middle of its range, and listed on Nasdaq under SPT. The stock opened at $18.05 and closed the day at $16.60. Ryan Barretto, who joined the company in 2016, became CEO in 2024. In July 2025 Sprout bought NewsWhip, a Dublin company that tracks stories as they spread. Sprout still trades on Nasdaq under SPT.

cover.theme: young plants (a sprout)

dek: Jamf let schools and companies set up, update, and secure thousands of Apple devices from one console.
lede: Jamf began with one student worker in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, who had to keep 400 university Macs running. Zach Halmstad found plenty of tools for Windows and almost none for Apple. So he wrote his own. Apple devices were spreading through offices and classrooms, and Jamf managed Apple hardware and nothing else. When it went public in July 2020, remote work had sent millions of laptops home, and its stock rose 51 percent on the first day.

sections.heading: Only Apple, Nothing Else
sections.body: Halmstad and Chip Pearson founded Jamf in 2002. The name comes from a character in Thomas Pynchon's novel Gravity's Rainbow. The bet was that Apple would win in schools and businesses, and that its customers would want a specialist. Jamf's software let IT teams set up a new iPad or MacBook without touching it, push updates, and lock lost devices. In 2017 Vista Equity Partners bought a majority stake.

sections.heading: Back to Private Hands
sections.body: Jamf priced at $26 a share on July 21, 2020, and opened on Nasdaq the next day. It closed its first session at $39.20. The stock later drifted far below its offer price. In 2025 Francisco Partners agreed to buy Jamf for $13.05 a share in cash. The deal closed in January 2026, valuing the company at about $2.2 billion, and Jamf left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: apples under a gable (Apple devices)

tagline: The Same Pill, a Lower Price
dek: GoodRx showed Americans how much their prescriptions cost at each pharmacy, then gave them coupons to pay less.
lede: Doug Hirsch started GoodRx after a pharmacy quoted him an alarming price for a prescription, and he went shopping for a better one. He found no single place to compare. GoodRx became that place. Its free app showed the price of a drug at every nearby pharmacy, plus a coupon to pay less. Millions of Americans used it. GoodRx went public in September 2020, in the middle of the pandemic, and closed its first day up 53 percent.

sections.heading: A Shock at the Counter
sections.body: Hirsch, a former Facebook executive, founded GoodRx in Santa Monica in 2011 with Trevor Bezdek and Scott Marlette. The bet was that drug prices were hidden from the people paying them, and that showing those prices would pull in millions of users. GoodRx made its money from fees paid by pharmacy benefit managers when people used its coupons. Unlike most startups of its size, it was profitable when it filed.

sections.heading: Amazon Enters the Aisle
sections.body: GoodRx priced at $33 a share on September 22, 2020, above its first range of $24 to $28. It opened on Nasdaq at $46 and closed at $50.50. Two months later Amazon launched its own pharmacy, and GoodRx shares fell 23 percent that day. The company added telehealth and subscriptions, and later sold tools to drug makers. Its stock spent the following years far below the offer price. GoodRx still trades on Nasdaq under GDRX.

cover.theme: an apothecary (the pharmacy counter)

fate: Delisted from Nasdaq, 2023; trades on the Moscow Exchange
dek: Ozon delivered almost anything to Russian homes, across eleven time zones, from a website that began by selling books.
lede: Ozon started in 1998 as an online bookshop in Moscow. Twenty-two years later it sold everything from phones to diapers across Russia, a country with eleven time zones and long stretches of bad road. The pandemic had pushed millions of Russians to shop online for the first time. Ozon went public on Nasdaq in November 2020, valued at $6.2 billion, and its stock rose 34 percent on the first day.

sections.heading: Books First, Then Everything
sections.body: Ozon was set up in Moscow by Reksoft, a Russian software house. In 1999 ru-Net Holdings, led by Leonid Boguslavsky, bought a controlling stake. The bet was that Russia would shop online as the West did, if someone built the warehouses and delivery network first. Ozon built both. It opened its site to outside sellers and became a marketplace. Pickup points and lockers filled in where couriers could not reach.

sections.heading: Cut Off From Nasdaq
sections.body: Ozon priced an upsized offering at $30 a share on November 23, 2020, well above its range, and raised about $990 million. After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Nasdaq halted trading in Ozon's shares and moved to delist them. Ozon appealed twice and lost. In October 2023 it announced a voluntary delisting. Its shares now trade on the Moscow Exchange.

cover.theme: a troika (Russian winter delivery)

dek: Mytheresa sold designer fashion online to the world's biggest spenders, picked with a boutique buyer's eye.
lede: Mytheresa began as a single boutique in Munich called Theresa, opened by Susanne and Christoph Botschen in 1987. Nearly twenty years later they put it online. By 2021 the site shipped Gucci, Bottega Veneta, and The Row to wealthy shoppers around the world. Luxury had been slow to trust the internet. The pandemic closed the stores, and rich customers moved online for good. Mytheresa went public in January 2021.

sections.heading: Small Edits for Big Spenders
sections.body: The Botschens launched mytheresa.com in 2006. The bet was that the richest shoppers would buy online if the selection felt as tight as a good boutique. Mytheresa bought less, chose carefully, and courted its top customers with private events. A small group of big spenders drove most of its sales. In 2014 the American department store Neiman Marcus bought the business, and Michael Kliger later became its CEO.

sections.heading: Buying Its Biggest Rival
sections.body: The parent company priced its offering at $26 a share on January 20, 2021, at the top of a raised range. It raised $407 million on the New York Stock Exchange, and the stock closed its first day up 19 percent. In April 2025 Mytheresa bought Yoox Net-a-Porter from Richemont, which took a 33 percent stake in return. The company renamed itself LuxExperience and now trades on the NYSE as LUXE.

cover.theme: Parisian fashion plates (designer fashion)
cover.artwork: "Costume Parisien" Fashion Plates from Journal des Dames et Des Modes

tagline: The Brain Inside the Smart Lamp
dek: Tuya gave appliance makers a ready-made cloud and app, so a cheap lamp or plug could join the smart home.
lede: The smart plug or light bulb you bought on sale may run on software from a company you have never heard of. Tuya, based in Hangzhou, sold appliance makers a ready-made kit: a chip module, a cloud, and an app. A factory could make an ordinary product smart without building its own software team. When Tuya went public in New York in March 2021, it raised $915 million and its stock rose 19 percent on day one.

sections.heading: Smart Homes, Sold Wholesale
sections.body: Wang Xueji founded Tuya in Hangzhou in 2014. The bet was that thousands of small brands wanted smart products and had no engineers to build the software. Tuya did the hard part once and rented it to all of them. Its platform ran lights, plugs, cameras, and vacuums for brands around the world. The company earned money on modules and on software that makers paid for each year.

sections.heading: Two Listings, Two Cities
sections.body: Tuya priced at $21 a share on March 17, 2021, above its range, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under TUYA. The stock later fell far below its offer price as Chinese tech stocks slumped. In July 2022 Tuya added a second primary listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It trades in both cities today, under TUYA in New York and 2391 in Hong Kong.

cover.theme: a lamp (the connected home)
cover.artwork: Lamp with Hanging Head Dragonfly Shade and Mosaic and Turtleback Base

tagline: From Game Studio to Ad Machine
dek: AppLovin found paying users for mobile app makers, with software that decides which ad to show to whom.
lede: AppLovin's stock fell 18.5 percent on its first day of trading. Four years later the company joined the S&P 500. The Palo Alto company made money from mobile games in two ways. It owned studios that made the games, and it ran the ad software that other game makers used to find players. When it went public in April 2021, investors could not tell which half mattered more. The answer turned out to be the ads.

sections.heading: Three Founders, One Feed of Ads
sections.body: Adam Foroughi, John Krystynak, and Andrew Karam founded AppLovin in 2012. The bet was that app makers would pay well for software that found the users most likely to spend. AppLovin bought game studios to feed its ad business with data and traffic. Its AI ad engine, called Axon, grew into the main source of profit. Foroughi ran the company as CEO.

sections.heading: Selling the Games
sections.body: AppLovin priced at $80 a share on April 14, 2021, and opened on Nasdaq at $70. The stock spent two years in a slump. Then its new ad engine took off, and profits soared. In June 2025 AppLovin sold its game studios to Tripledot Studios to focus on advertising. It joined the S&P 500 on September 22, 2025, and trades on Nasdaq as APP.

cover.theme: a juggler (keeping many apps in the air)

tagline: A Dorm-Room Site Builder Grows Up
dek: Squarespace let anyone build a good-looking website, store, or portfolio without hiring a designer.
lede: Squarespace began as a blog tool that Anthony Casalena wrote for himself while he was a student at the University of Maryland. His father put in $30,000. He had 300 beta testers. Seventeen years later the company hosted sites for photographers, restaurants, and small shops, and its ads were a fixture of podcasts. It skipped the usual IPO and went straight to the New York Stock Exchange through a direct listing in May 2021.

sections.heading: One Founder, No Rush
sections.body: Casalena founded Squarespace in 2003 and launched it to the public in January 2004. The bet was that people would pay for a site that looked designed, with no code at all. Squarespace sold templates that made a one-person business look polished. It added online stores, domains, and scheduling. In 2021 it bought Tock, the restaurant booking service. Casalena served as CEO the whole way.

sections.heading: Direct to the Floor
sections.body: Squarespace began trading on the NYSE on May 19, 2021, under SQSP, through a direct listing with a $50 reference price. It sold no new shares. The stock closed its first day below the reference price and spent most of its public life lower still. In 2024 Permira agreed to take the company private. The deal closed in October 2024, valued at about $7.2 billion.

cover.theme: a grid of squares (the site builder)

tagline: Apple's Old CEO Bets on Data
dek: Zeta Global let big brands find and reach customers, using its own data on millions of consumers.
lede: One of Zeta Global's two founders was John Sculley, the former Apple CEO best known for the 1985 fight that pushed Steve Jobs out. The other, David Steinberg, ran the company. They started it in 2007 as XL Marketing and built it into a marketing cloud that sold brands data on what consumers wanted. When Zeta went public in June 2021, it had to cut the size of its offering and price at the bottom of its range.

sections.heading: From XL Marketing to Zeta
sections.body: Steinberg and Sculley founded the company in New York in 2007. The bet was that marketers would pay for software tied to a large store of data on consumers, plus the tools to act on it. Zeta bought companies to grow that data and its email and ad tools. It renamed itself Zeta Global along the way. Steinberg runs it as CEO.

sections.heading: A Small Offering, Then Growth
sections.body: Zeta priced a downsized offering at $10 a share on June 9, 2021, the low end of its range. The stock closed its first day on the New York Stock Exchange down 11 percent. Revenue kept growing, and in fiscal 2025 it reached $1.3 billion. In October 2025 Zeta launched Athena, an AI agent for marketers. It still trades on the NYSE under ZETA.

cover.theme: a Greek Doric order (zeta, the Greek letter)
cover.artwork: Orders of Architecture, Greek Doric Order from the Parthenon, Elevation

fate: Delisted from NYSE, 2022; trades over the counter (DIDIY)
dek: DiDi let hundreds of millions of people in China hail a taxi or private car from their phones.
lede: Two days after DiDi listed in New York, China's internet regulator opened a cybersecurity review of the company. Two days after that, it ordered DiDi's app pulled from app stores. DiDi had just raised $4.4 billion at a value near $70 billion. It was China's dominant ride-hailing service, the company that had bought out Uber's China business five years earlier. Within a year it would leave the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: Beating Uber at Home
sections.body: Cheng Wei founded the company in Beijing in June 2012 as Didi Dache, a taxi-hailing app. It merged with its main rival, Kuaidi, in 2015. The bet was that China's huge cities and short supply of taxis would make ride-hailing a daily habit. DiDi spent heavily to win. In August 2016 it bought Uber's China business, and Uber took a stake in DiDi in return.

sections.heading: Listed, Then Delisted
sections.body: DiDi priced its shares at $14 and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on June 30, 2021. The stock closed the first day up 1 percent. Days later regulators pulled its apps. In July 2022 they fined the company 8.026 billion yuan, about $1.2 billion. DiDi left the NYSE on June 13, 2022. Its shares now trade over the counter as DIDIY.

cover.theme: a hired sedan chair (a ride for hire in China)
cover.artwork: A Hong-Kong Sedan Chair; A Chinese School-Boy; A Chinese Girl; A Hong-Kong Coolie

dek: Couchbase sold a fast, flexible database for apps that needed to stay quick under heavy traffic and offline.
lede: Couchbase was born from a merger of two small database startups in 2011. One was Membase, first called NorthScale. The other was CouchOne, built around CouchDB, the open-source database whose name stands for 'cluster of unreliable commodity hardware'. Together they sold a NoSQL database for apps that had to answer millions of users at once. When Couchbase went public in July 2021, its stock rose 27 percent on day one.

sections.heading: NoSQL for the Enterprise
sections.body: NorthScale was founded in 2009 by James Phillips, Steve Yen, and Dustin Sallings. CouchOne grew from the work of Damien Katz, the creator of CouchDB. The merged company bet that big businesses would leave old relational databases for something faster and more flexible. Airlines, banks, and retailers used Couchbase to power apps. Its rival MongoDB went public first, in 2017.

sections.heading: Four Years on Nasdaq
sections.body: Couchbase priced at $24 a share on July 21, 2021, above its range, and listed on Nasdaq as BASE. The stock closed its first day up about 27 percent, then drifted lower for years. In June 2025 Haveli Investments agreed to buy Couchbase for $24.50 a share in cash, about $1.5 billion. The deal closed in September 2025, and Couchbase went private.

cover.theme: a sofa (the couch)
cover.artwork: The Corner of the Sofa, No. 3

tagline: Paying for the Fraud It Misses
dek: Riskified approved more online orders for retailers, and paid them back for any fraud it let through.
lede: Riskified made online stores a simple offer: we judge each order, and if we approve one that turns out to be fraud, we pay for it. Most fraud tools just flagged risky orders and left the merchant to eat the loss. Riskified took the loss on itself. That let stores approve more good customers they would once have turned away. The Tel Aviv company went public in July 2021, and its stock rose 24 percent on day one.

sections.heading: A Guarantee on Every Order
sections.body: Eido Gal and Assaf Feldman founded Riskified in 2012, with Gal as CEO and Feldman as CTO. The bet was that machine learning could judge online orders better than human reviewers and rigid rules. Riskified charged a fee on each approved order and covered the cost of chargebacks. Large retailers and travel sites signed on, because a declined good customer was a lost sale.

sections.heading: Trading Below Its Price
sections.body: Riskified priced at $21 a share on July 28, 2021, above its range, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as RSKD. The offering valued it at about $4.3 billion, and the stock closed its first day up 24 percent. It soon fell well below its offer price, along with most 2021 listings. Riskified still trades on the NYSE under RSKD.

cover.theme: a tightrope walker (balancing risk)

dek: Amplitude showed product teams what users did inside their apps, so they could build what people kept using.
lede: Amplitude began as a failed voice-texting app. Its founders, Spenser Skates and Curtis Liu, built Sonalight in 2012 to let Android users send texts by speaking. The app never caught on. The analytics tool they built to study it did. Other companies asked for it, and the founders turned it into a business. Amplitude skipped a traditional IPO and joined Nasdaq through a direct listing in September 2021.

sections.heading: The Tool Behind the Flop
sections.body: Skates and Liu turned their internal tracker into Amplitude. The bet was that product teams, as well as marketers, needed analytics. Amplitude showed which features kept users coming back and where they dropped off. Companies could test a change and measure its effect. Customers paid by subscription. The company grew by adding experiments, customer data tools, and session replay. Its customers ranged from startups to large consumer brands.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing Jump
sections.body: Amplitude listed on Nasdaq under AMPL on September 28, 2021, through a direct listing with a $35 reference price. It sold no new shares. The stock closed its first day up about 57 percent, lifting the company's value from about $5 billion to more than $7 billion. It later fell far below that level. Amplitude still trades on Nasdaq under AMPL.

cover.theme: a breaking wave (amplitude)

dek: Weave gave dental, eye care, and veterinary offices one system for calls, texts, reminders, reviews, and payments.
lede: Weave sold its software to a customer most tech companies ignore: the front desk of a dental office. Its system showed the patient's name and history the moment the phone rang. It sent appointment reminders by text, asked for reviews, and took payments. The Utah company built a business around small medical offices. When it went public in November 2021, it priced below its range, and its stock fell 22 percent on day one.

sections.heading: Built for the Front Desk
sections.body: Weave was founded in 2008 and grew up in Lehi, Utah, in the tech corridor known as Silicon Slopes. The bet was that small practices wasted time juggling phones, paper, and separate tools. Weave tied its phone system to the practice's patient records, so staff knew who was calling before they picked up. Dentists came first. Optometrists, veterinarians, and other specialty clinics followed.

sections.heading: A Rough First Day
sections.body: Weave priced at $24 a share on November 10, 2021, below its expected range, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as WEAV. Its shares fell about 22 percent in the first session. The stock spent the following year far below its offer price as the market turned on unprofitable software companies. Weave still trades on the NYSE under WEAV.

cover.theme: a woman spinning thread (weave)

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: MBLY), majority owned by Intel
tagline: One Camera That Watches the Road
dek: Mobileye built the chips and software that let a car see lanes, cars, and people with a single camera.
lede: Mobileye went public twice. The first time was on the New York Stock Exchange in 2014. Three years later Intel bought it for $15.3 billion. In October 2022 Intel sold a slice back to the public on Nasdaq, while keeping control. By then Mobileye's camera chips were in millions of cars, warning drivers when they drifted from a lane or closed too fast on the car ahead.

sections.heading: A Professor's Camera Bet
sections.body: Amnon Shashua, a computer vision professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, founded Mobileye in 1999 with Ziv Aviram and Norio Ichihashi. The bet was that one cheap camera and smart software could do the job of costly radar. Mobileye sold its EyeQ chips to carmakers' suppliers. Each new generation took on more of the driving, from lane warnings toward hands-free systems.

sections.heading: Intel's Partial Exit
sections.body: Mobileye priced at $21 a share on October 25, 2022, and raised about $861 million. Intel kept all the Class B shares and nearly all the voting power. The stock rose 38 percent on its first day. In January 2026 Mobileye agreed to buy Mentee Robotics, a humanoid robot startup, for about $900 million. It still trades on Nasdaq under MBLY.

cover.theme: eyes (machine vision)

tagline: A Diagnosis That Started a Company
dek: Tempus ran genetic tests on cancer patients and used the data to help doctors choose treatments.
lede: Eric Lefkofsky, a cofounder of Groupon, started Tempus soon after his wife was diagnosed with breast cancer. He found that her doctors had little data to guide their choices. Tempus set out to sequence tumors, collect clinical records, and use AI to match patients with treatments. By the time it filed to go public in 2024, it had built a large library of clinical and molecular data on cancer patients.

sections.heading: Data for Every Tumor
sections.body: Lefkofsky founded the company in Chicago in 2015 as Tempus Labs. The bet was that genomic testing would become routine in cancer care, and the data behind it would be worth more than the tests. Tempus sold sequencing to doctors and sold data to drug makers. It later moved into cardiology, radiology, and depression. Lefkofsky ran it as CEO, and he still does.

sections.heading: Bigger After the Bell
sections.body: Tempus priced at $37 a share on June 13, 2024, the top of its range, and listed on Nasdaq as TEM. It raised about $411 million, and the stock closed the first day up about 9 percent. In November 2024 Tempus agreed to buy Ambry Genetics for $600 million. In July 2026 it announced a deal for Personalis, valued at about $1.5 billion. Tempus still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Father Time (tempus)

dek: eToro let ordinary investors trade stocks and crypto, and copy the trades of other users automatically.
lede: eToro's best-known feature let you hand your portfolio to a stranger. Pick another user whose trades you liked, and eToro copied every move into your account. The Israeli company started in 2007 as a currency-trading site called RetailFX. By 2025 it had millions of funded accounts across Europe and beyond. It had tried to go public through a SPAC in 2021 and walked away. In May 2025 it listed on Nasdaq the traditional way.

sections.heading: Trading as a Social Network
sections.body: Yoni Assia, his brother Ronen Assia, and David Ring founded the company in Tel Aviv in 2007. The bet was that trading could feel like a game, then like a social network. In 2010 eToro launched OpenBook, which let users follow and copy each other. It added stocks and, later, crypto. In 2021 it agreed to merge with a SPAC, FinTech Acquisition Corp. V. Both sides ended that deal in July 2022.

sections.heading: The IPO It Waited For
sections.body: eToro priced at $52 a share on May 13, 2025, above its range of $46 to $50, and listed on Nasdaq as ETOR. It raised about $620 million. The stock closed its first day up about 29 percent. In August 2026 eToro agreed to buy TradeZero, an American brokerage, in a deal worth up to $231 million. It still trades on Nasdaq under ETOR.

cover.theme: a young bull (a bull market)

dek: MIAX built electronic exchanges for options and futures, competing with the giants that run Wall Street's markets.
lede: Exchange companies rarely go public, because only a few exist. Miami International Holdings was one of the newcomers. Founded in 2007, it built a family of electronic options exchanges under the MIAX name, then bought its way into futures. Its rivals were the giants that run Wall Street's markets. When it went public in August 2025, it priced above its range, and its stock rose 34 percent on day one.

sections.heading: Building Exchanges From Scratch
sections.body: The company was founded in 2007 and is based in Princeton, New Jersey. The bet was that options trading would keep growing, and that a new exchange with fast technology could take a share from incumbents. It launched MIAX Options, then added more options and equities exchanges. It also bought older markets to enter futures trading. Its customers were the market makers and brokers who route orders every second.

sections.heading: A Rare Exchange IPO
sections.body: MIAX priced at $23 a share on August 13, 2025, above its range of $19 to $21. It sold 15 million shares and raised about $345 million. The stock began trading on the New York Stock Exchange the next day and closed up about 34 percent. The company announced plans to open a trading floor in Miami. It still trades on the NYSE under MIAX.

cover.theme: a Florida river at morning (Miami)

dek: Liftoff found new users for mobile apps and let their makers earn money from ads shown inside them.
lede: Liftoff's first try at an IPO stalled. In February 2026 it postponed an offering marketed at $26 to $30 a share, as software stocks sold off. Four months later it came back with a lower range and priced above it. The Redwood City company sold AI software that helped mobile apps find users and earn money from ads. Its June 2026 listing was the first ad tech IPO since 2025.

sections.heading: Growth Engine for Apps
sections.body: Liftoff began as a company that bought ads to win new users for mobile apps. Over time it added software that lets app makers sell ad space inside their own apps. It calls itself a growth and monetization engine for the app economy. Machine learning decides which ad a user sees and how much to bid. Its customers include game studios and consumer apps around the world.

sections.heading: Above the Range
sections.body: Liftoff priced 19 million shares at $23 on June 3, 2026, above its range of $20 to $22. Trading began on Nasdaq under LFTO the next day. The stock closed its first session up about 24 percent. The offering valued the company at close to $4 billion. It was the second time in four months that Liftoff had tried to price a deal. Liftoff still trades on Nasdaq under LFTO.

cover.theme: a woman lighting a rocket (liftoff)
cover.artwork: Woman Lighting a Rocket, also called Peace Gets Me Going, from Communia Gaudia (The Wide-Spread Rejoicing at the Siege of Namur)

tagline: Two Students and a Number Called Googol
dek: Google let anyone type a question into a plain white box and find the right page in under a second.
lede: Google sold its shares the way you sell a painting: by auction. Wall Street banks usually picked who got stock in a hot offering. Larry Page and Sergey Brin let ordinary investors bid online instead. In 2004 the dot-com crash was still a fresh bruise, and tech offerings were rare. Google arrived with a famous search box, a fast-growing ad business, and a pair of founders who wanted to go public on their own terms.

sections.heading: A Garage in Menlo Park
sections.body: Page and Brin met as PhD students at Stanford. Their search engine ranked a web page by how many other pages linked to it, and by how important those pages were. In September 1998 they founded Google and set up in a friend's garage in Menlo Park. The bet was that better answers would win users, and that small text ads next to those answers could pay for everything. The company grew up in Mountain View, California.

sections.heading: The Dutch Auction
sections.body: Google first hoped for $108 to $135 a share. Demand from the auction came in lower, and the stock priced at $85 on August 18, 2004. It began trading on Nasdaq the next day and closed near $100, up about 18 percent. In 2015 Google reorganized under a new parent company called Alphabet. Sundar Pichai became Google's chief executive that October. Alphabet still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker GOOGL.

cover.theme: a lantern held out into the dark night, searching for fireflies (search)

dek: Twitter let anyone post a short message that the whole world could read, reply to, and pass along.
lede: Twitter opened its first day of trading at $45.10, 73 percent above the price its bankers set the night before. By 2013 the short public post had become how news broke, how celebrities talked to fans, and how protests got organized. The San Francisco company had hundreds of millions of users and a young ad business. Facebook had stumbled through its own debut the year before, and every investor wanted to see if Twitter would do better.

sections.heading: A Side Project at Odeo
sections.body: Twitter began in 2006 inside Odeo, a San Francisco podcasting startup. Jack Dorsey, Biz Stone, Evan Williams and Noah Glass built a service for sending short status updates, sized to fit in a text message. The bet was that tiny public posts, stacked into a live feed, would add up to something people checked all day. Users invented the hashtag and the retweet themselves. The company later built its business on ads placed inside that feed.

sections.heading: A Pop, Then a Takeover
sections.body: Twitter sold 70 million shares at $26 each on November 6, 2013, raising $1.82 billion. It listed on the New York Stock Exchange the next day and closed at $44.90. Profits came slowly in the years that followed. In October 2022 Elon Musk bought the company for about $44 billion and took it private. He renamed it X in July 2023. In March 2025 his AI company, xAI, acquired X in an all-stock deal.

cover.theme: a small songbird on a branch (the tweet)

tagline: The Snowboard Shop That Sold Stores
dek: Shopify let small sellers open an online store in an afternoon, without hiring a programmer.
lede: Shopify started as a website for selling snowboards. Tobias Lütke, a German programmer in Ottawa, could not find store software he liked, so he wrote his own. The store mattered less than the code behind it. By 2015 Amazon set the pace of online shopping, and millions of small brands wanted a way to sell on their own websites. Shopify sold them the tools, and it went public on two exchanges at once, in New York and Toronto.

sections.heading: Snowdevil on Rails
sections.body: Lütke and Scott Lake opened Snowdevil, an online snowboard shop, in Ottawa in 2004. Lütke built the store with Ruby on Rails, then a new open-source web framework. In June 2006 the founders launched that store software as Shopify. Daniel Weinand is also named as a co-founder. The bet was that thousands of merchants had the same problem Snowdevil had. Shopify charged them a monthly fee to run their shops.

sections.heading: A Fifty Percent Pop
sections.body: Shopify priced its offering at $17 a share on May 20, 2015, above its raised range. It sold 7.7 million shares and raised $131 million. On the first day the stock opened at $28 on the New York Stock Exchange and closed at $25.71, up 51 percent. In March 2025 Shopify moved its U.S. listing from the NYSE to Nasdaq. It still trades as SHOP on Nasdaq and the Toronto Stock Exchange.

cover.theme: a small shopfront (the merchant's own store)

fate: Taken private by KKR and CD&R, 2021 ($5.3B)
dek: Cloudera let big companies store and sift huge piles of data using Hadoop, free software named after a toy elephant.
lede: Cloudera built a business on free software named after a toy elephant. Hadoop let companies spread enormous data sets across racks of cheap servers and query them all at once. Banks, phone carriers and retailers wanted that power, but few knew how to run it. Cloudera sold them a supported version, plus the people to make it work. When it went public in April 2017, big data was a boardroom phrase and the cloud giants were moving in.

sections.heading: Hadoop for Everyone Else
sections.body: Cloudera was incorporated in June 2008 and based in Palo Alto, California. Its founders came from Google, Yahoo and Facebook, where engineers had learned to handle data at web scale. Mike Olson, Amr Awadallah, Christophe Bisciglia and Jeff Hammerbacher bet that ordinary companies would soon face the same flood. They gave away the core software. Cloudera charged for subscriptions, management tools and support.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars a Share
sections.body: Cloudera priced at $15 a share on April 27, 2017, above its $12 to $14 range, and raised about $225 million. It closed its first day on the NYSE near $18, up about 20 percent. In January 2019 it merged with Hortonworks, its closest Hadoop rival. Growth slowed as customers moved data to cloud services. In 2021 KKR and Clayton, Dubilier & Rice took Cloudera private for $16 a share, about $5.3 billion.

cover.theme: an elephant (Hadoop's mascot)

dek: Futu let investors in Hong Kong and mainland China trade stocks from a phone app with a social feed.
lede: Futu put a stock exchange, a chat room and a news desk inside one phone app. Its Hong Kong app was called Futubull, and its customers were mostly young, mobile, and new to trading. In 2019 Chinese investors wanted easy access to Hong Kong and U.S. stocks, and the old brokers felt slow and paper-bound. Futu went public on Nasdaq that March, selling itself as the broker built for that crowd.

sections.heading: Trading as a Social App
sections.body: Leaf Hua Li founded Futu in 2011 and served as its chairman and chief executive. The company is based in Hong Kong. The bet was that a generation raised on social apps would want a broker that felt like one. Futu built trading, market data and a community feed into the same screen. It earned money from commissions, from lending to clients who traded on margin, and from interest on client balances.

sections.heading: From Futubull to Moomoo
sections.body: Futu priced its offering at $12 per American depositary share in March 2019. It sold 7.5 million shares and raised $90 million. The stock closed its first day up about 28 percent. Futu later took its moomoo app to the United States, Singapore, Australia and Malaysia. It ended 2025 with 3.37 million funded accounts and about $2.94 billion in revenue. It still trades on Nasdaq as FUTU.

cover.theme: two bulls locking horns (Futubull, a bull market)

dek: Fastly kept big websites quick by serving their pages from servers close to each reader.
lede: On June 8, 2021, one Fastly customer changed a setting, and a large slice of the internet went dark. News sites, shops and government pages returned errors at once. That outage showed how much of the web ran through a company most readers had never heard of. Two years earlier, Fastly had gone public as a challenger in content delivery, selling speed and control to developers at sites that could not afford to be slow.

sections.heading: A Wikia Engineer's Edge
sections.body: Artur Bergman founded Fastly in San Francisco in 2011. He had been chief technical officer at Wikia, a busy wiki host, and knew the pain of serving pages fast at scale. The bet was that developers wanted a delivery network they could program and update in seconds. Fastly placed servers at the edge of the network, close to readers. Customers paid by how much traffic they sent through it.

sections.heading: Forty-Nine Minutes
sections.body: Fastly priced 11.25 million shares at $16 on May 16, 2019. It opened on the NYSE the next day and closed at $23.99, up about 50 percent. In February 2020 Bergman handed the chief executive job to Joshua Bixby. The 2021 outage hit 85 percent of the network, and Fastly had 95 percent running normally within 49 minutes. Todd Nightingale, a Cisco executive, became chief executive in September 2022. Fastly still trades on the NYSE as FSLY.

cover.theme: a falcon (speed at the edge)

dek: Health Catalyst gave hospitals one place to pull their scattered records together and use the data to improve care.
lede: Health Catalyst's shares jumped 51 percent on the same July day that Livongo, another health tech company, made its debut. By 2019 American hospitals had spent billions moving patient records onto computers. The records sat in dozens of systems that did not talk to each other. Health Catalyst, a Salt Lake City company, sold a data platform and the analysts to make sense of it all. Its pitch was simple: use the data you already have to treat patients better for less.

sections.heading: A Three-Person Start
sections.body: Health Catalyst was founded in 2008 and is based in Salt Lake City. Dan Burton joined in January 2011 as an investor and adviser, when the company had three people. He later became chief executive. The bet was that hospitals would pay to pull clinical, financial and operational data into one warehouse. Health Catalyst sold that platform alongside services from its own analysts and improvement experts.

sections.heading: Up Fifty-One Percent
sections.body: Health Catalyst priced 7 million shares at $26 on July 24, 2019, above its $24 to $25 range. On Nasdaq the next day it reached $39.69 and closed at $39.17. In August 2025 the company said Burton would step down as chief executive. Ben Albert, who joined as president that September, took the top job. The company cut about 9 percent of its workforce in a restructuring. It still trades on Nasdaq as HCAT.

cover.theme: a woman on the mend by the sea (health care, getting better)

tagline: Ping An's Tech, Rented to Rival Banks
dek: OneConnect sold China's banks and insurers the cloud software Ping An had built for itself.
lede: OneConnect sold software to the rivals of its own biggest shareholder. The company began inside Ping An, the Chinese insurance and banking giant, as the group's fintech arm. It then packaged Ping An's systems for smaller banks and insurers across China. In December 2019 Chinese tech companies still listed in New York often, and fintech was a crowded field. OneConnect still had to cut its price and its size to get the deal done.

sections.heading: Born Inside Ping An
sections.body: OneConnect was founded in 2015 and is based in Shenzhen. It ran as a separate company within Ping An Group until November 2017, when Ping An stopped consolidating it. Ping An stayed a partner and its flagship customer. The bet was that thousands of Chinese financial firms could not build modern technology on their own. OneConnect offered them a core banking system, cloud platforms and other tools as a service.

sections.heading: A Flat Debut
sections.body: OneConnect first aimed to sell 36 million shares at $12 to $14 each. It settled for 31.2 million American depositary shares at $10, the top of a reduced range, and raised $312 million. The shares opened on the NYSE on December 13, 2019, and closed the first day at $10, unchanged. A Ping An subsidiary later offered to buy out the other shareholders. The deal closed in late 2025, and OneConnect left both the New York and Hong Kong exchanges.

cover.theme: a bridge (connecting banks to technology)

dek: Vertex worked out the right sales tax and VAT on every invoice, so big companies did not have to.
lede: Vertex took 42 years to go public, and it got there by doing one dull job well: sales tax. Every sale a large company makes can owe a different tax in each city, state and country. The rules change all the time. Vertex sold the software that kept track. By July 2020 the pandemic had pushed more shopping online, and tax rules for online sellers were growing more complex. Investors who wanted steady software revenue saw a rare old company coming to market.

sections.heading: A Consulting Shop in Pennsylvania
sections.body: Ray Westphal founded Vertex in 1978. It started as a small tax systems consulting firm and grew into a software company based in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania. The bet was that tax compliance was too complex for big companies to handle by hand. Vertex built engines that plug into a company's accounting and ordering systems. They calculate sales and use taxes and value-added taxes, and they handle filing and reporting.

sections.heading: Priced Above the Range
sections.body: Vertex priced 21.15 million shares at $19 on July 28, 2020, well above its $14 to $16 range. It raised $402 million and began trading on Nasdaq the next day as VERX. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal. The company kept growing as a subscription business. In 2026 it guided to between $825 million and $830 million in revenue. Vertex still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a mountain summit (the vertex)

tagline: From Memory Chips to Gaming Rigs
dek: Corsair sold the keyboards, mice, memory and cases that serious PC gamers and streamers build their setups with.
lede: Corsair started out making memory modules for computer makers, a part almost nobody ever saw. Twenty-six years later it went public as a brand that gamers showed off on their desks. In September 2020 millions of people were stuck at home, buying PCs, playing games and streaming them. Corsair sold the glowing keyboards, mice, headsets and parts for those setups. A private equity firm owned most of it, and the pandemic boom gave it a window to list.

sections.heading: Cache on a Stick
sections.body: Andy Paul, Don Lieberman and John Beekley founded Corsair Microsystems in Fremont, California, in January 1994. Its first products were cache modules sold to computer makers. When Intel moved that cache onto its processors, Corsair switched to memory modules. Later it turned to PC enthusiasts who tuned their machines for speed. From there it grew into power supplies, cases, cooling and gaming gear. In 2017 EagleTree Capital bought a majority stake for $525 million.

sections.heading: A Pandemic Listing
sections.body: Corsair priced 14 million shares at $17 on September 22, 2020, the middle of its $16 to $18 range. The company sold 7.5 million shares and EagleTree sold the rest, raising $238 million in all. At that price the company was worth about $1.5 billion. The stock began trading on Nasdaq the next day as CRSR. Corsair is now based in Milpitas, California. It still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: sailing warships (the corsair)

dek: C3.ai sold big companies and governments ready-made software for building and running AI applications.
lede: C3.ai went public under the stock ticker AI, and on its first day the shares more than doubled. The founder was Tom Siebel, who had built Siebel Systems into a $2 billion software company in the 1990s. In December 2020, investors were piling into anything that promised the next wave of software. Artificial intelligence was still mostly a lab word for the public. C3.ai offered a way for oil companies, utilities and the military to put it to work.

sections.heading: Three Name Changes
sections.body: Siebel founded the company in January 2009 as C3. The bet was that cloud computing, sensors and machine learning would remake how large companies ran, and that they would need one platform to build on. In 2016 the company became C3 IoT, for the internet of things. In June 2019 it changed its name again, to C3.ai. It sold large subscriptions to a short list of big customers, from its base in Redwood City, California.

sections.heading: Up 120 Percent
sections.body: C3.ai sold 15.5 million shares at $42 on December 8, 2020, above its $36 to $38 range, and raised about $651 million. On the NYSE the next day the stock closed at $92.49. Stephen Ehikian, a Salesforce veteran, became chief executive in September 2025, after Siebel stepped back for health reasons. In May 2026 Siebel returned as chief executive and Ehikian became president. C3.ai still trades on the NYSE as AI.

cover.theme: the head of a philosopher (machine intelligence)

tagline: Twenty Minutes to Sell a Used Car
dek: ACV let car dealers trade used cars with each other in 20-minute online auctions.
lede: ACV Auctions sold a used car to a dealer in 20 minutes, through an app. For generations dealers had traded cars at big physical auction yards, driving in to bid in person. ACV sent inspectors to the car instead and posted the report online. Buffalo, New York, was an unlikely place to start a tech marketplace. ACV went public in March 2021, after a year in which the pandemic had upended the dealers it served.

sections.heading: Starting in Buffalo
sections.body: ACV was incorporated in December 2014 and went live in Buffalo in 2015. The bet was that dealers would buy cars sight unseen if the inspection data was good enough. ACV built condition reports, then added transport, financing and assurance services on top. By the end of 2020 it covered 125 territories across the continental United States. That year 391,466 vehicles sold on its marketplace, worth $3.3 billion. Revenue was $208.4 million.

sections.heading: A Buyout by Copart
sections.body: ACV priced its offering at $25 a share in March 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as ACVA. It kept adding services such as transport and financing for dealers. In September 2026 Copart, the big salvage car auction company, agreed to buy ACV. Copart offered $10.50 a share in cash through a tender offer. The offer closed on October 15, 2026, and Copart took control. ACV's shares left Nasdaq that month.

cover.theme: an early motor car (the used-car trade)

dek: Alkami gave community banks and credit unions mobile and online banking as good as the giants offered.
lede: Alkami sold small banks the one thing they could not build: an app as good as Chase's. Community banks and credit unions held customers' trust, but their websites and phone apps lagged far behind. Customers noticed, and many drifted to the big banks. By April 2021 the pandemic had pushed even reluctant customers to bank on their phones. Alkami, based in Plano, Texas, went public with 151 banks and credit unions on its platform.

sections.heading: Leveling the Field
sections.body: Gary Nelson and Stephen Bohanon founded Alkami to level the playing field for smaller financial institutions. The company began business in 2009 and incorporated in Delaware in 2011. The bet was that banks would pay a subscription for one cloud platform that tied their old core systems to modern apps. Alkami linked more than 200 back-office and fintech tools behind a single login. By the end of 2020 it served nearly 9.7 million of its clients' customers.

sections.heading: Thirty Dollars a Share
sections.body: Alkami priced 6 million shares at $30 in April 2021 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as ALKT. Its prospectus cited an analysis that ranked it among the fastest-growing digital banking platforms in the United States, measured by registered users. New clients were also buying more: the 2020 group of new clients averaged 15 products each. Alkami still trades on Nasdaq as ALKT.

cover.theme: a small-town main street (community banking)

tagline: Software Born on a Job Site
dek: Procore put every drawing, change order and budget for a building project in one app the whole crew could share.
lede: Procore began because its founder could not find out what was happening on his own house. Tooey Courtemanche, a former carpenter turned tech founder, was building a home in Santa Barbara. Simple questions about what work was done, or where the budget stood, took days to answer. Construction was one of the largest industries in the world and one of the least digital. When Procore went public in May 2021, it was betting that builders were finally ready to trade paper for software.

sections.heading: A House in Santa Barbara
sections.body: Courtemanche started Procore in 2002, in Carpinteria, California, to fix the frustrations of his own building project. He wrote software that kept owners, general contractors, specialty contractors and architects on the same page. The bet was that construction firms would pay for one shared platform instead of a pile of spreadsheets, faxes and phone calls. Procore charged by the volume of construction work its customers ran through it, with unlimited users.

sections.heading: Nineteen Years to the NYSE
sections.body: Procore priced its offering at $67 a share and began trading on the NYSE on May 20, 2021. It raised about $634.5 million, and the shares closed the first day up more than 30 percent. Revenue reached $1.32 billion in 2025. Ajei Gopal later took over as chief executive, with Courtemanche as chairman. In July 2026 Procore agreed to buy DroneDeploy, a maker of drone mapping software. It still trades on the NYSE as PCOR.

cover.theme: a monument under construction (building the world)
cover.artwork: Sir Walter Scott's Monument, Edinburgh; as it appeared when nearly finished

dek: WalkMe laid step-by-step pop-up guides over business software, so employees could learn it without a manual.
lede: WalkMe started life in 2011 under the name Make Tutorial. Its idea fit in that name. Big companies spent fortunes on software that their own staff struggled to use. WalkMe laid a layer of pop-up tips and walkthroughs on top of those apps, guiding people click by click. By June 2021 the pandemic had sent office work online, and companies were rolling out new tools faster than ever. The Israeli company went public selling what it called digital adoption.

sections.heading: Make Tutorial, Renamed
sections.body: Dan Adika, Rafael Sweary, Eyal Cohen and Yuval Shalom Ozanna founded the company in Israel in October 2011. It became WalkMe in March 2012 and launched its product that April. The bet was that every company running big business software needed a guide that lived inside the screen. WalkMe sold it by subscription. By March 2021 it had about 2,000 customers in 42 countries, including 155 of the Fortune 500.

sections.heading: Bought by SAP
sections.body: WalkMe sold 9.25 million shares at $31 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as WKME in June 2021. Revenue had reached $148.3 million in 2020. By 2024 the shares traded far below the $31 offer price. In June 2024 SAP agreed to buy WalkMe for $14 a share in cash, about $1.5 billion. The deal closed in September 2024, and WalkMe left Nasdaq to become part of SAP.

cover.theme: a wilderness guide (showing the way)

dek: Xometry let engineers upload a part design, get an instant price, and have a machine shop make it.
lede: Xometry's founders saw people buying books online with a click and wanted custom metal parts to work the same way. An engineer who needed a machined bracket or a run of molded plastic usually phoned around for quotes and waited days. Xometry priced the job in seconds and routed it to a shop with spare capacity. By June 2021 supply chains were snarled and factories wanted flexible capacity. The Maryland company went public with a network of nearly 5,000 sellers.

sections.heading: NextLine Manufacturing
sections.body: Randy Altschuler and Laurence Zuriff founded the company in Gaithersburg, Maryland, in 2013, under the name NextLine Manufacturing. It became Xometry in June 2015. The bet was that the vast on-demand manufacturing business, local and barely digital, would move to an online marketplace. Xometry used its data to price jobs on the spot. It then added tools, supplies and financial services for the machine shops that did the work.

sections.heading: Fifty Percent on Day One
sections.body: Xometry priced its offering at $44 a share on June 29, 2021, and raised about $300 million. Its shares began trading on Nasdaq the next day and rose more than 50 percent. Revenue reached about $687 million in 2025. In July 2026 Sanjeev Singh Sahni became chief executive, and Altschuler became executive chairman. The company is now based in North Bethesda, Maryland. It still trades on Nasdaq as XMTR.

cover.theme: a blacksmith's shop (making parts to order)

dek: VTEX gave big brands and retailers the cloud software to run online stores and marketplaces in many countries at once.
lede: VTEX promised the world's largest retailer an online store in Brazil within eight months, from kickoff to launch. It delivered, and the Walmart project shaped everything that followed. The two engineers who founded VTEX in Rio de Janeiro decided big companies needed a commerce platform they could switch on, not build from scratch. When VTEX went public in July 2021, the pandemic had pushed shoppers online across Latin America, and it served over 2,000 customers in 32 countries.

sections.heading: Two Engineers from Rio
sections.body: Geraldo do Carmo Thomaz Júnior and Mariano Gomide de Faria, both mechanical engineering graduates of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, started VTEX's operations in Brazil in 2000. They ran it as co-chief executives. The bet was that enterprises wanted speed to market more than custom code. VTEX built a cloud platform with marketplace features at its core. It opened its first office outside Brazil in 2013 and reached the United States in 2017.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars a Share
sections.body: VTEX priced its offering at $19 a share in July 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as VTEX. Customers on the platform included Whirlpool, which used it to run online stores in Latin America, its largest online market. By the end of 2025 VTEX served 2,200 customers and 3,100 active online stores across 44 countries. It still trades on the NYSE as VTEX.

cover.theme: the bay of Rio de Janeiro (its birthplace)
cover.artwork: Rio Jnhomerim in the Bay of Rio de Janeiro, plate two from Landscapes

dek: Sportradar sold live sports data to betting companies and media, and watched games for signs of match fixing.
lede: Sportradar started in Norway as software that collected betting odds from online sportsbooks. Twenty years later it fed live game data to bookmakers, broadcasters and leagues around the world. In 2021 American states were legalizing sports betting one after another, and the NBA, MLB and NHL wanted partners who could sell their data safely. Sportradar held many of those rights. Its founder still controlled most of the votes when it listed in New York.

sections.heading: From Trondheim to St. Gallen
sections.body: Petter Fornæss and Tore Steinkjer built the first software in Trondheim, Norway, in 2001, under the name Market Monitor. Carsten Koerl, a veteran of early online betting, became a major investor and later chief executive. The bet was that betting companies would pay for fast, accurate data and that leagues would pay for protection against match fixing. Sportradar won betting data rights from the NBA, MLB and NHL. It moved its base to St. Gallen, Switzerland.

sections.heading: Koerl Keeps Control
sections.body: Sportradar sold 19 million shares at $27 in September 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as SRAD on September 14. The offering valued it at about $8 billion. After the deal Koerl held about 82 percent of the voting power. The company kept adding league partners, including a ten-year NHL deal signed in 2021. It reported about €1.29 billion in revenue for 2025. Sportradar still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a day at the races (sports and betting)

tagline: Built in a House Without Water
dek: GitLab gave software teams one app to store code, review it, test it and ship it.
lede: GitLab was written in a house in Ukraine with no running water. In 2011 Dmitriy Zaporozhets decided that a good tool for working together on code mattered more than his daily trip to the communal well. A Dutch programmer, Sid Sijbrandij, found the project online a year later. By the time GitLab went public in October 2021, it had no headquarters office at all. Every one of its employees worked remotely, and it was one of the largest all-remote companies in the world.

sections.heading: Code by the Well
sections.body: Zaporozhets released GitLab as an open-source project in 2011. Sijbrandij discovered it from his home in the Netherlands in 2012 and began building a business around it. The company was incorporated in Delaware in September 2014. The bet was that developers wanted one application for the whole software life cycle, from planning to deployment. GitLab gave away a free community edition and sold paid tiers with more features.

sections.heading: Seventy-Seven Dollars a Share
sections.body: GitLab priced its offering at $77 a share and began trading on Nasdaq as GTLB on October 14, 2021. It raised about $650 million, and the stock closed its first day well above the offer price. Sijbrandij later handed the chief executive role to Bill Staples and stayed on as chairman. GitLab reported more than 10,000 customers paying at least $5,000 a year. It still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a badger (GitLab's tanuki)
cover.artwork: Badger, from the series "Mirror of Stone Rubbings of Views of the Provinces"

tagline: Snap the Receipt, Skip the Report
dek: Expensify let workers snap a photo of a receipt and file their expense report without the paperwork.
lede: "The next 100 years are going to be nuts," David Barrett wrote at the top of his letter in Expensify's prospectus. Few founders open an IPO filing that way. Barrett had built a company around a chore everyone hated: the expense report. Employees photographed receipts, and Expensify turned them into reports their bosses could approve. By November 2021 an average of 639,000 paid members across 53,000 companies used it each quarter, and tech stocks were near their peak.

sections.heading: A Chore Worth Fixing
sections.body: Barrett had led engineering at Red Swoosh, a file-sharing startup that Akamai bought in 2007. He founded Expensify in 2008, and it was incorporated in April 2009. The bet was that small and midsize businesses would adopt a tool their employees chose for themselves, then pay for it. Expensify connected to QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite and other accounting systems. In early 2020 it launched the Expensify Card to earn money on spending itself.

sections.heading: A Long Slide
sections.body: Expensify priced its offering at $27 a share in November 2021 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as EXFY. The offering raised about $263 million and valued the company near $3.87 billion after a strong debut. Then the market for small-cap software turned. The stock has since fallen more than 95 percent from its debut. Barrett still runs the company from Portland, Oregon, and it still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a traveling trunk (business travel and its receipts)

dek: Arm designed the energy-sipping chip blueprints that nearly every smartphone, and many other devices, are built on.
lede: Arm's chip designs were inside more than 99 percent of the world's smartphones, yet Arm made no chips at all. It licensed blueprints to the companies that did, and collected a royalty on each one sold. More than 250 billion Arm-based chips had shipped by the time it filed. In September 2023 the AI boom had made chips the hottest corner of the market. SoftBank, which had bought Arm seven years earlier, brought it back to the public markets.

sections.heading: Acorn, Apple and VLSI
sections.body: Arm began in Cambridge, England, in November 1990 as a joint venture of Acorn Computers, Apple and VLSI Technology. Its job was to design processors that used little power. The bet was to sell designs, not silicon, and let partners build the chips. That model put Arm in phones, cars, sensors and servers. SoftBank bought Arm in 2016 for about £24 billion and took it private.

sections.heading: SoftBank Sells a Slice
sections.body: In 2020 Nvidia agreed to buy Arm for about $40 billion. Regulators in Europe, Britain and the United States pushed back, and the deal fell apart in February 2022. SoftBank chose an IPO instead. It sold 95.5 million American depositary shares at $51 each, and Arm listed on Nasdaq on September 14, 2023. The sale raised $4.87 billion at a $54.5 billion valuation, and SoftBank kept about 90 percent. Arm still trades on Nasdaq as ARM.

cover.theme: studies of an arm (the name, and the reach)
cover.artwork: Study of a Nude Seen from the Back, and Two Studies of an Arm

dek: OneStream gave finance chiefs one platform to close the books, plan budgets and report results.
lede: OneStream's founders had already built the software most big finance teams used, then watched it get bought. Tom Shea's first company, UpStream, was acquired by Hyperion. There he worked with Craig Colby and Bob Powers, who had been key to building Hyperion's financial management product. Their new company set out to replace the patchwork of tools that grew up around it. By July 2024 OneStream had 1,423 customers and was controlled by KKR when it went public.

sections.heading: Starting Over in Michigan
sections.body: Shea, Colby and Powers formed OneStream in 2012, based in Birmingham, Michigan. They launched with a single customer, a global company worth billions. The bet was that the office of the chief financial officer wanted consolidation, planning, reporting and reconciliation on one platform instead of many. OneStream sold it as a cloud subscription. KKR bought a majority stake in 2019. The company passed $450 million in annual recurring revenue in 2023.

sections.heading: Bought Out by Hg
sections.body: OneStream sold 24.5 million shares at $20 in July 2024 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as OS. Once the deal closed, KKR held about 52 percent of the voting power. In January 2026 OneStream agreed to be acquired by affiliates of Hg, the software investor. Shareholders received $24 a share in cash. The deal closed on April 1, 2026, and OneStream left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a single brook running through a gorge (one stream of data)

tagline: A Broken Leg and a Torn ACL
dek: Hinge Health gave people with back, joint and muscle pain physical therapy at home, guided by an app.
lede: Hinge Health's two founders each spent a year in rehab. Daniel Perez broke his arm and leg in a bike crash. Gabriel Mecklenburg tore his ACL on the judo mat. Both liked their physical therapists but struggled to keep up with the appointments. Their company turned physical therapy into an app, sensors and a remote care team. By May 2025 employers were hunting for ways to cut spending on back and joint pain. Hinge Health went public that month.

sections.heading: Physical Therapy by Phone
sections.body: Perez and Mecklenburg built Hinge Health around their own recoveries. They launched their first U.S. client in 2016, selling to employers and health plans. The bet was that most musculoskeletal care could be delivered at home. Members exercise while TrueMotion, the company's AI motion tracking, checks their form. A wearable device called Enso eases pain with electrical nerve stimulation. Licensed physical therapists and health coaches oversee the plan.

sections.heading: Thirty-Two Dollars a Share
sections.body: Hinge Health priced 13.7 million shares at $32 in May 2025 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as HNGE. Revenue had reached $390 million in 2024, up 33 percent. The founders kept voting control through a dual-class share structure. The company is based in San Francisco, with offices in Montreal and Bangalore. It reports about 25 million contracted lives and still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: acrobats on a ladder (bodies in motion)

dek: Klarna let shoppers get their order first and pay for it later, in installments.
lede: Klarna started in 2005 with a simple promise: get the goods first, pay afterward. Three young founders in Stockholm called it Kreditor, taking the credit and fraud risk off merchants' hands. Two decades later the Swedish company served about 111 million shoppers and 790,000 merchants in 26 countries. It had also become a loud voice on AI, saying an assistant did the work of 700 customer service agents. In September 2025 it finally went public in New York.

sections.heading: From Kreditor to Klarna
sections.body: Sebastian Siemiatkowski, Niklas Adalberth and Victor Jacobsson founded the company in Stockholm with help from the Stockholm School of Economics' business incubator. Angel investor Jane Walerud offered SEK 600,000 for 10 percent early on. The name changed to Klarna in 2009. The bet was that shoppers would buy more if they could pay later, and that merchants would pay Klarna for the extra sales. It grew into a shopping app, a card and a bank.

sections.heading: Forty Dollars a Share
sections.body: Klarna priced 34.3 million shares at $40 and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as KLAR on September 10, 2025. Klarna itself sold 5 million of them, and existing shareholders sold the rest. Siemiatkowski, still chief executive, kept special high-vote shares. By 2026 Klarna reported more than 119 million active consumers and more than one million merchants. It still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a hat shop counter (shopping, buy now, pay later)

dek: Quantinuum builds quantum computers from trapped atoms, aimed at problems ordinary computers struggle to solve.
lede: Quantinuum's computers hold single charged atoms in place with electric fields and work with them using lasers. Its Helios machine has 98 of these trapped-ion qubits. In June 2026 quantum computing was moving from physics labs toward real customers, and investors were eager for a pure play backed by a big industrial name. Honeywell owned a large stake. The company listed on Nasdaq that month at a valuation of about $17.6 billion.

sections.heading: Hardware Meets Software
sections.body: Quantinuum was formed in 2021 by combining Honeywell Quantum Solutions with Cambridge Quantum, a software company. Both had started in 2014. The bet was that one company owning both the machines and the software would reach useful quantum computing first. It built the H-Series trapped-ion computers and software such as TKET and InQuanto. Its research teams published work on error correction and logical qubits. It has bases in Broomfield, Colorado, and Cambridge, England.

sections.heading: Sixty Dollars a Share
sections.body: Quantinuum sold 28 million shares at $60 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as QNT in June 2026. The shares opened at $68.
