Rajeeb Hazra, chief executive since 2023, led the company to market. Honeywell kept about 48 percent of the voting power. In May 2026 it agreed to terms with the Commerce Department for up to $100 million in CHIPS Act funding, paid for in stock. It trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a rainbow (light split into its states)

dek: Salesforce let sales teams track every customer in a web browser, with nothing to install and a monthly bill.
lede: Salesforce's logo was the word "software" inside a red circle with a line through it. The company sold a tool for tracking customers and deals, and it ran entirely on the web. Customers paid by the month and never installed a thing. When it filed to go public in December 2003, the dot-com crash was still fresh, and most big companies still bought software on discs with large upfront licenses.

sections.heading: An Oracle Man's Apartment
sections.body: Marc Benioff was a senior executive at Oracle when he started Salesforce in 1999 with Parker Harris, Dave Moellenhoff, and Frank Dominguez. They built the first version in a San Francisco apartment. The bet was that business software could work like a website. Salesforce would host everything, fix bugs once for every customer, and charge a subscription. Rivals sold the same kind of tool as a license, plus months of installation work.

sections.heading: Two Price Hikes, Then a Pop
sections.body: Demand pushed Salesforce to raise its price range twice. It priced at $11 a share on June 22, 2004, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as CRM. The stock closed its first day at $17.20, up 56 percent. Salesforce then grew into one of the largest software companies in the world. It bought Tableau in 2019 and Slack in 2021, and it still trades on the NYSE as CRM.

cover.theme: clouds over the sea (the cloud)

tagline: Drag a Column, Draw a Chart
dek: Tableau let ordinary office workers turn a spreadsheet into a chart by dragging and dropping, with no code.
lede: Tableau listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker DATA, and one of its founders had built rendering software at Pixar. The Seattle company made software that turned rows of numbers into charts and maps as fast as a person could drag a mouse. When it went public in May 2013, companies were drowning in data from the web, and most of it sat in reports that only analysts could build.

sections.heading: A Stanford Lab Project
sections.body: Tableau grew out of a Stanford research project. Chris Stolte, a graduate student, worked with professor Pat Hanrahan on a way to turn a database query into a picture. Hanrahan had earlier worked at Pixar on its RenderMan software. Christian Chabot, a Stanford MBA, joined them to found the company in 2003. Their bet was that people who knew the business best should explore the data themselves, without waiting for the IT department.

sections.heading: A 64 Percent First Day
sections.body: Tableau priced at $31 a share on May 16, 2013, above a range it had already raised. The stock opened at $47 and closed at $50.75, up 64 percent. Marketo also soared that day. Six years later, Salesforce agreed to buy Tableau in an all-stock deal worth about $15.7 billion. The deal closed in August 2019, and Tableau's stock left the NYSE.

cover.theme: a star chart (a picture made from data)
cover.artwork: Celestial Map of the Northern Sky with the Twelve Zodiac Signs

dek: Atlassian sold Jira and Confluence to software teams cheaply online, and let the tools spread through companies on their own.
lede: Atlassian went public in New York with almost no sales force. Two university friends in Sydney had built a company that sold Jira and Confluence on its website at low prices, and teams bought them with a credit card. The tools spread from one team to the next. When Atlassian filed in November 2015, it was a rare Australian tech company listing in the United States, and enterprise software usually came with a large sales team attached.

sections.heading: Two Friends and a Credit Card
sections.body: Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar met at the University of New South Wales. They founded Atlassian in Sydney in 2002 and funded it with about A$10,000 on a credit card. Their first big product, Jira, tracked bugs and tasks for software teams. Confluence, a shared wiki, followed. The bet was that good, cheap tools sold online would find their own buyers. Atlassian spent its money on product instead of salespeople.

sections.heading: TEAM on the Nasdaq
sections.body: Atlassian priced at $21 a share on December 9, 2015, above its range, and listed on the Nasdaq as TEAM. The stock closed its first day at $27.78, up 32 percent, and the company was worth about $5.8 billion. In 2022 Atlassian moved its legal home from the United Kingdom to the United States. Farquhar stepped down as co-CEO in 2024, and the company still trades on the Nasdaq as TEAM.

cover.theme: Atlas holding up the world (the titan behind the name)

dek: Spotify let people play almost any song on demand, free with ads or for a monthly fee.
lede: Spotify went public without selling a single new share. Most companies hire banks to price an offering and hand stock to big investors. Spotify simply let its existing shares start trading on the New York Stock Exchange, a direct listing. The Swedish streaming service filed in February 2018, when music piracy had faded and paying a monthly fee for every song had become normal. Spotify had done much to make it so.

sections.heading: A Better Deal Than Piracy
sections.body: Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon founded Spotify in Stockholm in 2006. File-sharing sites had gutted music sales. Their bet was that a free, legal service that played songs instantly could beat piracy, and that some listeners would pay to drop the ads. Spotify signed licenses with the major record labels. Those royalty deals became its largest cost, and its subscribers became its main source of revenue.

sections.heading: $132, Then $165.90
sections.body: The NYSE set a reference price of $132 a share the night before trading began on April 3, 2018. Spotify opened at $165.90 under the ticker SPOT and closed at $149.01. The direct listing raised no money for the company, and it became a model that Slack and others later followed. Spotify added podcasts and audiobooks, and it still trades on the NYSE as SPOT.

cover.theme: a street musician cranking a hurdy-gurdy (music on demand)

dek: Lyft let anyone with a phone call a ride from a nearby driver in a personal car.
lede: Lyft's first cars wore fuzzy pink mustaches on their grilles, and riders were told to sit up front and fist-bump the driver. By March 2019 the mustaches were gone and Lyft was racing Uber to the stock market. It won by about six weeks. The San Francisco company was the first ride-hailing app to go public in the United States, and investors were still guessing whether the business could ever turn a profit.

sections.heading: From Zimride to Lyft
sections.body: Logan Green and John Zimmer first built Zimride in 2007, a carpool board for college students making long trips. In 2012 they launched Lyft, which matched riders with nearby drivers for short trips across town. The bet was that ordinary people would share their own cars with strangers if an app handled the payment and the trust. Lyft focused on the United States and Canada while Uber spread worldwide.

sections.heading: A Pop That Faded
sections.body: Lyft priced at $72 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq as LYFT on March 29, 2019. It opened at $87.24 and closed at $78.29, up 8.7 percent. Within days the stock fell below its offering price. Green and Zimmer stepped back from running the company in 2023. In 2025 Lyft bought FreeNow, a European taxi app, and it still trades on the Nasdaq as LYFT.

cover.theme: a hansom cab (a ride for hire)

dek: Revolve sold young shoppers the clothes they saw on Instagram, picked by data and promoted by influencers.
lede: Revolve paid Instagram stars to wear its dresses before most brands knew what an influencer was. The Los Angeles-area retailer flew them to resorts and festivals, and their followers bought the looks online. Revolve chose what to stock by watching sales data closely. When it went public in June 2019, shopping malls were closing across the country, and Revolve was selling to millennial women almost entirely through their phones.

sections.heading: Two Engineers Sell Dresses
sections.body: Michael Mente and Mike Karanikolas founded Revolve in 2003. Both came from technology, not fashion. Their bet was that an online store could read its own data better than a department store buyer could read a runway. Revolve tracked what sold and reordered fast. It later built its own house brands and launched FWRD for luxury labels. Its marketing leaned on a large network of social media influencers.

sections.heading: An 89 Percent First Day
sections.body: Revolve priced at $18 a share, the top of its range, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as RVLV on June 7, 2019. The stock opened about 40 percent higher and closed its first day at $34, up 89 percent. It was one of the year's best debuts. Mente and Karanikolas still run the company as co-CEOs, and Revolve still trades on the NYSE as RVLV.

cover.theme: a society portrait in an evening gown (the look of the season)

dek: Dynatrace watched over companies' software and told engineers what broke, where, and why, before customers noticed.
lede: Dynatrace started in Linz, Austria, changed owners twice, and reached the stock market as a private equity spinout. Its software watched every request moving through a company's apps and servers, then pointed to the cause when something slowed down. When it went public in August 2019, businesses were moving to the cloud, and their software had become a tangle of small services that no human could monitor alone.

sections.heading: From Linz to Thoma Bravo
sections.body: Bernd Greifeneder founded Dynatrace in Linz in 2005 to trace slow transactions through complex software. Compuware, the Detroit software company, bought it in 2011. In 2014 the private equity firm Thoma Bravo took Compuware private for about $2.4 billion and later set Dynatrace up on its own. The new bet was a single platform that used automation to find the root cause of a problem across a whole cloud system.

sections.heading: A 49 Percent Jump
sections.body: Dynatrace priced at $16 a share, above a range it had raised, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as DT on August 1, 2019. The stock closed its first day at $23.85, up 49 percent. Thoma Bravo kept a controlling stake and sold down over the following years. Dynatrace kept buying smaller tools, including DevCycle in 2026, and it still trades on the NYSE as DT.

cover.theme: a lighthouse (watching over the traffic)

tagline: Air Mattresses to a Pandemic IPO
dek: Airbnb let travelers stay in strangers' homes and let hosts earn money from a spare room or an empty house.
lede: Airbnb began with three air mattresses on a San Francisco apartment floor, rented to guests during a design conference. Twelve years later it went public in the middle of a pandemic that had stopped travel cold. In the spring of 2020 bookings collapsed and the company cut about a quarter of its staff. By the time it filed in November, people were renting cabins and beach houses close to home, and Airbnb had bounced back.

sections.heading: Cereal Boxes and Spare Rooms
sections.body: Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia were roommates who could not cover their rent. They rented out air mattresses in 2007, then founded the company with Nathan Blecharczyk in 2008. Early on, they kept it alive by selling election-themed cereal boxes. The bet was that strangers would trust each other enough to share a home, if reviews, photos, and payments made it feel safe. Investors doubted it for years.

sections.heading: Doubled by Lunch
sections.body: Airbnb priced at $68 a share on December 9, 2020, and began trading on the Nasdaq as ABNB the next day. It opened at $146, more than double the offer price, and closed at $144.71, up 112 percent. The debut valued it at about $86.5 billion. Airbnb joined the S&P 500 in 2023, and it still trades on the Nasdaq as ABNB.

cover.theme: a cottage (a home to stay in)

dek: BigCommerce gave merchants an online store they could run without building or hosting the software themselves.
lede: BigCommerce's stock opened at nearly three times its offering price, then got halted for volatility within minutes. It was August 2020. The pandemic had shut stores, and every shop that wanted to survive needed to sell online. BigCommerce rented those shops their storefront software. It was smaller than its Canadian rival Shopify, and it pitched itself to larger brands that wanted more control over how their stores worked.

sections.heading: From Sydney to Austin
sections.body: Eddie Machaalani and Mitchell Harper founded BigCommerce in Sydney in 2009, after building online software together. The company later moved its headquarters to Austin, Texas. The bet was that merchants wanted a hosted store they could switch on fast, with an open design that let them plug in other tools. BigCommerce sold to small sellers and to well-known brands that had outgrown simpler platforms.

sections.heading: From BIGC to CMRC
sections.body: BigCommerce priced at $24 a share, above a range it had already raised, and began trading on the Nasdaq as BIGC on August 5, 2020. It opened near $68 and closed at $72.27, up 201 percent. The gains did not last as online shopping cooled. In 2025 the company renamed itself Commerce.com and changed its ticker to CMRC. In April 2026 Rezolve Ai made an unsolicited bid, and the board adopted a rights plan.

cover.theme: a market square (a place to sell)

dek: Bentley made the software engineers use to design and run roads, bridges, rail lines, and power plants.
lede: Bentley Systems filed to go public in 2002, pulled back, and stayed private for 18 more years. The family company from Exton, Pennsylvania, made software that engineers used to design roads, bridges, water systems, and plants. Its tools were deep inside the world's infrastructure and almost unknown outside it. When it finally listed in September 2020, governments were talking about large new infrastructure spending and digital models of whole cities.

sections.heading: MicroStation and the Brothers
sections.body: Keith and Barry Bentley founded the company in 1984. Keith wrote MicroStation, a design program for engineers, and his brothers Greg and Ray later joined the business. The bet was that civil engineers needed their own software, separate from the general drafting tools most designers used. Bentley sold to engineering firms, transit agencies, and utilities. Over the years it bought dozens of specialist tools for bridges, pipes, and geology.

sections.heading: Thirty-Six Years to Nasdaq
sections.body: Bentley priced at $22 a share on September 22, 2020, and began trading on the Nasdaq as BSY the next day. Only existing shareholders sold stock, so the company raised no new money. The shares rose about 52 percent on the first day. The Bentley family kept voting control. Greg Bentley handed the CEO role to Nicholas Cumins in 2024, and Bentley still trades on the Nasdaq as BSY.

cover.theme: engineers restoring an aqueduct (infrastructure)
cover.artwork: Restoration of the Aqueduct of Pisa, from The Life of Ferdinand de' Medici

dek: PubMatic let websites and apps sell their ad space to the highest bidder, in the split second a page loads.
lede: PubMatic made money in ad tech, a business known for burning cash. The company ran auctions for publishers: each time a page or app loaded, advertisers bid for the slot, and PubMatic's software picked a winner in milliseconds. It ran much of that work on its own servers to keep costs low. When it went public in December 2020, the pandemic had pushed more people online, and ad budgets were moving to streaming TV and apps.

sections.heading: Working for the Seller
sections.body: Brothers Rajeev and Amar Goel founded PubMatic in 2006 with Anand Das and Mukul Kumar. Much of its engineering team worked in Pune, India. Most ad tech firms worked for the buyers, the brands and agencies placing ads. PubMatic's bet was the other side of the trade. It worked for publishers, helping them earn more from every visit by putting their ad space in front of many buyers at once.

sections.heading: A Profitable Debut
sections.body: PubMatic priced at $20 a share, above its range of $16 to $18, and began trading on the Nasdaq as PUBM on December 9, 2020. The stock rose sharply on its first day. PubMatic was already profitable when it filed. It went on to sell more ads on connected TV and in mobile apps, and it still trades on the Nasdaq as PUBM.

cover.theme: a newspaper stall (publishers and their pages)

tagline: The Survey Company That Went Public Twice
dek: Qualtrics let companies ask customers and employees how they felt, then showed them what to fix.
lede: Qualtrics was days from its first IPO in November 2018 when SAP bought it for $8 billion. Two years later SAP took it public anyway. The Utah company sold survey software, then rebranded the idea as experience management: measuring how customers, workers, and patients felt about a product or a job. When it listed in January 2021, the pandemic had sent offices home, and employers were desperate to know how their people were doing.

sections.heading: A Father's Survey Idea
sections.body: Scott Smith, a marketing professor, wanted better online survey tools for his research. His son Ryan left school to help build them, and with Jared Smith and Stuart Orgill they founded Qualtrics in 2002, working from a basement in Utah. Universities were the first customers. The bet was that every business would want to run its own research, fast and online, without hiring a market research firm.

sections.heading: SAP's Spin, Silver Lake's Buy
sections.body: Qualtrics priced at $30 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq as XM on January 28, 2021. It closed its first day at $45.50, up about 52 percent. SAP kept a majority stake. In 2023 SAP sold Qualtrics to Silver Lake and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board for about $12.5 billion, or $18.15 a share, and the stock left the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a land survey of the American West (the survey)
cover.artwork: Geographical Explorations and Surveys West of the 100th Meridian

dek: DigitalOcean rented simple cloud servers to developers and small businesses at low, flat prices.
lede: DigitalOcean let a developer rent a server for $5 a month and have it running in under a minute. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google fought over giant companies with long contracts. DigitalOcean went after the solo coder, the startup, and the small business, and it won them with plain prices and free tutorials. When it went public in March 2021, it was the rare cloud company small enough that its customers could read their own bill.

sections.heading: Brothers, Droplets, and Tutorials
sections.body: Ben and Moisey Uretsky founded DigitalOcean in New York in 2011 with Mitch Wainer, Jeff Carr, and Alec Hartman. The brothers had run a web hosting business before. They called each server a droplet. The bet was that millions of developers wanted a cloud that was simple and cheap, without the hundreds of services big providers sold. Its free how-to guides drew huge search traffic and brought in new customers.

sections.heading: A Drop on Day One
sections.body: DigitalOcean priced at $47 a share, the top of its range, raising about $775 million. It began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as DOCN on March 24, 2021. It opened at $41.50 and closed at $42.50, down about 10 percent. In 2023 it bought Paperspace to rent graphics chips for AI work, and DigitalOcean still trades on the NYSE as DOCN.

cover.theme: small boats on a big sea (the ocean)

dek: TuSimple built software to let big freight trucks drive themselves on long highway routes.
lede: TuSimple was the first self-driving truck company to sell shares on a U.S. exchange. Its software used cameras, radar, and lidar to steer heavy trucks on long highway runs across the Southwest. Trucking companies faced a shortage of drivers, and investors were pouring money into anything autonomous. When TuSimple went public in April 2021, it had test trucks hauling freight in Arizona and Texas, still with safety drivers in the cab.

sections.heading: Highways Before City Streets
sections.body: Xiaodi Hou and Mo Chen founded TuSimple in 2015, with offices in San Diego and China. Most self-driving efforts chased robotaxis on busy city streets. TuSimple's bet was simpler roads. Long, straight highways between freight hubs had fewer surprises than downtown traffic, and every mile without a human driver saved real money. It partnered with truck makers and shipping companies to build a freight network.

sections.heading: Flat Debut, Hard Fall
sections.body: TuSimple priced at $40 a share, above its range, and began trading on the Nasdaq as TSP on April 15, 2021. It closed its first day at exactly $40. In 2022 the board removed Hou as CEO amid a federal review of the company's ties to a Chinese startup. TuSimple wound down its U.S. trucking work, delisted from the Nasdaq in 2024, and renamed itself CreateAI.

cover.theme: a long mountain road with travelers (the open highway)

tagline: One Job Post, Every Job Board
dek: ZipRecruiter let small businesses post a job once, send it everywhere, and get matched with good candidates.
lede: ZipRecruiter started as a side project: four friends wanted a way to post one job to dozens of job boards at once. It grew into a marketplace that used software to match employers with job seekers, and it spent heavily on TV ads to reach small businesses. When it went public in May 2021, the economy was reopening, employers were struggling to hire, and help-wanted signs hung in shop windows across the country.

sections.heading: Built for the Small Employer
sections.body: Ian Siegel, Ward Poulos, Joe Edmonds, and Willis Guo founded ZipRecruiter in Santa Monica in 2010. Big companies had recruiters and expensive hiring software. A dentist or a plumber hiring one person did not. ZipRecruiter's bet was that small employers would pay a simple fee to post a job widely and have the software rank applicants for them. It paid for growth with radio and TV ads.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing
sections.body: ZipRecruiter went public through a direct listing on the New York Stock Exchange on May 26, 2021, selling no new shares. The NYSE set a reference price of $18, the stock opened at $19.80, and it closed at $21.10, up 17 percent. Hiring cooled after 2022, and revenue shrank. By August 2026 the shares traded below $5, and ZipRecruiter still trades on the NYSE as ZIP.

cover.theme: workmen at a quarry (people at work)

tagline: An Ad Company Built From Acquisitions
dek: Nexxen sold video and TV advertising software to both the brands buying ads and the publishers selling them.
lede: Nexxen has carried three names. It began as Taptica, a mobile ad firm listed in London, then became Tremor International after buying Tremor Video. When it sold shares in New York in June 2021, as Tremor, it was an Israeli ad tech company already trading on London's AIM market. Streaming TV was pulling ad money away from cable, and Tremor wanted to reach the deeper pool of American investors.

sections.heading: Buying Both Sides
sections.body: The company grew mostly by buying other businesses. It took over Tremor Video's buyer-side business in 2017. In 2020 it bought Unruly, a video ad marketplace, from News Corp. The bet was that one company should serve both ends of a video ad: the brands paying for it and the publishers showing it. Owning both sides meant more data and a larger cut of each ad sold.

sections.heading: From TRMR to NEXN
sections.body: Tremor priced its U.S. offering at $19 per American depositary share on June 17, 2021, and its shares began trading on the Nasdaq as TRMR the next day. In 2022 it bought Amobee from Singtel. The company renamed itself Nexxen in 2023. In February 2025 it left London's AIM market, and Nexxen now trades only on the Nasdaq as NEXN.

cover.theme: the 1906 San Francisco earthquake (Tremor, its old name)

tagline: Checking That a Human Saw It
dek: Integral Ad Science told brands whether their online ads were seen by real people, in safe places.
lede: Online advertisers had a problem they could not see: many of their ads loaded below the fold, beside ugly content, or in front of bots. Integral Ad Science sold them the evidence. Its software checked each ad for viewability, brand safety, and fraud, and reported back. When IAS went public in June 2021, ad spending was surging after the pandemic slump, and big brands wanted proof their money reached actual human eyes.

sections.heading: An Auditor for Ads
sections.body: IAS was founded in New York in 2009, as brands moved more of their budgets to automated ad buying. In that system, a brand might never know which site showed its ad. The bet was that advertisers would pay an independent referee to check every placement. IAS grew into one of the main ad verification firms, with DoubleVerify as its chief rival. The private equity firm Vista Equity Partners took control in 2018.

sections.heading: From Vista to Novacap
sections.body: IAS priced at $18 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq as IAS on June 30, 2021. The stock closed its first day up about 14 percent, valuing the company near $3.3 billion. Its shares later slid as growth slowed. In December 2025 the Canadian private equity firm Novacap took IAS private for $10.30 a share in cash, valuing it at about $1.9 billion.

cover.theme: an old man with a magnifying glass (verification)
cover.artwork: Old Man with a Book, Old Man with a Magnifying Glass, Old Man Holding a Medallion

dek: DISCO let lawyers search, sort, and review mountains of documents and email for lawsuits, using cloud software.
lede: DISCO listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker LAW. The Austin company sold software for e-discovery, the slow and costly work of reviewing every email and file that might matter in a lawsuit. Law firms had long paid armies of junior lawyers and outside vendors to do it. When DISCO went public in July 2021, cloud software stocks were near their peak and legal tech was still a small corner of the market.

sections.heading: Built by a Lawyer
sections.body: Kiwi Camara, a lawyer, co-founded DISCO and ran it as CEO. The company was founded in 2013 and based in Austin, Texas. Its bet was that the cloud and machine learning could shrink document review, letting a small team search millions of records quickly and flag the ones that mattered. DISCO charged by the amount of data a case used, so big lawsuits meant big bills.

sections.heading: LAW on the Big Board
sections.body: DISCO priced at $32 a share on July 20, 2021, above a range it had already raised. It began trading on the NYSE as LAW the next day and traded above $42 that afternoon. The shares later fell hard as growth slowed. Eric Friedrichsen replaced Camara as CEO, and in June 2026 the stock traded under $4. DISCO still trades on the NYSE as LAW.

cover.theme: the old gate of the Palace of Justice (the law)
cover.artwork: The Old Gate of the Palace of Justice, Paris

dek: Definitive Healthcare sold data on hospitals, doctors, and clinics to the companies trying to sell to them.
lede: Definitive Healthcare's stock opened 38 percent above its offering price, and five years later its largest backer offered about a dollar a share. The Massachusetts company sold a database of the U.S. healthcare system: which hospitals had which equipment, which doctors performed which procedures, and who made the buying decisions. Drug makers, device companies, and staffing firms used it to find customers. It went public in September 2021, when healthcare data was a hot investment theme.

sections.heading: Who Buys in a Hospital
sections.body: Jason Krantz founded Definitive Healthcare in 2011 and led it as CEO. Selling to hospitals was hard. Decisions were spread across departments, and public data was scattered and messy. The bet was that a single, constantly updated database of providers, procedures, and contacts would save sales teams months of guesswork. The private equity firm Advent International took a majority stake in 2019 before the IPO.

sections.heading: From $27 to a Buyout Bid
sections.body: Definitive priced at $27 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq as DH in September 2021, opening at $37.25. Growth slowed, the company took large write-downs, and the stock sank. In September 2026 Advent proposed taking it private at $1.02 a share, and a special committee of the board began reviewing the offer. Clay Ritchey became CEO that month. DH still trades on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a portrait of the physician Vesalius (the doctors in the data)
cover.artwork: Portrait of Doctor Andreas Vesalius of Brussels

fate: Taken private by TPG and Corpay, 2025 ($2.2B)
dek: AvidXchange let midsize companies receive, approve, and pay their bills electronically instead of shuffling paper and checks.
lede: Millions of American businesses still paid their suppliers with paper checks, long after their customers paid by card. AvidXchange went after that gap. The Charlotte company scanned incoming invoices, routed them for approval, and paid suppliers electronically, keeping a small fee on many payments. When it went public in October 2021, fintech stocks were near their peak, and offices emptied by the pandemic had no one left to open the mail.

sections.heading: The Midsize Back Office
sections.body: Michael Praeger co-founded AvidXchange in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 2000. The company focused on the midsize market: property managers, builders, and other firms too big for spreadsheets and too small for costly corporate systems. The bet was that automating the accounts payable office would pay twice. Customers would save on paperwork, and AvidXchange would earn money from the payments that flowed through its network.

sections.heading: Public, Then Private Again
sections.body: AvidXchange priced an upsized offering at $25 a share, the top of its range, raising about $660 million. It began trading on the Nasdaq as AVDX on October 13, 2021. The stock drifted far below its offering price. In October 2025 the private equity firm TPG and the payments company Corpay took AvidXchange private for $10 a share, valuing it at about $2.2 billion.

cover.theme: a couple reading a letter (the mail that brings the bills)

dek: Backblaze backed up people's computers and stored companies' data in its own cloud, for far less than the giants charged.
lede: Backblaze built its own storage servers, red metal boxes it called Storage Pods, and then published the designs for anyone to copy. It also published the failure rates of every hard drive it ran, a report engineers read like box scores. The cheap hardware let it sell online backup and cloud storage for a fraction of what Amazon charged. When Backblaze went public in November 2021, it was a small company in a market ruled by giants.

sections.heading: Five Founders, No Big Checks
sections.body: Gleb Budman, Brian Wilson, Casey Jones, Tim Nufire, and Damon Uyeda founded Backblaze in 2007. They started with unlimited backup for a flat monthly price per computer. To make that price work, they designed their own low-cost servers. The company grew for years on little outside funding. Later it added B2, a cloud storage service for developers and businesses, and B2 became its main growth engine.

sections.heading: Storage for the AI Boom
sections.body: Backblaze priced at $16 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq as BLZE on November 11, 2021, raising $100 million. The stock spent years below its offering price. Then AI companies needed huge amounts of storage. In June 2026 Backblaze signed a five-year, $335 million storage deal with CoreWeave, and it still trades on the Nasdaq as BLZE.

cover.theme: a prairie fire (the blaze)

dek: Klaviyo let online shops send emails and texts based on what each shopper had browsed and bought.
lede: Klaviyo grew up inside Shopify's world, and Shopify owned a stake in it by the time it went public. The Boston company's software sent online shoppers emails and texts based on what they had looked at or left in their cart. More than 130,000 businesses used it. When Klaviyo listed in September 2023, the IPO market had been closed for most of two years, and its debut came the day after Instacart's.

sections.heading: Data First, Then the Email
sections.body: Andrew Bialecki and Ed Hallen founded Klaviyo in Boston in 2012. Most email tools sent the same blast to everyone. Their bet was that a store's own customer data should drive every message: a reminder for an abandoned cart, a note when an item came back in stock. Klaviyo connected tightly to Shopify and other store platforms, and it grew for years with little outside money.

sections.heading: A Test for the IPO Window
sections.body: Klaviyo priced at $30 a share on September 19, 2023, above a range it had already raised, and sold about $576 million of stock. It began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as KVYO the next day. It opened at $36.75 and closed up about 9 percent. Klaviyo still trades on the NYSE as KVYO.

cover.theme: a pianist at the keys (one message, tuned to the listener)

dek: Ingram Micro moved computers, chips, and cloud subscriptions from tech makers to the resellers who sell them to businesses.
lede: Ingram Micro went public on the New York Stock Exchange for the second time in October 2024. It had first listed in 1996, then spent eight years owned by a Chinese conglomerate and a private equity firm. The Irvine, California, company is one of the world's largest tech distributors. It buys laptops, servers, and software in bulk from makers like Apple and Cisco, then sells them to the resellers who supply businesses.

sections.heading: Micro D to Ingram
sections.body: Geza Csige and Lorraine Mecca started the business in 1979 as Micro D, a distributor of computer products. Ingram Industries, a Nashville family company, bought into it in the 1980s and built Ingram Micro around it. The bet was scale: tech makers did not want to deal with tens of thousands of small resellers, and resellers did not want dozens of suppliers. A distributor sitting in the middle could serve both.

sections.heading: Owners Come and Go
sections.body: China's HNA Group bought Ingram Micro for about $6 billion in 2016. Platinum Equity bought it in 2021. Platinum then took it public again, pricing at $22 a share on October 23, 2024. Shares began trading on the NYSE as INGM the next day and closed at $24.60, up about 12 percent. Platinum kept a majority stake, and Ingram Micro still trades on the NYSE as INGM.

cover.theme: a supply wharf stacked with goods (distribution)

dek: Via sold cities and transit agencies software to run on-demand shuttles, school buses, and smarter routes.
lede: Via started as a shared-van service in Manhattan and ended up selling software to city governments. Riders on its early app shared rides along the same route for a flat fare. The real business turned out to be the code that matched them. When Via went public in September 2025, hundreds of transit agencies used its software to run on-demand shuttles, paratransit, and school transport, often in places where a fixed bus route made little sense.

sections.heading: From Rides to Routes
sections.body: Daniel Ramot and Oren Shoval founded Via in 2012, with offices in New York and Tel Aviv. The bet was that algorithms could fill vans with riders heading the same way, making a shared ride nearly as convenient as a private one. Via then licensed that system to public transit agencies, which paid it to plan routes and dispatch vehicles. Government contracts became the core of the business.

sections.heading: A Slow Start, Then a Slide
sections.body: Via priced at $46 a share on September 11, 2025, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as VIA the next day. The stock opened at $44, below its offering price, then recovered to close at $49.51, up about 7.6 percent. Over the following months the shares fell well below the offering price. Via still trades on the NYSE as VIA.

cover.theme: the Via Appia outside Rome (the road, the name)
cover.artwork: View of Rome, with via Appia

tagline: Rockets That Land, Then Ring the Bell
dek: SpaceX launched rockets that land and fly again, and sold satellite internet from thousands of its own satellites.
lede: SpaceX raised about $75 billion when it went public, the largest IPO ever. By the end of its first day of trading it was worth about $2.1 trillion. The company had spent two decades as a private firm, landing rocket boosters on ships at sea and filling the sky with Starlink internet satellites. When it listed in June 2026, it launched most of the world's satellites, and Starlink sold service to millions of customers.

sections.heading: Reuse the Rocket
sections.body: Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002. His bet was that launch costs would only fall if rockets could be reused instead of thrown away after each flight. Its first three Falcon 1 launches failed, and the fourth reached orbit in 2008. NASA contracts for cargo and then astronauts followed. Falcon 9 boosters began landing in 2015, and Starlink later turned SpaceX's launch business into a global internet company.

sections.heading: A Fixed Price of $135
sections.body: SpaceX skipped the usual price range and set a fixed price of $135 a share. It priced on June 11, 2026, and began trading on the Nasdaq as SPCX the next day. The stock opened at $150 and closed near $161, up about 19 percent. Musk's stake made him the first person worth more than $1 trillion. SpaceX still trades on the Nasdaq as SPCX.

cover.theme: a comet streaking across the night sky (spaceflight)

dek: VMware let one server act like many, so companies could do more work with fewer machines.
lede: VMware's stock closed its first day at $51, up 76 percent, in the biggest tech IPO since Google. The company sold a trick that sounded like magic: software that split one physical computer into several make-believe ones, each running its own operating system. Data centers were full of servers that sat mostly idle. VMware let companies pack that work onto fewer boxes. By the summer of 2007, it was the quiet engine inside corporate computer rooms.

sections.heading: A Stanford Lab Idea
sections.body: Diane Greene, her husband Mendel Rosenblum, and three colleagues founded VMware in Palo Alto in 1998. Rosenblum's research at Stanford showed that a thin layer of software could fool an operating system into thinking it had a whole machine to itself. Their first product let a single PC run Windows and Linux side by side. The bigger prize was the server room. In 2004 EMC, the storage giant, bought VMware and kept it running as its own business.

sections.heading: Passed From Owner to Owner
sections.body: EMC sold a slice of VMware to the public at $29 a share on August 13, 2007, and the stock began trading on the NYSE the next day. EMC kept control. In 2008 it replaced Greene as chief executive with Paul Maritz. Dell bought EMC in 2016, and VMware came along with it. Dell spun VMware off in 2021. In November 2023 Broadcom closed its purchase of VMware for about $69 billion.

cover.theme: a river and its mirror image in the mist (a virtual copy)
cover.artwork: Branch of the Seine near Giverny (Mist)

dek: Marketo told marketers which people were ready to buy, and sent each one the right email at the right time.
lede: Marketo's stock jumped almost 78 percent on its first day, on the same morning Tableau went public. Wall Street wanted software in the cloud, and Marketo sold it to the marketing department. Its tools watched what a prospect did on a company's website and in its emails. Then they scored that person and sent the next message on their own. By 2013, marketers had budgets and data of their own, and Marketo gave them a way to prove what they earned.

sections.heading: Three Friends From Epiphany
sections.body: Phil Fernandez, Jon Miller, and David Morandi had worked together at Epiphany, an earlier marketing software company. They founded Marketo in 2006 and set up in San Mateo, California. Their bet was that marketers would pay a monthly fee for one tool to run campaigns, track leads, and hand the warm ones to sales. Jon Miller became the public voice of the idea. He wrote guides that taught a new trade its playbook.

sections.heading: Private, Then Adobe
sections.body: Marketo priced at $13 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq on May 17, 2013. The stock closed its first day at $23.10. Growth was strong, but profits never came, and the shares drifted. In 2016 Vista Equity Partners took Marketo private for about $1.79 billion. Two years later Vista sold it to Adobe for $4.75 billion. The product lives on today as Adobe Marketo Engage.

cover.theme: a family on the road to market

dek: Fitbit counted your steps and your sleep, and nudged millions of people to move a little more.
lede: Fitbit went public two months after the Apple Watch went on sale, and investors still bid it up almost 50 percent on day one. The little clip-on tracker had turned walking into a game. It counted steps, distance, and calories, and it sent the numbers to your phone. Friends raced each other on weekly leaderboards. By June 2015, Fitbit was the name people knew in fitness trackers, and the question was whether a watch would swallow them.

sections.heading: A Sensor in a Clip
sections.body: James Park and Eric Friedman incorporated Fitbit in San Francisco in April 2007. Park had bought a Nintendo Wii and loved its motion sensors, but the game kept players stuck in the living room. He wanted a gadget that used the same kind of sensor to get people out of the house. The first Fitbit was a small clip you wore on your clothes. The bet was that people would move more if they could see their numbers.

sections.heading: The Watch Arrives
sections.body: Fitbit priced at $20 a share on June 17, 2015, above its range. It opened on the NYSE the next day under the ticker FIT and closed at $29.68. Then cheaper bands and smartwatches cut into sales, and the stock sank well below its offer price. Fitbit moved toward watches and health services. In January 2021 Google closed its purchase of Fitbit for $2.1 billion.

cover.theme: a figure in motion, frame by frame (counting every step)

dek: DocuSign let people sign contracts on a screen, so deals closed in minutes instead of days of printing and faxing.
lede: DocuSign turned a pen stroke into a verb. By 2018, people said they would "DocuSign" a lease or an offer letter. Before it, a contract meant printing, signing, scanning, and faxing, or waiting days for the mail. DocuSign put a bright tab on the page that said sign here, and the deal closed from a laptop or a phone. When it filed to go public, the e-signature was a habit, and DocuSign wanted to own everything around the agreement.

sections.heading: The Real Estate Start
sections.body: Tom Gonser, Court Lorenzini, and Eric Ranft founded DocuSign in 2003. Gonser had run NetUpdate, a company that built online tools for real estate and mortgages, and home sales ran on stacks of paper. A 2000 federal law had made electronic signatures binding. The bet was that a signature on a screen could be legal, safe, and faster. Sales began in 2005, when the real estate forms maker zipForm built DocuSign into its software.

sections.heading: Fifteen Years to the Bell
sections.body: DocuSign priced at $29 a share on April 26, 2018, above its range. It began trading on the Nasdaq the next day under the ticker DOCU, and the stock rose more than 30 percent. The pandemic sent the shares soaring in 2020, when signing in person became hard. They fell back as offices reopened. Private equity firms explored a buyout in early 2024, but no deal came. DocuSign is still public on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a hand with a quill pen (the signature)

fate: Still public (NYSE: HUYA), controlled by Tencent
dek: Huya let millions of Chinese gamers watch their favorite players stream live and tip them with virtual gifts.
lede: Huya's name means "tiger's tooth," and it bit hard on its first day: up 34 percent in May 2018. The Guangzhou company ran one of China's biggest sites for watching people play video games live. Fans sent streamers virtual gifts that cost real money, and Huya kept a share. Esports was booming, and phones made it easy to watch anywhere. That spring iQiyi and Bilibili both fell on their debuts. Huya did the opposite.

sections.heading: Spun Out of YY
sections.body: Huya began inside YY, the Chinese live video company. In November 2014, YY announced that its game streaming service would run on its own as Huya Live. The bet was that watching games would grow as large as playing them. Huya signed popular streamers and broadcast esports tournaments. Most of its money came from viewers who bought virtual gifts for the players they liked.

sections.heading: Tencent Takes the Wheel
sections.body: Huya priced at $12 a share, the top of its range, and began trading on the NYSE on May 11, 2018. It raised $180 million and closed its first day at $16.06. In April 2020 Tencent became Huya's largest shareholder and took control of the vote. A planned merger with rival DouYu fell apart in 2021. Streaming revenue then shrank for several years. As of 2025, Tencent owned about 67 percent of Huya and held 95 percent of the votes.

cover.theme: a tiger ready to spring (Huya means tiger's tooth)

dek: CrowdStrike guarded company computers from hackers with software that lived in the cloud and learned from every attack.
lede: CrowdStrike first hoped to sell its shares for about $20. Demand pushed the price to $34, and the stock still closed its first day at $58. The company sold one product, Falcon, a small program that sat on every laptop and server and reported back to CrowdStrike's cloud. Old antivirus software looked for known bad files. Falcon watched for suspicious behavior. In June 2019, companies were tired of breaches, and investors wanted security that ran in the cloud.

sections.heading: One Sensor, One Cloud
sections.body: George Kurtz and Dmitri Alperovitch founded CrowdStrike in 2011. Kurtz became chief executive and Alperovitch chief technology officer. Their bet was that a light sensor on each machine, joined to one big cloud, could spot attackers faster than antivirus on each computer working alone. Every attack seen on one customer's machine taught the system to protect the rest. Customers paid by subscription, and they could add new modules without new software.

sections.heading: Blue Screens Worldwide
sections.body: CrowdStrike priced at $34 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12, 2019, under the ticker CRWD. The stock rose more than 70 percent that day. The company kept growing and moved its headquarters to Austin, Texas. On July 19, 2024, a faulty Falcon update crashed Windows computers around the world and grounded flights. CrowdStrike pulled the update within 80 minutes. The company is still public on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a hawk on watch (the Falcon sensor)
cover.artwork: Hawk, from The Picture Book of Realistic Paintings of Hokusai

tagline: A Shield in Front of the Web
dek: Cloudflare made more than 20 million websites faster and kept attackers out, often for free.
lede: Cloudflare began as a side project that tracked spammers. Matthew Prince and Lee Holloway built that tool, Project Honey Pot, years before they built a company. Then Prince told a business school classmate, Michelle Zatlyn, about it. She saw a bigger idea: stop the attacks as well as track them. Cloudflare's network sat between websites and their visitors. It sped up pages and blocked attacks before they landed. By September 2019, more than 20 million websites, apps, and domains used it, many on the free plan.

sections.heading: From Honey Pot to Network
sections.body: Prince, Holloway, and Zatlyn founded Cloudflare in July 2009, while Prince and Zatlyn were students at Harvard Business School. They wrote the business plan in class. Holloway built the first working version. The bet was to give the basic service away to small sites, learn from all that traffic, and sell bigger plans to large companies. Holloway stepped down in 2015 after he fell ill with frontotemporal dementia.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars on Day One
sections.body: Cloudflare priced at $15 a share on September 12, 2019. It began trading on the NYSE the next day under the ticker NET. The stock rose as much as 30 percent during the day and closed at $18, up 20 percent. The offering raised $525 million. Cloudflare kept adding products on top of the same network that served its free customers. It is still public on the NYSE.

cover.theme: sunlight flaring through clouds
cover.artwork: Mist Rising at Sunset in the Catskills

dek: Kingsoft Cloud rented computing power and storage to Chinese companies, from video apps to phone makers.
lede: Kingsoft Cloud shot up to $74.67 a share after its IPO, then lost more than 95 percent of that in two years. It went public in May 2020, the first big U.S. IPO from China after the Luckin Coffee scandal shook trust in Chinese listings. Kingsoft Cloud rented servers, storage, and networks to companies in China. It had a powerful friend in Xiaomi, the phone maker, which was an early investor and a major customer.

sections.heading: Kingsoft's Cloud Arm
sections.body: Kingsoft, the Beijing software company, formed Kingsoft Cloud in 2012 as its cloud services arm. Xiaomi put in about $1.8 million that same year for a 9.9 percent stake. The bet was that China's fast-growing apps would rather rent computing than build their own. Yuri Milner put in $20 million in 2013, and IDG joined a later round. By the IPO, Kingsoft owned about 53 percent and Xiaomi about 16 percent.

sections.heading: Listed Twice, Down Hard
sections.body: Kingsoft Cloud priced at $17 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq on May 8, 2020. It raised $510 million and closed its first day at $23.84. The shares then slid with the rest of Chinese tech. In December 2022 the company added a second listing in Hong Kong under the code 3896. Revenue grew 23 percent in 2025, to 9.56 billion yuan. It is still listed in New York and Hong Kong.

cover.theme: mountains in the mist (a Chinese cloud)

dek: Rackspace ran and fixed other companies' servers and clouds, and sold itself on answering the phone.
lede: Rackspace went public twice. The first time, in 2008, its shares sold for $12.50 and later climbed to about $80. The second time, in August 2020, the stock fell more than 20 percent on its first day. In between, Apollo had bought the company for $4.3 billion and loaded it with debt. Rackspace's trade had changed too. It once rented out its own servers. By 2020 it also ran customers' computing on the big public clouds.

sections.heading: Three Students in San Antonio
sections.body: Richard Yoo, Dirk Elmendorf, and Patrick Condon met at Trinity University in San Antonio. They launched Rackspace in October 1998 to host websites on servers they ran for customers. Graham Weston and Morris Miller put in seed money and joined to run the business. The bet was service. Rackspace called it Fanatical Support, and customers paid more to reach a person who would fix their problem.

sections.heading: Debt After the Buyout
sections.body: Rackspace sold 33.5 million shares at $21 each and began trading on the Nasdaq on August 5, 2020. The offering raised $704 million. The shares closed the first day at $16.17. Part of the money went to pay down the debt from Apollo's 2016 buyout, about $3.9 billion. The stock kept falling. In 2024 Rackspace swapped its debt with lenders and raised $275 million of new money. In mid 2026 its shares traded under $4. It is still public.

cover.theme: objects lined up on shelves (racks of servers)
cover.artwork: Articles of China on Four Shelves

dek: Chindata built giant data centers near Chinese cities and filled them with servers for ByteDance.
lede: One customer paid for more than 80 percent of Chindata's revenue: ByteDance, the company behind TikTok and Douyin. Chindata built huge data centers on cheap land outside big Chinese cities, close to power and fiber. It leased whole buildings to a few large tech companies. In September 2020, people worked and watched video from home, and investors wanted anything that powered the cloud. Bain Capital, which controlled the company, took it public at the top of its range.

sections.heading: Built for a Few Giants
sections.body: Jing Ju, Chindata's chief executive, founded its China data center business in 2015. The company began building its own hyperscale data centers in July 2016, many of them in Hebei and Shanxi provinces. The bet was size. Instead of renting racks to thousands of small clients, Chindata built whole campuses for a few giant ones. The group also ran Bridge Data Centres, with sites near Kuala Lumpur and Mumbai.

sections.heading: Bain Takes It Back
sections.body: Chindata priced at $13.50 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq on September 30, 2020, under the ticker CD. It raised $540 million and closed its first day at $16.23. In 2023 China Merchants Group made a bid for the company. Bain Capital, which already held most of the votes, won with an offer of $8.60 per share. The deal took Chindata private for about $3.16 billion.

cover.theme: long rows of buildings in China (server halls)

dek: DoorDash brought food from local restaurants, and later groceries and more, to your door within the hour.
lede: DoorDash started as a website called PaloAltoDelivery.com, built by Stanford students who asked local shops what they needed. The answer was delivery. Outside New York, most restaurants had no way to get food to people's homes. By December 2020, the pandemic had closed dining rooms across the country, and DoorDash was how many restaurants stayed open. Its drivers, called Dashers, had already hit a million deliveries in a single day.

sections.heading: A Website Called PaloAltoDelivery
sections.body: Tony Xu, Andy Fang, Stanley Tang, and Evan Moore launched the service in Palo Alto in January 2013 and incorporated as DoorDash that June. As students, they had canvassed Bay Area businesses and were surprised how few could deliver. Outside New York City, delivery barely existed. The bet was that a network of local drivers could serve the suburbs. DoorDash expanded to the East Coast in 2014. By 2020 it served all 50 states, plus Canada and Australia.

sections.heading: A Pandemic Debut
sections.body: DoorDash priced at $102 a share on December 8, 2020, and began trading on the NYSE the next day. It raised $3.37 billion. The stock closed its first day up about 86 percent, near $190. In 2023 DoorDash moved its listing to the Nasdaq. In 2025 it bought Deliveroo, the British delivery company, for about $3.9 billion. DoorDash is still public under the ticker DASH.

cover.theme: an open doorway

dek: ON24 ran webinars and virtual events for businesses, and told sales teams which viewers were ready to buy.
lede: ON24 waited 23 years to go public, and then the whole world moved online at once. The San Francisco company started in 1998 under the name NewsDirect. It grew into the platform that businesses used for webinars and virtual events. When the pandemic cancelled trade shows in 2020, marketers had nowhere else to meet buyers. ON24 powered more than 159,000 webinars and other online events in the first nine months of that year, and it tracked who watched.

sections.heading: From NewsDirect to Webinars
sections.body: Sharat Sharan co-founded the company in January 1998 as NewsDirect, and it took the name ON24 a year later. Sharan served as chief executive from the start. The bet was that companies would talk to their customers through online video, and that every click during a webinar was a signal. ON24 sold its platform to business marketers. It gave their sales teams lists of the most engaged viewers.

sections.heading: Back to the Conference Hall
sections.body: ON24 priced at $50 a share and began trading on the NYSE in February 2021 under the ticker ONTF. The stock rose about 42 percent on its first day. Then offices and conference halls reopened, and demand for virtual events cooled. The shares fell far below the offer price. In December 2025 ON24 agreed to sell itself to Cvent, the event software company, for $8.10 a share in cash. The deal closed on April 1, 2026.

cover.theme: a crowd facing a screen (the webinar audience)

dek: Semrush showed marketers how people found them online, and how to beat rivals in search results.
lede: Semrush raised only $37 million in its first twelve years, then went public worth more than a billion dollars. Its tools showed marketers why a competitor showed up first on Google. Semrush tracked keywords, ads, and links across the web, and it sold that view by subscription. Most customers signed up on their own, with no sales call. By the end of 2020, it had 67,000 paying customers in 142 countries.

sections.heading: One Tool Became Fifty
sections.body: Oleg Shchegolev and Dmitry Melnikov founded Semrush in 2008. It began as a single product for search engine optimization. The founders kept costs low and grew mostly on their own revenue. The bet was a free tier and a cheap self-serve plan, so customers could find the tool, try it, and pay without talking to anyone. By its IPO, Semrush sold more than 50 products, tools, and add-ons.

sections.heading: A Slow Start, Then Adobe
sections.body: Semrush cut the size of its offering and priced at $14 a share, the low end of its range, in March 2021. It began trading on the NYSE under the ticker SEMR and fell about 20 percent on its first day. The company kept growing its subscriptions. In November 2025 Adobe agreed to buy Semrush for $1.9 billion. Adobe closed the deal on April 28, 2026.

cover.theme: a lookout over a valley (seeing who is visible)
cover.artwork: Chattanooga Valley from Lookout Mountain, No. 2

dek: UiPath sold software robots that clicked, typed, and copied data so office workers did not have to.
lede: UiPath started in Bucharest, Romania, under the name DeskOver, and kept that name for ten years. Then it found its product: software robots that copy what a person does on a screen. They log into apps, read documents, fill in forms, and move files. Big companies had rooms full of people doing that work by hand. By early 2021, UiPath counted 7,968 customers, including eight of the ten biggest companies in America.

sections.heading: DeskOver Finds Its Robots
sections.body: Daniel Dines and Marius Tîrcă founded the company in Bucharest in 2005. It took the name UiPath in 2015 and incorporated in Delaware that June. The bet was that most office work runs through screens, and a robot that could see a screen could do much of it. UiPath used computer vision so its robots worked on old systems with no other way in. It moved its headquarters to New York.

sections.heading: A Big New York Debut
sections.body: UiPath priced at $56 a share on April 20, 2021, and began trading on the NYSE the next day under the ticker PATH. It raised $1.3 billion, and the stock rose 23 percent on its first day. The shares later fell far below the offer price as growth slowed. UiPath turned toward AI agents that plan and carry out work. In 2025 it launched its platform for agentic automation. It is still public on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a sunlit path through a wood
cover.artwork: A Sunlit Path through a Wood

dek: Paymentus let people pay their power, water, and insurance bills online, any way they liked.
lede: When Dushyant Sharma tried to patent his bill payment idea in 2004, he was turned down and told that a fax machine could solve the problem. He built Paymentus anyway. Utilities, insurers, and cities still mailed billions of paper bills, and people still paid many of them by check. Paymentus gave those billers one cloud platform to send bills and take payment by card, bank, app, or voice. Unusually for a 2021 IPO, it made money.

sections.heading: Born in Ontario
sections.body: Sharma founded the company in Ontario, Canada, in 2004 as Bizpective Technologies, and renamed it Paymentus the next year. It first served mid-size billers to prove the system worked. In 2011 Accel-KKR invested and Paymentus moved up to larger clients. By 2020 it served more than 1,300 billers and processed more than 195 million transactions. PayPal and Walmart joined as the first partners in its payment network.

sections.heading: Profitable at the Bell
sections.body: Paymentus priced at $21 a share, the top of its range, on May 25, 2021, and began trading on the NYSE under the ticker PAY. The stock rose about 36 percent on its first day. Paymentus came to market with $302 million in 2020 revenue and $13 million in profit. Accel-KKR and Sharma kept almost all of the votes. It is still public on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a gas lamp on a city street (the utility bill)
cover.artwork: The rue Mosnier with Gas Lamp

tagline: Freight Loads From a Chat Group
dek: Full Truck Alliance matched Chinese shippers with truck drivers on an app, so fewer trucks drove home empty.
lede: Full Truck Alliance began as freight listings posted in QQ and WeChat chat groups. Its two founding apps, Huochebang and Yunmanman, turned that chatter into China's biggest digital freight market. A factory posted a load, and a nearby trucker took it. In 2020, more than 2.8 million truckers completed 71.7 million orders through the platform. Two weeks after its June 2021 IPO, Beijing ordered a security review and froze new sign-ups.

sections.heading: Two Rivals Merge
sections.body: Huochebang started in 2011 and Yunmanman in 2013. Both began by posting loads in chat groups, then built apps, and both grew into leading freight platforms. In 2017 they merged to form Full Truck Alliance. Peter Hui Zhang, the founder, became chairman and chief executive. The bet was that China's millions of small trucking outfits wasted time and fuel hunting for loads, and one big network could match them faster.

sections.heading: A Review Two Weeks In
sections.body: Full Truck Alliance priced at $19 a share, the top of its range, on June 21, 2021. It began trading on the NYSE under the ticker YMM and rose 13 percent on its first day. On July 5, 2021, China's cyberspace regulator opened a security review of both apps and stopped new user sign-ups. The freeze lasted until June 29, 2022. The company is still public on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a horse-drawn cart on an open road (freight)
cover.artwork: Two Horse Cart at Juncture in Road

dek: Intapp built the software that big law, accounting, and investment firms use to run their deals and clients.
lede: Ninety-six of America's 100 largest law firms ran Intapp software when it went public. Most people had never heard of it. Intapp sold to professionals who bill by the hour: lawyers, accountants, consultants, and dealmakers. Its tools checked conflicts of interest, tracked time, and kept client data in one place. By 2021, those firms were moving to the cloud, and Intapp had more than 1,600 clients in over 40 countries.

sections.heading: Built for Law Firms First
sections.body: Intapp was founded in 2000 as Integration Appliance. Its first job was to connect and manage the data that law firms kept in many separate systems. Thad Jampol co-founded the company and later ran its products. The bet was that professional firms had needs too specific for general business software. Intapp grew into accounting and consulting. In 2018 it bought DealCloud, which brought in private equity and investment banking clients.

sections.heading: A Steady Climb
sections.body: Intapp priced at $26 a share on June 29, 2021, and began trading on the Nasdaq the next day under the ticker INTA. The stock rose about 8 percent on its first day. Great Hill Partners and Temasek, existing investors, had offered to buy up to $60 million of the shares. Intapp kept selling to law, accounting, and private capital firms. In July 2026 it signed a new $150 million credit line. It is still public on the Nasdaq and based in Palo Alto.

cover.theme: the steps of a palace of justice (law firms)
cover.artwork: Main Staircase of the Palace of Justice

fate: Taken private by KKR and Dragoneer, 2024 ($4.8B)
dek: Instructure made Canvas, the online classroom where millions of students turn in homework and teachers post grades.
lede: Instructure went public twice in six years. It first listed in 2015. Thoma Bravo bought it for $2 billion in 2020, then sold shares to the public again in July 2021. In between, the pandemic sent every school online at once. Canvas, Instructure's learning system, was where many of them landed. Students turned in work there and teachers posted grades. By the end of 2020, Canvas had 30 million contracted users and more than 6,000 school and college customers.

sections.heading: Two Grad Students in Utah
sections.body: Brian Whitmer and Devlin Daley were graduate students at Brigham Young University when they founded Instructure in 2008. Their product, Canvas, ran in the cloud and let schools plug in other education apps. The bet was that colleges would switch learning systems if teachers and students liked the tool. Instructure grew from Salt Lake City. By its second IPO, it served colleges and K-12 districts in more than 90 countries.

sections.heading: Thoma Bravo, Then KKR
sections.body: Instructure first listed on the NYSE in November 2015. Thoma Bravo took it private in March 2020. The second IPO priced at $20 a share in July 2021 under the ticker INST, and the stock rose about 5 percent on its first day. In November 2024 KKR and Dragoneer bought the company for $23.60 a share, about $4.8 billion. In 2026 hackers breached Canvas, and Instructure faced lawsuits.

cover.theme: a lesson between teacher and student

fate: Taken private by Apax Partners, 2024 ($4.40 a share)
dek: Thoughtworks built custom software for big companies and taught the industry new ways to write it.
lede: Thoughtworks' chief scientist, Martin Fowler, co-wrote the Agile Manifesto in 2001. That short document changed how much of the world builds software. Thoughtworks was the consulting firm that practiced it. Its teams of developers built custom systems for large companies, and its staff wrote books that other programmers learned from. When it went public in September 2021, companies were rushing to rebuild their old systems for the digital age.

sections.heading: A Chicago Basement Start
sections.body: Roy Singham started the business in a Chicago basement as a management consultancy in the late 1980s. It took the name Thoughtworks in 1990 and incorporated in 1993. Fowler joined in 1999. The bet was that small teams of strong engineers, shipping working code often, beat the long, rigid projects of big consultancies. Thoughtworks also published its Technology Radar twice a year. In 2017 Singham sold the firm to Apax Partners for $785 million.

sections.heading: Apax Comes Back
sections.body: Thoughtworks priced at $21 a share, above its range, in September 2021. It listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker TWKS on September 15 and rose 40 percent on its first day. The stock then fell for most of the next three years. Guo Xiao stepped down as chief executive in 2024. In November 2024 Apax took Thoughtworks private again, paying $4.40 a share.

cover.theme: a philosopher at his desk (thought at work)

fate: Still public (NYSE: IHS); sale to MTN at $8.50 a share pending
dek: IHS built and rented out the cell towers that carry phone calls and data across Africa and other emerging markets.
lede: IHS Towers was the largest U.S. listing ever for a company with African roots. It owned the steel towers that hold up the cell networks in Nigeria and beyond. Phone companies rented space on them for their antennas and paid every month. By mid 2021, IHS ran 30,207 towers in nine countries, across Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. In six of those markets it was the biggest tower operator.

sections.heading: Built in Lagos
sections.body: Sam Darwish, an engineer, co-founded IHS in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2001. In Nigeria, phone companies had begun hiring outside firms to build their towers. The bet was that carriers would rather share towers than each build their own. IHS bought towers from carriers, built new ones, and leased the space. It grew across Africa, then into Latin America and Kuwait.

sections.heading: MTN Comes Calling
sections.body: IHS cut the size of its offering and priced at $21 a share, the low end of its range, in October 2021. It began trading on the NYSE under the ticker IHS and fell 19 percent on its first day. The company later sold assets, including its Latin American towers in 2026. In February 2026 MTN Group, the African phone company, agreed to buy the rest of IHS for $8.50 a share. Shareholders approved the deal on August 4, 2026.

cover.theme: towers rising over a city

fate: Taken private by Thoma Bravo, 2023 ($7.50 a share)
tagline: Watch a Stranger Use Your App
dek: UserTesting let companies watch videos of real people trying their websites and apps, and hear what confused them.
lede: UserTesting sold a simple, humbling experience: watching a stranger get lost on your website. Companies posted a task, and real people recorded their screens and voices as they tried it. Designers heard exactly where they got stuck. More than half of the world's 100 most valuable brands used it by 2021. UserTesting went public that November, and its stock barely moved on day one. Fourteen months later, it was private again.

sections.heading: Video First
sections.body: Darrell Benatar co-founded UserTesting in California in June 2007. It launched a platform for large companies in 2012, though it put real money behind that push only later. The bet was that video of real people would settle arguments inside a company faster than charts. The platform added machine learning to find the key moments in each video. By September 2021 it had more than 2,100 customers, each paying about $67,000 a year on average.

sections.heading: Fourteen Months on the NYSE
sections.body: UserTesting priced at $14 a share on November 16, 2021, and began trading on the NYSE under the ticker USER. The stock ended its first day almost exactly where it started. Software stocks fell hard in 2022. In October 2022 Thoma Bravo agreed to buy the company for $7.50 a share in cash. The deal closed on January 12, 2023, and UserTesting left the stock market.

cover.theme: people looking over a reader's shoulder (watching real users)
cover.artwork: Woman Reading at Table While Man and Woman Listen In

tagline: A Maple Leaf and a Bear
dek: Instacart sent personal shoppers to pick groceries off store shelves and bring them to your door.
lede: Instacart's legal name is Maplebear: maple for Canada, where Apoorva Mehta grew up, and bear for California, where he moved later. Instacart sent shoppers into local supermarkets to fill orders placed on an app. Grocers got online sales without building their own delivery. By 2023 it worked with more than 1,400 retail banners, which together made up more than 85 percent of the U.S. grocery market. Its IPO that September valued it at about $10 billion.

sections.heading: The Store Comes to You
sections.body: Mehta, Max Mullen, and Brandon Leonardo founded Instacart in San Francisco in 2012. The bet was that people would pay to skip the grocery run, and that stores would rather partner with Instacart than fight it. Its shoppers picked from the stores' own shelves, so it needed no warehouses. In 2021 Fidji Simo became chief executive, and Mehta moved to executive chairman.

sections.heading: Thirty Dollars to Start
sections.body: Instacart priced at $30 a share on September 18, 2023, and began trading on the Nasdaq the next day under the ticker CART. It raised $660 million and rose about 12 percent on its first day. Mehta left the board after the IPO. In 2025 Simo left for OpenAI, and Chris Rogers became chief executive. Instacart earned $450 million on $3.74 billion of revenue in 2025. It is still public on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a basket of fresh groceries
cover.artwork: Still Life with a Basket of Fruit and a Bunch of Asparagus

dek: WeRide built self-driving taxis, buses, vans, and street sweepers, and ran them in cities from Guangzhou to Abu Dhabi.
lede: WeRide was described as the first robotaxi company to list on a stock market. Its cars, buses, vans, and street sweepers drove themselves, and by its IPO they were operating or testing in 30 cities across seven countries. The company was born in Silicon Valley and grew up in Guangzhou. It went public in October 2024, raising about $440 million, and priced at the bottom of its range.

sections.heading: From Baidu to Guangzhou
sections.body: Tony Xu Han had been chief scientist of Baidu's self-driving unit. He founded WeRide in 2017 with Yan Li, who became chief technology officer. The company started in Silicon Valley and made Guangzhou its home. The bet was to build one driving system and put it in many kinds of vehicles, from taxis to sweepers. WeRide says it was the first company in the world to sell robotaxi rides to the public.

sections.heading: Driverless in Dubai
sections.body: WeRide priced at $15.50 a share, the low end of its range, on October 24, 2024. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker WRD and rose about 7 percent on its first day. A partnership with Uber put its robotaxis on the Uber app, starting in Abu Dhabi. In April 2026 WeRide began fully driverless, paid rides in Dubai. It is still public on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a riderless horse (no one at the wheel)

dek: Circle issued USDC, a digital dollar backed one to one by cash, and earned interest on the reserves behind it.
lede: Circle's stock rose 168 percent on its first day of trading. Three years earlier, its plan to go public through a SPAC had collapsed. Circle issued USDC, a digital token that anyone could redeem for one U.S. dollar. More than $61 billion of it was in circulation by May 2025. Circle held the matching reserves in cash and cash equivalents, and the interest on them brought in most of its money.

sections.heading: Boston, Then the Stablecoin
sections.body: Jeremy Allaire and Sean Neville founded Circle in Boston in October 2013. In 2018 Circle and Coinbase formed the Centre consortium and launched USDC. The bet was that a fully backed dollar on a blockchain could move money around the world at any hour. By March 2025, USDC had carried more than $25 trillion in transactions. Circle's revenue and reserve income rose from $15.4 million in 2020 to $1.7 billion in 2024.

sections.heading: SPAC Failed, IPO Soared
sections.body: Circle agreed in July 2021 to merge with Concord Acquisition Corp, a SPAC. The deal ended in December 2022. Circle then priced a regular IPO at $31 a share on June 4, 2025, above a range it had already raised. The stock began trading on the NYSE under the ticker CRCL. The Senate passed the GENIUS Act, a stablecoin law, that same month. In July 2026 Circle won final approval to form a national trust bank.

cover.theme: a full moon (a perfect circle)
cover.artwork: Full Moon and Autumn Flowers by the Stream

dek: Netskope watched how employees used cloud apps and the web, and stopped company data from leaking out.
lede: Netskope spent thirteen years as a private company before it rang the bell. It sat between employees and the internet. It saw which cloud apps they used, what data they moved, and whether a file should leave the company at all. By 2025, workers were also pasting company data into AI tools, and Netskope sold security for cloud and AI. It went public that September with $707 million in annual recurring revenue, up 33 percent in a year.

sections.heading: Thirteen Years Private
sections.body: Sanjay Beri and Krishna Narayanaswamy founded Netskope in May 2012. Beri became chief executive and Narayanaswamy chief technology officer. The bet was that security had to follow data into the cloud, since the old office firewall could no longer see it. Netskope combined security and networking in one service. It grew from Santa Clara, California, and stayed private until 2025.

sections.heading: Top of the Range
sections.body: Netskope priced at $19 a share, the top of its range, on September 17, 2025. It sold 47.8 million shares and raised $908.2 million. The stock began trading on the Nasdaq the next day under the ticker NTSK and rose about 18 percent on its first day. For the fiscal year that ended in January 2026, revenue reached $709 million, up from $538 million a year earlier. It is still public on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: fishermen casting a net at night

tagline: Forty Thousand Dollars and a Spoon
dek: Bending Spoons bought tired internet brands like Evernote, Vimeo, and AOL, cut costs, and raised prices.
lede: Bending Spoons started with $40,000 left over from a failed startup and paid $10,000 for its first acquisition. Thirteen years later it owned Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo, AOL, and Eventbrite. The Milan company bought apps that people still used and ran them lean. Many of those companies saw deep layoffs and higher prices after the deal. By March 2026 its products had more than 500 million monthly users and 9 million paying customers.

sections.heading: After Evertale Failed
sections.body: Some of the founders first built Evertale, an app that used AI to write a diary for its users. It raised a million dollars and earned almost nothing. In 2013 they wound it down. With the $40,000 left, Luca Ferrari, Francesco Patarnello, Matteo Danieli, Luca Querella, and Tomasz Greber started Bending Spoons in Copenhagen, then moved to Milan. The bet was that buying proven apps beat inventing new ones. Revenue reached $1.31 billion in 2025, up from $387 million in 2023.

sections.heading: Still Buying After the IPO
sections.body: Bending Spoons priced at $29 a share, above its range, on June 30, 2026. It began trading on the Nasdaq the next day under the ticker BSP and rose about 40 percent on its first day. It kept buying. Airtable joined in September 2026 and Miro in October. That same month Berkshire Hathaway agreed to buy $330 million of new shares at $33 each.

cover.theme: a single silver spoon

tagline: A Sports Car Full of Laptop Batteries
dek: Tesla made electric cars that people wanted to drive fast, then pushed the whole car industry toward batteries.
lede: Tesla went public having built one car, a two-seat electric Roadster powered by thousands of laptop-style battery cells. It was 2010. Detroit had just come out of bankruptcy and bailouts, and most people thought electric cars were slow and dull. Tesla had borrowed $465 million from the U.S. Department of Energy to build a family sedan, the Model S. Its filing asked investors to bet that a small Silicon Valley startup could make cars at scale.

sections.heading: Batteries Before Brakes
sections.body: Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning started Tesla in 2003, naming it after the inventor Nikola Tesla. Elon Musk led the first big funding round and became chairman. A legal settlement later let Musk, JB Straubel, and Ian Wright also call themselves founders. The plan was simple to state and hard to do. Start with an expensive sports car for rich buyers. Use that money to build a cheaper sedan. Then use the sedan to build a car for everyone.
