sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars a Share
sections.body: Tesla priced its IPO at $17 a share on June 28, 2010, and began trading on Nasdaq the next day. The stock opened at $19 and closed at $23.89, a gain of about 40 percent. The Model S arrived in 2012. The Model 3 followed, and Tesla grew into the most valuable carmaker in the world. It moved its headquarters from Palo Alto to Austin, Texas, and still trades on Nasdaq as TSLA.

cover.theme: a gathering storm (electric charge)

fate: Still public (NYSE: BABA; also listed in Hong Kong)
dek: Alibaba gave Chinese shoppers and small merchants one giant place to buy and sell almost anything online.
lede: Alibaba raised $25 billion when it went public, the most any company had ever raised in an IPO. Fifteen years earlier, Jack Ma had started it in his apartment in Hangzhou with a small group of friends. By 2014 its sites Taobao and Tmall were where much of China shopped online. China's middle class was growing fast. American investors had no simple way to own that growth, and Alibaba offered them one on the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: An English Teacher's Marketplace
sections.body: Jack Ma was a former English teacher who had seen the internet on a trip to the United States. In 1999 he and 17 co-founders, including the lawyer Joe Tsai, launched Alibaba.com to connect Chinese factories with buyers abroad. Taobao came next, a consumer marketplace that charged sellers nothing to list. Alibaba made its money from ads and services sold to merchants. Alipay, its payment service, gave strangers a reason to trust each other with money.

sections.heading: Ninety-Three Dollars by Close
sections.body: Alibaba priced its shares at $68 on September 18, 2014. They opened the next day at $92.70 and closed at $93.89, up 38 percent. Bankers then sold extra shares, lifting the total to $25 billion. Years of growth followed. In 2020 Chinese regulators halted the IPO of Ant Group, Alibaba's payments affiliate, and Jack Ma stepped back from public life. Alibaba added a Hong Kong listing in 2019 and still trades in New York as BABA.

cover.theme: a cave mouth (open sesame)
cover.artwork: Sagami Province: Entrance to the Caves at Enoshima (Sagami, Enoshima iwaya no guchi)

fate: Still public, renamed Everpure in 2026 (NYSE: P)
dek: Pure Storage replaced the slow spinning disks in company data centers with fast, simple flash memory.
lede: Pure Storage started life inside a venture capital office under the code name OS76. Its founders believed the spinning hard disk, the workhorse of every corporate data center, was finished. Flash memory was getting cheap enough to replace it. When Pure filed to go public in 2015, it was selling all-flash storage arrays to big companies and fighting giants like EMC and NetApp. Investors had to decide whether a six-year-old company could take that market from the incumbents.

sections.heading: Born in a VC's Spare Room
sections.body: John Colgrove, a founding engineer at Veritas Software, joined Sutter Hill Ventures as an entrepreneur in residence. There he met John Hayes, and in 2009 the two started Pure Storage in Sutter Hill's offices. Colgrove wanted to stay an engineer, so the company hired Scott Dietzen as CEO. Their bet was that flash could cost about the same as disk once software squeezed more data into it. Faster storage would then sell itself.

sections.heading: A Dip Below Seventeen
sections.body: Pure priced its IPO at $17 a share in October 2015 and raised $425 million on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock fell on day one and closed at $16.01, down 5.8 percent. The company kept growing and sold storage for AI workloads. In February 2026 it renamed itself Everpure to reflect a broader push into data management. In April 2026 its ticker changed from PSTG to a single letter, P.

cover.theme: a stored harvest under snow (data kept safe)
cover.artwork: Stack of Wheat (Snow Effect, Overcast Day)

tagline: A Firewall Up in the Cloud
dek: Zscaler let companies protect workers anywhere by checking their internet traffic in the cloud instead of in office boxes.
lede: Jay Chaudhry grew up in a village in the Himalayas, and Zscaler was the fifth company he started. The first four had all been sold. By 2018, office workers were spread across laptops, phones, and coffee shops, yet most companies still guarded their networks with hardware firewalls in a server room. Zscaler ran the checks in its own data centers around the world. When it filed to go public, it was the first big tech IPO of the year.

sections.heading: Moving the Wall
sections.body: Chaudhry founded Zscaler with K. Kailash. The idea was to stop routing traffic back to headquarters for inspection. Instead, every user connected to the nearest Zscaler data center, which scanned for threats and enforced company rules before passing traffic on. The pitch fit a world where email, files, and sales tools were moving to the cloud too. Customers paid a subscription per user. They had no boxes to buy, ship, or patch.

sections.heading: Double on Day One
sections.body: Zscaler priced 12 million shares at $16 each on March 15, 2018, above its expected range, and raised about $192 million. On Nasdaq the next day the stock opened at $27.50 and more than doubled. It closed with a market value near $4 billion. Remote work during the pandemic made its model the norm. Zscaler still trades on Nasdaq as ZS, with Chaudhry as CEO.

cover.theme: a Himalayan peak above the clouds

tagline: The Phone That Rings at 3 A.M.
dek: PagerDuty woke up the right engineer the moment a website or app broke, so outages got fixed faster.
lede: Three former Amazon engineers built PagerDuty because they were tired of being woken up the wrong way. At Amazon they had carried pagers for on-call shifts, and the tools for it were clumsy. By 2019, nearly every business ran on software, and every minute of downtime cost money. PagerDuty listened to a company's monitoring tools and called, texted, or pinged the right person when something failed. It filed to go public in a busy spring for software IPOs.

sections.heading: Waterloo Grads on Call
sections.body: Alex Solomon, Andrew Miklas, and Baskar Puvanathasan studied at the University of Waterloo and worked together at Amazon. In 2009 they started PagerDuty in Toronto, then moved it to San Francisco. The product began as a simple scheduler that knew who was on call and kept trying until someone answered. It grew into a platform for managing incidents. Teams paid a monthly fee per user.

sections.heading: A Fifty-Nine Percent Jump
sections.body: PagerDuty priced its IPO at $24 a share on April 10, 2019, above a range it had already raised. It listed on the New York Stock Exchange as PD the next day and closed up 59 percent. Growth later slowed. The company explored a sale, and in August 2026 it cut about 15 percent of its staff. PagerDuty still trades on the NYSE as PD.

cover.theme: sailors on watch (eight bells, the change of shift)

dek: Fiverr let anyone hire a freelancer for a logo or a translation as easily as buying a book online.
lede: Fiverr took its name from a price tag. When it launched, every job on the site cost $5, whether a business card design or a short voiceover. By 2019 sellers charged far more, and the Tel Aviv company had handled over 50 million transactions between 5.5 million buyers and 830,000 sellers. Freelance work was growing, but hiring a stranger online still felt risky. Fiverr pitched itself to Wall Street as a store where services came with a fixed price and a clear description.

sections.heading: Services on a Shelf
sections.body: Micha Kaufman and Shai Wininger started Fiverr in 2010. Most freelance sites made buyers post a job and wait for bids. Fiverr flipped that. Sellers listed a packaged service, called a gig, with a set price and delivery time, and buyers picked one like a product off a shelf. Fiverr took a cut of each order. Its apps for iPhone and Android followed in 2013 and 2014.

sections.heading: Ninety Percent on Day One
sections.body: Fiverr priced its IPO at $21 a share on June 12, 2019, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange the next day. The stock opened at $26 and closed at $39.90, up 90 percent. It had never turned a profit. The pandemic brought a rush of remote work, then a long slide. In September 2025 Fiverr cut about 250 jobs, roughly 30 percent of its staff, to become an AI-first company. It still trades on the NYSE as FVRR.

cover.theme: a craftsman at work (a trade for hire)
cover.artwork: The Carpenter, from Arts et Métiers

dek: Datadog gave engineers one screen to watch all their servers and apps, and a warning when something broke.
lede: Before Datadog went public, Cisco offered more than $7 billion to buy it. The founders said no and rang the Nasdaq bell instead. It was 2019, and companies were moving their software onto Amazon, Microsoft, and Google clouds. Their systems had become sprawling and hard to see. Datadog collected the numbers from all of it, put them on shared dashboards, and warned teams before customers noticed a problem. It was a rare New York software company in a Silicon Valley game.

sections.heading: Two Friends From Paris
sections.body: Olivier Pomel and Alexis Lê-Quôc met as students at École Centrale Paris. They later spent nine years together at Wireless Generation, an education software company in New York. There they watched developers and system administrators work at cross purposes. In 2010 they started Datadog to give both groups the same view of their infrastructure. It began with monitoring for cloud servers and added application tracing in 2016, then logs and security.

sections.heading: Twenty-Seven Dollars and Up
sections.body: Datadog priced its IPO at $27 a share on September 18, 2019, selling 24 million shares and raising $648 million. The stock rose about 37 percent on its first day on Nasdaq, and the company ended the day worth nearly $10 billion. It kept buying smaller companies, including Sqreen, Metaplane, and Eppo. By 2024 it had about 6,500 employees in 33 countries. Datadog still trades on Nasdaq as DDOG.

cover.theme: a watchful hound

dek: ZoomInfo sold sales teams a giant, constantly updated directory of companies and the people who make buying decisions inside them.
lede: ZoomInfo went public under a name it had bought. The company began in 2007 as DiscoverOrg, and in 2019 it acquired its rival Zoom Information and took its name. Its product was a database of businesses and the people who work there, with titles, emails, and phone numbers. Salespeople used it to find out who to call. ZoomInfo filed for its IPO in the spring of 2020, as the pandemic pushed nearly every sales team onto phones and video calls.

sections.heading: From DiscoverOrg to ZoomInfo
sections.body: Henry Schuck and Kirk Brown founded DiscoverOrg in 2007. It sold contact data to sales teams that needed to know who made buying decisions at each company. DiscoverOrg bought rivals and tools for checking email addresses, including RainKing, NeverBounce, and Datanyze. Then it bought Zoom Information, a company founded in 2000 as Eliyon Technologies. Customers paid yearly subscriptions to search the combined data.

sections.heading: A New Ticker Named GTM
sections.body: ZoomInfo sold 44.5 million shares at $21 each in June 2020, raising about $935 million on Nasdaq under the ticker ZI. Later it bought Chorus.ai and other tools that listen to sales calls. The company has faced lawsuits over how it collects personal data and over what it told investors. In May 2025 it changed its ticker to GTM, short for go-to-market. ZoomInfo still trades on Nasdaq and bought DoubleO.ai in 2026.

cover.theme: a mountain lookout (seeing the whole market)

fate: Acquired by Vista Equity Partners, 2023 ($19 a share in cash)
dek: Duck Creek sold insurers the software that writes policies, handles claims, and sends bills, delivered from the cloud.
lede: Duck Creek went public in the middle of a pandemic as a company Accenture had spun out four years earlier. Its customers were property and casualty insurers, many still running policy, claims, and billing on aging in-house systems. Duck Creek offered them modern software as a service. When it filed in 2020, insurers were rushing to move work online, and investors were paying high prices for any cloud software that showed steady growth.

sections.heading: Out of Accenture
sections.body: Accenture owned Duck Creek until August 2016, when it sold control to the private equity firm Apax and kept a large stake. The company sold to insurers of every size. Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance, founded in 2013 with no IT systems of its own, used Duck Creek to launch more than forty products in eighteen months. The bet was that insurers would rather rent their core systems than build them.

sections.heading: Bought Back for Nineteen
sections.body: Duck Creek sold 15 million shares at $27 each in August 2020 and listed on Nasdaq as DCT. After the IPO, Apax and Accenture still controlled a majority of the votes. The stock fell as growth slowed. In January 2023 Duck Creek agreed to sell itself to Vista Equity Partners. The deal closed on March 30, 2023, and shareholders received $19 a share in cash, below the IPO price.

cover.theme: ducks on a creek

dek: Palantir built software that let spy agencies, armies, and big companies pull scattered data together and find patterns in it.
lede: Palantir is named after the seeing stones in The Lord of the Rings, and its offices carry names like the Shire and Rivendell. For years its CEO said the company would not go public. Then in 2020 it moved its headquarters from Palo Alto to Denver, criticized Silicon Valley on the way out, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It had never made a profit. Its biggest customers were governments, and many people did not trust it.

sections.heading: PayPal's Fraud Tools, Redeployed
sections.body: Peter Thiel founded Palantir in 2003 with Stephen Cohen, Joe Lonsdale, Alex Karp, and Nathan Gettings. Thiel paid for a prototype built by Gettings, a PayPal engineer, with Lonsdale and Cohen, then Stanford students. He hired Karp, a friend from Stanford Law School, as CEO. The idea was to turn software like PayPal's fraud detection toward catching terrorists. Private investors valued it at $20 billion by late 2015.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing, Then the S&P
sections.body: Palantir skipped a traditional IPO. On September 30, 2020, it went public through a direct listing, letting existing holders sell shares on the NYSE with no underwriters. The exchange set a reference price of $7.25. In February 2023 it reported its first profitable quarter. It joined the S&P 500 in September 2024 and moved its listing to Nasdaq that November. In February 2026 it announced a move to Miami.

cover.theme: a seer (the seeing stone)

dek: Certara let drug makers test medicines on simulated patients first, saving time and money before real trials began.
lede: Since 2014, more than 90 percent of new drugs approved by the FDA came from customers of Certara's software. The company sells biosimulation: computer models that predict how a drug moves through different bodies, run as virtual trials on virtual patients. Seventeen drug regulators, including the FDA, license the same software to check the companies they oversee. Certara filed to go public in late 2020, as the world waited for COVID-19 vaccines.

sections.heading: A Dozen Deals, One Platform
sections.body: Certara grew by buying the tools it needed. By its IPO it had acquired 12 companies, including Simcyp, the core of its simulation platform, and Xenologiq, which started its work in quantitative systems pharmacology. Drug makers used its software to choose doses, plan trials, and answer regulators' questions. Certara also sold consulting and writing services for regulatory filings. Its customers included all of the top 35 drug companies by research spending in 2019.

sections.heading: Owned by EQT, Then Listed
sections.body: Certara priced its IPO at $23 a share in December 2020 and listed on Nasdaq as CERT. The company sold 14.6 million shares and existing holders sold 14.4 million more. A fund advised by the private equity firm EQT kept majority control after the offering. William Feehery, a former DuPont executive, ran the company as CEO. Certara still trades on Nasdaq as CERT.

cover.theme: an anatomical engraving (the virtual patient)
cover.artwork: Interiorum corporis humani partium viva delineatio, from the second edition

fate: Taken private by parent Telus, 2025 (renamed Telus Digital in 2024)
tagline: Born in a Philippine Call Center
dek: TELUS International answered customers, moderated content, and labeled AI training data for big tech brands.
lede: TELUS International began with a Canadian phone company buying a small call center in the Philippines. In 2005 Telus took control of Ambergris Solutions, a boutique customer service firm serving U.S. clients, and renamed it. By 2021 it had grown across Asia, Central America, and Europe. It answered customer calls for tech brands, moderated social media posts, and labeled the data that trains AI models. When it went public, the pandemic had pushed nearly every customer conversation online.

sections.heading: Buying Its Way Abroad
sections.body: Telus added countries one deal at a time. It bought Transactel in 2008 for operations in Guatemala and El Salvador. It took a stake in a Bulgarian and Romanian operator in 2012 and bought Ireland's Voxpro in 2017. Baring Private Equity Asia bought 35 percent of the company in 2016. Just before the IPO it agreed to buy Lionbridge AI, a data annotation business, for $935 million.

sections.heading: Back Home to the Parent
sections.body: TELUS International sold 37 million shares at $25 each in February 2021 and listed in New York and Toronto as TIXT. In 2023 it bought the app developer WillowTree for about $1.2 billion. Its CEO, Jeff Puritt, retired in 2024, and the company renamed itself Telus Digital. In 2025 Telus agreed to buy the shares it did not already own for $539 million. The deal closed on October 31, 2025.

cover.theme: a bridge across the river (connecting customers and brands)

tagline: A Bag for Your Old Clothes
dek: ThredUp let people mail in the clothes they no longer wore and buy secondhand fashion at a steep discount.
lede: ThredUp's business starts with a bag. Sellers order a Clean Out Kit, fill it with clothes they no longer want, and mail it back with a prepaid label. ThredUp sorts, photographs, prices, and lists what it can sell. By the end of 2020 the Oakland company had processed over 100 million secondhand items from 35,000 brands. It filed to go public in early 2021, pitching resale as a cheaper way to dress and a fix for fashion's waste.

sections.heading: Closets Full of Inventory
sections.body: James Reinhart, Chris Homer, and Oliver Lubin started ThredUp in 2009. Reinhart, its CEO, had earlier co-founded a network of charter schools. The bet was that most closets hold clothes nobody wears, and that sorting them at scale could turn them into a store. Buyers saved up to 90 percent off estimated retail prices. In 2018 ThredUp began running resale programs for brands and retailers too.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars a Share
sections.body: ThredUp priced its IPO at $14 a share in March 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as TDUP. At the end of 2020 it had 1.24 million active buyers and 428,000 active sellers. In 2020 it processed just over one million Clean Out bags. It estimated that the clothing Americans throw away each year could fill about one billion of those bags. ThredUp still trades on Nasdaq as TDUP.

cover.theme: laundresses carrying clothes (garments on the move)

dek: SkyWater made chips for other companies in Minnesota, as the only U.S.-owned pure-play silicon foundry.
lede: On April 12, 2021, days before SkyWater's IPO, President Biden held up one of its silicon wafers at the White House and called chips infrastructure. The Minnesota company was the only U.S.-owned pure-play foundry, a factory that makes chips designed by others. Most of the world's chipmaking had moved to Asia. A global chip shortage was stalling car plants. SkyWater went public in April 2021 as a small fab with a national security story.

sections.heading: Cypress's Old Fab
sections.body: SkyWater began in 2017, when the private equity firm Oxbow Industries bought Cypress Semiconductor's chip factory in Bloomington, Minnesota. The plant made chips on 200-millimeter wafers at older 90 and 130 nanometer sizes. SkyWater held the Pentagon's Trusted Foundry status, so it could build chips for defense programs. It also worked with customers to take new technologies from the lab to production. With Google and Efabless, it opened its 130 nanometer design kit to anyone in 2020.

sections.heading: Bought by a Quantum Company
sections.body: SkyWater sold 6.96 million shares at $14 each in April 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as SKYT. Oxbow kept about 73.6 percent of the stock. The company added a fab in Florida and, in June 2025, bought Infineon's 200-millimeter plant in Austin. In January 2026 the quantum computing company IonQ agreed to buy SkyWater for about $1.8 billion in cash and stock. The deal closed in July 2026.

cover.theme: sky over water (SkyWater)

dek: Flywire let students, patients, and travelers pay big bills abroad in their own currency, without wire transfer headaches.
lede: Flywire started out as peerTransfer, a Boston company built to help international students pay tuition. Sending money to a foreign university meant bank wires, unknown fees, and payments that arrived without a name attached. Flywire let students pay in their own currency through methods they already used, from bank transfers to Alipay. By its 2021 IPO it handled payments from over 240 countries and territories in more than 130 currencies, for schools, hospitals, and travel companies.

sections.heading: From peerTransfer to Flywire
sections.body: The company was formed in July 2009 as peerTransfer Corporation and took the name Flywire in 2016. Universities were its first market. Each school got one connection to Flywire, which handled currency conversion, tracked who paid, and settled the money. The same tools fit hospitals chasing bills sent as paper checks, and travel companies taking deposits from abroad. Flywire earned fees on the money it moved.

sections.heading: A Pandemic-Era Debut
sections.body: Flywire sold 10.44 million shares at $24 each in May 2021 and listed on Nasdaq as FLYW. Its engineers worked from Boston, Valencia, Cluj, Chicago, and Tel Aviv. COVID-19 had slowed international student travel, its first market, when the company went public. Its network connected to local payment methods such as Boleto, Trustly, and PayPal's Venmo, so a family in Brazil could pay tuition abroad the way it paid bills at home. Flywire still trades on Nasdaq as FLYW.

cover.theme: kites on the wind (money flying across borders)
cover.artwork: Fukuroi: Famous Kites of Enshu (Fukuroi, meibutsu Enshu dako)

dek: Sprinklr gave big brands one place to post, listen, advertise, and answer customers across every social network.
lede: Sprinklr's first servers sat in the basement of its founder's home. Ragy Thomas, a marketing technology executive, paid for the company himself in 2009. He named it after a garden sprinkler, an image of a brand tending its social media presence with care. Early customers included Cisco, Dell, and Virgin America. By the time Sprinklr filed to go public in 2021, big companies were trying to answer customers on dozens of social channels at once.

sections.heading: Buy the Tool, Rebuild It
sections.body: Thomas had worked at the email marketing company Bigfoot International before starting Sprinklr. The company grew from social posting into ads, listening, and customer care. It bought smaller firms like Dachis Group, TBG Digital, and Get Satisfaction. Then it did something unusual. It retired the tools it bought and had the acquired teams rebuild them inside Sprinklr's own platform. By 2018 it had more than 1,500 customers.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars on the NYSE
sections.body: Sprinklr priced 16.6 million shares at $16 each and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on June 23, 2021. It raised about $266 million, at a value of roughly $4 billion. Its ticker, CXM, stood for customer experience management. In November 2024 Rory Read became CEO, and Thomas moved to an advisory role as chairman. Sprinklr still trades on the NYSE as CXM.

cover.theme: filling watering cans (a brand tending its garden)

tagline: Bought Out of Bankruptcy, Waved Through
dek: Clear let travelers skip airport ID lines by proving who they were with their eyes and fingertips.
lede: Clear went bankrupt once before it went public. The first version, started in 2003 under the journalist Steven Brill, shut down in 2009. Caryn Seidman-Becker and Ken Cornick bought it out of bankruptcy and relaunched it in 2012. By 2021 its pods stood at airports and stadiums, scanning irises and fingerprints so members could skip ID checks. Travel was coming back after the pandemic lockdowns, and Clear filed to go public under the ticker YOU.

sections.heading: A Second Life at the Airport
sections.body: Seidman-Becker and Cornick bought Clear in 2010. Their bet was that people would pay a yearly fee to turn their body into their ID. Airports let Clear operate in exchange for a commission on new members. Airlines like Delta and United gave their frequent fliers discounts. Sports leagues signed on too, so the same scan could get a fan into a ballpark. Clear later gained a patent to use biometric identity as a ticket.

sections.heading: Thirty-One Dollars and a Line
sections.body: Clear sold 13.2 million shares at $31 each in June 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. Its two co-founders kept control through shares with 20 votes each. Security lapses followed. In 2022 a passenger with a false identity got through Clear's system, and lawmakers asked for tighter checks. Critics said it let wealthy flyers buy their way past a public service. Clear still trades on the NYSE as YOU.

cover.theme: a city gate (passing through)
cover.artwork: Raam Gate, from The Eight City Gates of Amsterdam

fate: Delisted from Nasdaq and deregistered with the SEC, 2026
dek: Zenvia let Latin American companies reach customers by SMS, WhatsApp, and chat, from marketing to fraud alerts.
lede: Twilio bought a piece of Zenvia on the day it went public. The American messaging giant agreed to purchase 3.85 million shares in a private placement alongside the IPO. Zenvia was Brazil's version of the same idea: software that lets a company text, call, and chat with its customers at scale. It had started 17 years earlier as a bootstrapped startup in a garage. By 2021 WhatsApp had become the way much of Brazil talked to businesses.

sections.heading: From a Brazilian Garage
sections.body: Cassio Bobsin, a computer science graduate of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, founded the company and ran it as CEO. Zenvia's platform combined channels like SMS, voice, WhatsApp, Instagram, and webchat with tools like chatbots and journey designers. Customers used it for marketing campaigns, onboarding, warnings, customer service, and fraud control. Zenvia earned most of its revenue from the volume of messages sent. It bought Sirena, a WhatsApp sales tool, in 2020.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Home
sections.body: Zenvia sold about 11.5 million shares at $13 each in July 2021 and listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market as ZENV. Bobsin and early investors kept about 94 percent of the voting power. In February 2026 Zenvia renegotiated an earnout it owed for Movidesk, then received a Nasdaq notice that it was out of compliance. Days later it announced a voluntary delisting. It left Nasdaq and deregistered with the SEC in March 2026.

cover.theme: a parrot (a talking bird, Brazil)
cover.artwork: Red Parrot on the Branch of a Tree

fate: Acquired by Thoma Bravo, 2023 ($2.3B); merged into Ping Identity
tagline: Forked From Sun, Forged in Norway
dek: ForgeRock managed logins for big companies, so billions of customers and workers could sign in safely to apps and services.
lede: ForgeRock was born when Oracle bought Sun Microsystems and planned to retire Sun's identity software. A group of former Sun employees in Norway took the open source code and kept building it themselves. The company formed there in 2009 and later moved to San Francisco. By its 2021 IPO it supported billions of identities, used for everything from shopping and banking to signing in at work. Its stated vision was simple: a world where you never log in again.

sections.heading: OpenAM Becomes a Business
sections.body: ForgeRock's products grew from Sun open source projects. Access management came from OpenAM, the directory from OpenDJ, and identity management from OpenIDM. The community versions stayed free, while companies paid for licenses to the enterprise platform. The pitch fit a world of apps and connected devices, where each customer needed one safe identity across many places. By April 2020 ForgeRock had raised $230 million from investors.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five, Then Thoma Bravo
sections.body: ForgeRock sold 11 million shares at $25 each in September 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as FORG. A year later, in October 2022, the private equity firm Thoma Bravo agreed to buy it for $2.3 billion in cash. The deal closed on August 23, 2023. Thoma Bravo folded ForgeRock into Ping Identity, another identity company it owned.

cover.theme: a walled fortress on a rock (ForgeRock, guarding identity)

tagline: One System for the Trading Desk
dek: Enfusion gave hedge funds and asset managers one cloud system for trading, risk, and accounting, replacing patched-together software.
lede: Enfusion began as two Chicago programmers who had seen how badly hedge funds ran their own technology. They had worked inside big funds and watched data leak between fragmented systems and patched-together spreadsheets. More than 24 years before its IPO, they started a fintech consultancy, then brought in a third developer to build one platform for the whole investment process. By 2021 Enfusion served 635 clients, and asset managers were moving their back offices to the cloud.

sections.heading: From the Trade to the Books
sections.body: Enfusion's software ran a fund from the trade to the books. Portfolio managers, traders, risk teams, and accountants worked from the same data. Its clients ranged from hedge funds and private equity funds to family offices and mutual funds. Almost all its revenue came from subscriptions. In 2020 it kept more than 120 percent of its prior-year revenue from existing clients and turned a profit.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars, Then Clearwater
sections.body: Enfusion priced its IPO at $17 a share in October 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ENFN. It sold 15.3 million shares, and existing holders sold 3.4 million more. A new CEO had taken over in March 2020, just as the pandemic hit. In January 2025 Clearwater Analytics agreed to buy Enfusion in cash and stock, valued at about $11.25 a share. The deal closed in April 2025.

cover.theme: LaSalle Street (Chicago's financial district)
cover.artwork: N. W. Corner of LaSalle and Randolph, Chicago, Showing Court House Square

fate: Agreed to be acquired by Salesforce, October 2026 ($47.50 a share in cash)
dek: Braze let apps send the right push, email, or text at the right moment, so customers kept coming back.
lede: Braze was sending more than 100 billion messages a month before it went public. Most were the small nudges people get from their apps: a push alert about a sale, a reminder to finish an order, an email about a new feature. The company began in 2011 as Appboy, built for a world that had just moved onto smartphones. By 2021 brands wanted to talk to customers across every channel at once, and Braze filed to go public.

sections.heading: Appboy Grows Up
sections.body: Bill Magnuson, Jon Hyman, and Mark Ghermezian founded Appboy in New York and raised $3 million to start it. In 2016 they launched Canvas, a tool for building customer journeys that span many messages. A $50 million round followed in 2017, and the company renamed itself Braze. By 2019 it had passed $100 million in annual recurring revenue. In 2020 it joined a boycott of Facebook advertising over content moderation.

sections.heading: From $65 to Salesforce
sections.body: Braze priced its IPO at $65 a share and began trading on Nasdaq as BRZE on November 17, 2021. It raised $520 million at a market value of $5.9 billion. Braze added AI tools under the name Sage and opened offices in Seoul, Dubai, and Bucharest. On October 19, 2026, it agreed to be bought by Salesforce for $47.50 a share in cash.

cover.theme: fishing by torchlight (drawing customers in)
cover.artwork: Fishing by Torch in Kai Province (Koshu hiburi), from the series One Thousand Pictures of the Ocean

tagline: A Whole Country in One App
dek: Kaspi.kz put shopping, payments, loans, and bills for millions in Kazakhstan into a single phone app.
lede: Kaspi.kz started as a small bank and became the app millions of people in Kazakhstan use to pay, shop, and borrow. In 2002 Vyacheslav Kim bought Caspian Bank, a privatized lender. Over the next two decades he and Mikheil Lomtadze turned it into a super app: payments, an online marketplace, and consumer loans in one place. It listed in London in 2020. In January 2024 it came to Nasdaq, in what became the largest U.S. IPO since the previous October.

sections.heading: From Caspian Bank to Kaspi
sections.body: Kim bought the bank in 2002, and the investment firm Baring Vostok took a stake in 2006. Lomtadze joined in 2007, and the two rebuilt it around technology. Caspian Bank became Kaspi Bank in 2008. In 2019 Kaspi launched instant payments between people and shops using its app and QR codes. It bought car, real estate, and classifieds sites in Azerbaijan in 2019 and the Ukrainian payment system Portmone in 2021.

sections.heading: Ninety-Two Dollars a Share
sections.body: Kaspi's Nasdaq debut priced 11.3 million American depositary shares at $92 each in January 2024. The company sold none of them. Kim, Lomtadze, and another holder sold shares, raising over $1 billion. Its London-listed depositary receipts had already traded for more than three years. The deal was one of the first big U.S. listings of 2024. American investors could now buy Kaspi on a U.S. exchange instead of through London. Kaspi.kz still trades on Nasdaq as KSPI.

cover.theme: a crowded market stall (everything in one place)
cover.artwork: Still Life with Dead Game, Fruits, and Vegetables in a Market

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: PONY; also listed in Hong Kong)
dek: Pony.ai built self-driving taxis and trucks, and ran paid driverless rides on public roads in Chinese cities.
lede: By the time Pony.ai went public, its robotaxis had driven more than 33.5 million autonomous kilometers. Over 3.9 million of those had no driver in the seat at all. Riders in Beijing and Guangzhou could summon one from an app. The company had started eight years earlier, founded by two former Baidu engineers in Silicon Valley. It filed in late 2024, as the race to put driverless cars on public roads moved from tests to paying fares.

sections.heading: Two Engineers From Baidu
sections.body: James Peng and Tiancheng Lou founded Pony.ai in December 2016, after working on Baidu's self-driving program in Silicon Valley. The company ran pilots in Guangzhou and in Irvine, California. In 2021 one of its cars hit a road divider in Fremont, and California suspended its driverless testing permit, the first such suspension. Pony kept building in China. It formed a joint venture with Toyota and its Chinese partner GTMC to mass-produce robotaxis.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars on Nasdaq
sections.body: Pony.ai sold 20 million American depositary shares at $13 each in November 2024 and raised about $260 million on Nasdaq. The shares opened around 15 percent above the offer price. In 2025 it tested driverless trucks between Beijing and the Port of Tianjin, signed a deal with Bolt to bring robotaxis to Europe, and added a second listing in Hong Kong in November 2025. Pony.ai still trades on Nasdaq as PONY.

cover.theme: a pony

tagline: Business Trips Without the Expense Report
dek: Navan let companies book work travel, hand out corporate cards, and track expenses in one app.
lede: Navan's name is a palindrome built from "navigate" and "avant," meaning navigating forward. Until 2023 it was called TripActions, a corporate travel booker that had grown into a $9.2 billion startup. Business travel had collapsed in the pandemic and then come back. Navan bet that companies wanted travel booking, company cards, and expense reports in one place, so nobody had to tape receipts to a form. It went public in October 2025 still losing money.

sections.heading: TripActions, Renamed
sections.body: Ariel Cohen and Ilan Twig had already sold one startup, StreamOnce, to Jive Software. In May 2015 they founded TripActions to fix corporate travel booking. Andreessen Horowitz led a $154 million round in 2018 that valued the company above $1 billion. In 2020 it launched TripActions Liquid, a payments and expense product. It bought the German travel company Comtravo in 2022 and rebranded as Navan in February 2023.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Dollars, Still Unprofitable
sections.body: Navan sold 30 million shares at $25 each, and existing holders sold 6.9 million more. It began trading on Nasdaq as NAVN on October 30, 2025. Revenue was growing about 30 percent a year, but the company was not yet profitable. Twig held about 43 percent of the voting power and Cohen about 24 percent. In September 2026 Navan bought BoomPop, an AI events platform.

cover.theme: a triumph of navigation (navigating forward)
cover.artwork: The Thames, or The Triumph of Navigation

dek: Lime put rentable electric scooters and bikes on city streets, unlocked by phone and left wherever the ride ended.
lede: Lime's valuation fell 79 percent in a single funding round in 2020. The scooter company had been worth $2.4 billion a year earlier, and the pandemic had forced it to pause service in 99 percent of its markets. Uber led a rescue round and handed Lime its Jump bike business. Six years later, Lime filed to go public as a growing company. In 2025 it carried about 19 million riders in roughly 230 cities across 29 countries, and its revenue rose 29 percent.

sections.heading: Neutron, Doing Business as Lime
sections.body: Brad Bao and Toby Sun, both executives at the venture arm of China's Fosun International, founded LimeBike in January 2017. Andreessen Horowitz led its first $12 million round. Riders found a scooter or bike on an app map, unlocked it with their phone, and left it at the end of the trip. A 2018 round made it a unicorn. The legal company was named Neutron Holdings, a name it kept through the IPO.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Dollars on Nasdaq
sections.body: Wayne Ting became CEO in 2020, and Lime spent the next years building its own vehicles and its relationships with cities. It filed for its IPO in May 2026 after reporting $886.7 million in revenue for 2025. Lime priced its shares at $25 in July 2026, selling about 6.7 million of them, and listed on Nasdaq as LIME. It still trades there today.

cover.theme: a bicycle on the street

tagline: Half Off, If Enough People Click
dek: Groupon emailed millions of people one half-price local deal a day, unlocked once enough of them bought it.
lede: Groupon said no to Google. In late 2010 the search giant offered about $6 billion for a two-year-old Chicago company that emailed one coupon a day. Groupon turned it down and went to Wall Street instead. Its deals were simple: a spa, a pizza place, or a yoga studio at half off, unlocked only when enough buyers signed up. Inboxes filled with copycats, and investors argued over whether the model could last. When Groupon filed in June 2011, it was the hottest name on the internet.

sections.heading: A Petition Site Finds a Coupon
sections.body: Andrew Mason started a site called The Point in 2007. It let people rally around a cause, and the cause only kicked in once enough people joined. Users kept using it to buy things together. So in November 2008 Mason, with backers Eric Lefkofsky and Brad Keywell, launched Groupon in Chicago. Each day it offered one deal in each city. Merchants gave up their margin for a flood of new customers, and Groupon kept a large cut of every sale.

sections.heading: Twenty-Eight at the Open
sections.body: Groupon priced its IPO at $20 a share on November 3, 2011, above its range. It raised $700 million, the largest offering by a U.S. internet company since Google in 2004. The stock opened at $28 and closed its first day at $26.11. The glow faded fast as growth slowed and deal fatigue set in. The board fired Mason in 2013. Groupon did a 1-for-20 reverse split in 2020, and Dusan Senkypl became CEO in 2023. It still trades on Nasdaq as GRPN.

cover.theme: hucksters bargaining on a beach (the daily deal)
cover.artwork: Fishing Boats with Hucksters Bargaining for Fish

tagline: Let the Customers Come to You
dek: HubSpot gave small businesses the tools to pull in customers with blogs, search, and email instead of cold calls.
lede: HubSpot's founders thought the cold call was dying. Brian Halligan and Dharmesh Shah met at MIT and noticed that people had stopped answering ads and sales pitches. Buyers searched, read blogs, and made up their own minds. So the pair built software to help a business get found online and turn readers into leads. They called the idea inbound marketing and preached it everywhere. When HubSpot filed to go public in August 2014, it sold that idea to thousands of small and midsize companies.

sections.heading: Two Classmates in Cambridge
sections.body: Halligan and Shah founded HubSpot in June 2006 in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Their first product put the pieces of online marketing in one place: a blog, landing pages, email, search tools, and reports on what worked. The customers were small and midsize firms that had no marketing department. HubSpot charged a monthly subscription. Later it added a free customer database and sales tools, so a company could run its whole funnel from one login.

sections.heading: Thirty Dollars by Close
sections.body: HubSpot priced its IPO at $25 a share on October 8, 2014, and began trading on the NYSE as HUBS the next day. The stock rose about 20 percent and closed just over $30, valuing the company near $900 million. HubSpot then grew into a full suite of marketing, sales, and service software. Yamini Rangan became CEO in 2021. Google looked at buying the company in 2024 and walked away. Revenue passed $3.1 billion in 2025, and HubSpot still trades as HUBS.

cover.theme: a quiet harbor (inbound: ships coming to you)

dek: Match Group owned the apps where millions of single people met, from Match.com to OkCupid to Tinder.
lede: The company behind Tinder went public just as swiping became the way a generation dated. Match Group was a bundle of dating brands that Barry Diller's IAC had gathered for years. It started with Match.com, a 1995 website, and grew to include OkCupid, PlentyOfFish, and Tinder. Tinder was barely three years old and already the brand everyone talked about. When Match Group filed in October 2015, investors had to price a business built on people looking for love on their phones.

sections.heading: Personal Ads Go Online
sections.body: Gary Kremen founded Match.com in 1995 as one of the first dating sites on the web. IAC bought it in 1999 and kept adding brands. In February 2009 IAC formed Match Group to hold them all, run from Dallas. Its bet was breadth. Different apps fit different people, from older singles who wanted long profiles to students who wanted a quick swipe. Most use was free. Match Group earned its money from members who paid for subscriptions and extra features.

sections.heading: Priced at the Low End
sections.body: Match Group priced its IPO at $12 a share on November 18, 2015, at the bottom of its range. It raised about $400 million at a market value of $2.9 billion and rose in its first day of trading on Nasdaq as MTCH. IAC still held most of the stock. In July 2020 IAC split off its stake, and Match Group became a fully independent company. Spencer Rascoff took over as CEO in February 2025. The stock still trades as MTCH.

cover.theme: a pair of lovers (the match)

tagline: Card Machines for Brazil's Corner Shops
dek: StoneCo gave Brazilian shopkeepers card readers, fast payouts, and real people to call when something broke.
lede: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway bought into a Brazilian card-machine company on its way to Nasdaq. StoneCo's founders had spent twelve years starting and selling payment businesses in Brazil, where a few big banks controlled how shops took cards. Small merchants paid high fees and got poor service. Stone set out to win them one at a time with local sales teams and quick support. When it filed in 2018, Stone was betting that service could beat size.

sections.heading: Twelve Years of Payments
sections.body: André Street and Eduardo Pontes had built Braspag, a leading online payments gateway in Brazil, before the idea for Stone came to them in 2012. They started with online merchants and plugged them in through simple software. Then they moved into physical stores, where most Brazilian commerce happened. Stone placed sales and service staff in local hubs close to its clients. It earned fees on each card payment and on advancing merchants their money early.

sections.heading: A Billion-Dollar Debut
sections.body: StoneCo priced its IPO at $24 a share on October 24, 2018, above its $21 to $23 range. It raised about $1.1 billion, and Ant Financial bought $100 million more in a side deal. Berkshire Hathaway and T. Rowe Price were among the backers. The stock rose about 30 percent on its first day on Nasdaq. A push into lending went badly in 2021, and the stock fell far below its offering price. StoneCo still trades on Nasdaq as STNE.

cover.theme: a stone bridge (Stone, a bridge for payments)

tagline: Keeping Track of Every Firewall Rule
dek: Tufin let big companies see and change thousands of firewall rules from one screen without breaking anything.
lede: Tufin went private for a dollar less than its IPO price. In between, it sold a fix for a quiet mess inside large companies. Big firms ran hundreds of firewalls from different vendors, each stuffed with rules nobody remembered writing. One wrong change could cut off a business or open a hole for attackers. Tufin's software mapped those rules, tested changes before they went live, and kept a record for auditors. When it filed in 2019, more than 2,000 customers in over 70 countries had bought it.

sections.heading: One Console for Every Wall
sections.body: Ruvi Kitov and Reuven Harrison founded Tufin in Israel in 2005. Firewalls from Cisco, Check Point, and Palo Alto Networks each had their own tools, and security teams changed rules by hand. Tufin sat on top of all of them. Its suite showed how traffic could flow across the network and automated the routine requests that piled up in IT queues. It sold mostly perpetual licenses plus maintenance to banks, telecoms, and other large firms.

sections.heading: Fourteen In, Thirteen Out
sections.body: Tufin priced its IPO at $14 a share on April 11, 2019, and listed on the NYSE as TUFN. As a public company it struggled to keep growth steady while it shifted toward subscriptions, and the stock spent long stretches below its offering price. In April 2022 private equity firm Turn/River Capital agreed to buy Tufin for $13 a share in cash, valuing it at about $570 million. The deal closed in August 2022, and Tufin left the NYSE.

cover.theme: a gate in city ramparts (the firewall)
cover.artwork: Exterior View of the Italian Gate of the Ramparts of the Town of Dresden

dek: Chewy shipped pet food to your door on a schedule, with service reps who sent flowers when a pet died.
lede: PetSmart paid $3.35 billion for an online pet store in 2017, then the biggest e-commerce deal on record. Two years later it took that store public. Chewy had started in Florida as Mr. Chewy, selling heavy bags of food and litter that nobody wanted to carry home. Its customers signed up for Autoship and never had to think about running out. Its phone reps were famous for handwritten cards. When Chewy filed in 2019, it was one of the few online retailers Amazon had not crushed.

sections.heading: Mr. Chewy in South Florida
sections.body: Ryan Cohen and Michael Day founded the company in June 2011. They bet that pet owners were loyal and that pet food was a repeat purchase made for a subscription. Chewy shipped fast, took calls around the clock, and treated each pet as family. Sumit Singh replaced Cohen as CEO in March 2018. By then Chewy belonged to PetSmart, which private equity firm BC Partners controlled.

sections.heading: Fifty-Nine Percent on Day One
sections.body: Chewy priced its IPO at $22 a share in June 2019 and raised about $1 billion. It listed on the NYSE as CHWY and jumped about 59 percent on its first day. The pandemic sent new pet owners flooding to the site in 2020. Cohen moved on and later became chairman and then CEO of GameStop. BC Partners kept a large stake in Chewy and sold shares over time. Chewy still trades on the NYSE as CHWY.

cover.theme: a white dog (the pet at home)

tagline: One Login to Rule the Office
dek: Ping Identity let workers and customers sign in once and safely reach every app a big company ran.
lede: Ping Identity was bought by private equity twice in six years. In between, it went public. The Denver company sold the plumbing behind a simple promise: sign in once and get into everything. Big companies had piled up hundreds of apps, in their own data centers and in the cloud, each with its own password. Ping checked who you were and passed that trust along. When it filed in 2019, the old office firewall mattered less every year, and identity was becoming the new front door.

sections.heading: Passwords Without Borders
sections.body: Andre Durand and Bryan Field-Elliot founded Ping Identity in 2002. Their goal was to replace older controls such as VPNs and firewalls with security built around the person logging in. Ping co-wrote open standards that let one system vouch for a user to another. It added a cloud service in 2012, multi-factor sign-in in 2014, and tools that judged risk from device and behavior. In June 2016 Vista Equity Partners bought a majority stake for $600 million.

sections.heading: From Fifteen to Twenty-Eight Fifty
sections.body: Ping priced its IPO at $15 a share on September 19, 2019, and listed on the NYSE as PING. Goldman Sachs led the deal. Vista kept control after the offering. In August 2022 Thoma Bravo agreed to buy Ping for $28.50 a share in cash, about $2.8 billion. The deal closed on October 18, 2022, and Ping left the market. Thoma Bravo had also bought rival ForgeRock, and in August 2023 it combined the two companies under the Ping Identity name.

cover.theme: a masked portrait (who are you, really)

fate: Taken private by JD.com, 2025 ($2 per ADS)
tagline: Groceries Across Town Within an Hour
dek: Dada brought supermarket orders to Chinese homes within the hour, using hundreds of thousands of riders on call.
lede: Dada went public at $16 a share and left five years later at $2. In 2020 its riders were everywhere. In the year before the IPO, more than 634,000 of them delivered 822 million orders across China. Dada ran two linked businesses. Dada Now was an open delivery network any shop could hire. JD-Daojia let shoppers order from Walmart and local supermarkets on their phones. When it filed in May 2020, lockdowns had taught millions of people to buy groceries online.

sections.heading: A Rider Network, Then a Store
sections.body: Philip Kuai started Dada Now around 2014 as an on-demand delivery platform for merchants and individual senders. In 2016 it bought JD-Daojia, the local retail arm of e-commerce giant JD.com. The deal made JD a major shareholder, and Walmart invested too. The bet was that riders and storefronts work better together. Supermarkets got an online channel without building one, and Dada's riders had steady orders to carry between them.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars Down to Two
sections.body: Dada priced its IPO at $16 per American depositary share on June 5, 2020, and listed on Nasdaq as DADA. Goldman Sachs, BofA Securities, and Jefferies ran the deal. Growth slowed and the stock slid for years. JD.com raised its stake to a majority and in April 2025 agreed to buy the rest. The deal closed on June 16, 2025, at $2 per share, and Dada left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a courier on horseback (the delivery rider)

dek: Snowflake let companies pour all their data into the cloud and query it without managing a single server.
lede: Warren Buffett almost never buys IPOs. He bought Snowflake. Berkshire Hathaway and Salesforce each agreed to put $250 million into the data company at its offering price. Snowflake ran a data warehouse in the cloud. Companies loaded their sales records, logs, and customer data into it and paid for the computing they used. Storage and computing were split, so a team could scale either one up in seconds. When it filed in August 2020, much of the world was working from home.

sections.heading: Three Engineers From Oracle
sections.body: Benoît Dageville and Thierry Cruanes spent years building databases at Oracle. Marcin Żukowski had co-founded a database startup in the Netherlands. In July 2012 the three founded Snowflake in San Mateo. They built for the cloud from the first line of code, on top of Amazon's storage. Old warehouses had to be sized and tuned by experts. Snowflake ran itself. Frank Slootman, who had taken ServiceNow public, became CEO in May 2019.

sections.heading: Double by the Close
sections.body: Snowflake priced its IPO at $120 a share on September 15, 2020, and raised about $3.4 billion. It opened at $245 the next day on the NYSE and closed at $253.93, more than double the offering price. It ranked among the largest software IPOs ever. Sridhar Ramaswamy replaced Slootman as CEO in February 2024. Product revenue reached $4.72 billion in the fiscal year that ended January 2026. Snowflake still trades as SNOW.

cover.theme: a hill after snowfall (snowflake)

tagline: Facebook's Co-Founder Builds a To-Do List
dek: Asana gave teams one shared place to see who was doing what, by when, so fewer meetings got wasted.
lede: One of Facebook's co-founders left to build software for planning work. Dustin Moskovitz had watched Facebook's own teams lose hours chasing status updates. With engineer Justin Rosenstein he started Asana to fix that. Teams used it to track tasks, projects, and goals in one shared place, and many started on a free plan. By early 2020 more than 82,000 customers were paying. Asana went public by direct listing in September 2020, while offices sat empty and work had moved online.

sections.heading: An Internal Tool Escapes
sections.body: Moskovitz and Rosenstein founded Asana in December 2008. Rosenstein had worked at Google and Facebook, where he worked on the Like button. Their first version grew from a task tracker they had built inside Facebook. Asana spread from the bottom up. A single team would try it, then the rest of the company would follow and upgrade to a paid plan. Its name comes from the Sanskrit word for a yoga pose.

sections.heading: A Direct Listing at Twenty-One
sections.body: Asana skipped a traditional IPO and listed its shares directly on the NYSE as ASAN on September 30, 2020. The reference price was $21 a share. Moskovitz bought large blocks of stock in the years that followed. In March 2025 he said he would retire as CEO, and the shares fell 25 percent. Dan Rogers took over on July 21, 2025, with Moskovitz staying on as chairman. Asana still trades on the NYSE as ASAN.

cover.theme: a figure in balance (asana, a yoga pose)

dek: Upstart let banks approve more borrowers at lower rates by judging loans with AI instead of credit scores alone.
lede: Upstart told banks its model could approve up to three times as many borrowers at the same loss rates. Dave Girouard, who once ran Google's enterprise business, had built a lender around that claim. Upstart looked past the credit score at education, job history, and many other variables. Banks and credit unions used its platform to make personal loans online. When it filed in late 2020, interest rates were near zero and investors were hungry for fintech.

sections.heading: A Google Executive Starts Over
sections.body: Girouard left Google and founded Upstart in April 2012 with Anna Counselman and Paul Gu. Their bet was that the standard credit score shut out millions of people who would repay. Upstart trained models on loan outcomes and kept feeding them more data. Most loans went to bank partners or investors, so Upstart earned fees for sending borrowers and running the process.

sections.heading: Up Twentyfold, Then Down
sections.body: Upstart priced its IPO at $20 a share on December 15, 2020, and began trading on Nasdaq as UPST the next day. By the fall of 2021 the stock had climbed above $300. Then interest rates rose, the investors who bought its loans pulled back, and the shares lost more than 90 percent of their value. In May 2026 co-founder Paul Gu took over as CEO, and Girouard became executive chairman. Upstart still trades as UPST.

cover.theme: young colts on a marsh (upstarts)

dek: Viant gave advertisers software to buy ads on connected TVs, phones, streaming audio, and billboards from one screen.
lede: The ad-tech company that went public in 2021 still owned Myspace. Three brothers, Tim, Chris, and Russ Vanderhook, had started it in Irvine, California, in 1999 and run it ever since. By the time it filed, its core product was Adelphic, software that let marketers plan and buy ads across desktop, mobile, connected TV, audio, and digital billboards. Connected TV made up 34 percent of its revenue. Cookies were on their way out, and Viant pitched ads aimed at real households instead.

sections.heading: Twenty Years in the Family
sections.body: The Vanderhooks founded the business in 1999 and have led it the whole way, with Tim as CEO and Chris as chief operating officer. In 2011 the company, then called Specific Media, bought Myspace from News Corp. Later it rebuilt itself around a demand-side platform, the software ad buyers use to bid on ad space. Viant's pitch was people-based targeting. It matched ads to households rather than browser cookies, which mattered more as privacy rules tightened.

sections.heading: A Family Firm on Nasdaq
sections.body: Viant priced its IPO at $25 a share on February 9, 2021, and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker DSP, short for demand-side platform. BofA Securities and UBS led the deal. The brothers kept control through a separate class of voting shares. The stock fell well below its offering price as ad markets cooled after 2021. Viant kept investing in connected TV and automated buying tools. It still trades on Nasdaq as DSP.

cover.theme: a crowd watching a spectacle (the ad audience)

dek: Zhihu gave millions of Chinese readers a place to ask hard questions and get long, thoughtful answers from experts.
lede: Zhihu's name carries a question: "Do you know?" For its first two years you could only join if someone invited you. Zhou Yuan started the question-and-answer site in late 2010, and its early members wrote long, careful answers. It opened to everyone in 2013 and grew into one of China's largest content communities. By the end of 2020, 43.1 million creators had posted 315.3 million questions and answers. Zhihu filed for its New York IPO in March 2021.

sections.heading: Invitation Only
sections.body: Zhou Yuan founded Zhihu in late 2010, and the site went live in January 2011. Between 2010 and 2012 it stayed invite-only, which kept the answers careful and the tone serious. Once registration opened, the community spread from tech into careers, history, science, and daily life. Zhihu started selling ads in 2016. Later it added paid memberships for premium content.

sections.heading: New York, Then Hong Kong
sections.body: Zhihu priced its IPO at $9.50 per American depositary share and began trading on the NYSE as ZH on March 26, 2021. It had 75.7 million average monthly users in the last quarter of 2020. Affiliates of Tencent and JD.com bought shares alongside the offering. Beijing's crackdown on its tech giants hit Chinese stocks soon after. Zhihu added a second listing in Hong Kong in April 2022 and still trades in both cities.

cover.theme: a sage dictating to listeners (questions and answers)

fate: Agreed to be acquired by Nielsen, 2026 ($13.60 a share; pending)
dek: DoubleVerify told advertisers whether their online ads were real, seen by people, and kept away from ugly content.
lede: DoubleVerify went public at $27 a share. Five years later Nielsen agreed to buy it for $13.60. In between, it checked more than 5 billion digital ad transactions a day. Brands paid it to check each ad. It told them whether a person or a bot saw it, whether it ran in the right country, and whether it sat next to hate speech. When DoubleVerify filed in March 2021, ad budgets were pouring online, and so was fraud.

sections.heading: An Auditor for Every Ad
sections.body: DoubleVerify started in New York in 2008. Online ads ran across thousands of sites, apps, and exchanges, and advertisers had no neutral way to see where their money went. DoubleVerify sat in the middle as an independent referee. Its software could block a bad placement before the ad was bought and measure the ones that ran. It boiled the results into one score, the DV Authentic Ad. Providence Equity Partners bought a controlling stake in 2017.

sections.heading: From Twenty-Seven to Thirteen Sixty
sections.body: DoubleVerify priced its IPO at $27 a share on April 20, 2021, and listed on the NYSE as DV the next day. Tiger Global bought $60 million of stock alongside the deal. Growth slowed, and the stock slid. In August 2026 the parent of Nielsen agreed to buy DoubleVerify for $13.60 a share in cash, about half its IPO price. The deal was still pending in October 2026.

cover.theme: a reflection (seeing double, checking twice)

dek: 1stDibs let collectors anywhere buy vintage furniture, art, and jewelry from the world's top dealers.
lede: 1stDibs began with one man's trip to the Paris flea market. Michael Bruno loved the vintage furniture there and wanted to put the best dealers' stock online. He started a listings site in 2000, then moved it to New York and signed up American sellers. Over two decades it became the place designers went for a Danish sideboard or an Art Deco lamp. Each month in 2020 buyers and sellers traded more than 36,000 messages. It filed for its IPO in May 2021.

sections.heading: First Look for the Trade
sections.body: The name plays on "first dibs," the right to claim something before anyone else. Bruno built 1stDibs to give buyers that early look at the best dealers' stock. Over time the site became a marketplace that took a commission on each sale. Its sellers were mostly small businesses, and many called 1stDibs their main sales channel. David Rosenblatt, a former Google executive, became CEO and expanded into art, jewelry, and fashion.

sections.heading: Twenty Dollars a Share
sections.body: 1stDibs priced its IPO at $20 a share in June 2021 and began trading on Nasdaq as DIBS. The pandemic home boom faded soon after, and high-end furniture sales slowed with the housing market. Revenue fell 13 percent in 2023 to $84.7 million, and the company cut costs. In 2025 it posted its first full year of positive adjusted EBITDA as a public company. 1stDibs still trades on Nasdaq as DIBS.

cover.theme: secondhand dealers on a Paris street (the flea market)

tagline: A Network Only Doctors Could Join
dek: Doximity gave American doctors a private network to message colleagues, send faxes, and run video visits from their phones.
lede: Doximity saved up to 15 percent of its IPO shares for the doctors who used it. That was a lot of doctors. More than 80 percent of U.S. physicians were members, along with over 90 percent of graduating medical students. The network let them find colleagues, read medical news, and handle chores like faxing and phone calls from an app. When it filed in June 2021, the pandemic had pushed doctors into telehealth, and Doximity's free video calling tool had caught on.

sections.heading: From Epocrates to Doximity
sections.body: Jeff Tangney had co-founded Epocrates, a drug-reference app that lived on doctors' handheld devices. In April 2010 he started Doximity as a professional network for physicians only. Members verified that they were medical professionals. The tools were free for doctors. Doximity earned its money from drug makers and health systems that paid to reach its members with marketing and job listings. It was profitable years before its IPO.

sections.heading: Doctors Bought In
sections.body: Doximity priced its IPO at $26 a share on June 23, 2021, and listed on the NYSE as DOCS. The stock more than doubled in its first day of trading. By then it had over 1.8 million medical professional members. Tangney stayed on as CEO and kept outsized voting power through a dual-class share structure. Doximity still trades on the NYSE as DOCS.

cover.theme: an allegory of the physician (a network for doctors)
cover.artwork: The Physician Considered as God, plate one from Allegories of the Medical Profession

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: HEPS); controlled by Kaspi.kz since 2025
dek: Hepsiburada let shoppers across Turkey order almost anything online, from phones to groceries, with fast delivery.
lede: Hepsiburada means "everything is here" in Turkish, and the name was the plan. Hanzade Doğan Boyner, from one of Turkey's best-known business families, started the store in 2000, when few Turks shopped online. Two decades later it sold electronics, fashion, groceries, and more to millions of customers, with its own delivery network behind it. It called itself one of the few tech companies anywhere founded by a woman. It went public on Nasdaq in 2021, while the lira was sliding.

sections.heading: A Store Built in Istanbul
sections.body: Doğan Boyner founded Hepsiburada in 2000 as an online retailer that bought and sold its own stock. In 2015 it opened a marketplace to outside merchants, who paid commissions to reach its shoppers. It built its own warehouses and a delivery company, HepsiJet, which ran in 63 cities by 2021. It added HepsiPay for payments and HepsiExpress, which brought groceries in 30 to 60 minutes. The bet was that owning delivery would win Turkish shoppers' trust.

sections.heading: From Doğan to Kaspi
sections.body: D-Market, the company behind Hepsiburada, priced its IPO at $12 per American depositary share and listed on Nasdaq as HEPS in July 2021. The shares fell soon after as Turkey's currency crisis deepened. In October 2024 Doğan Boyner and her family agreed to sell their controlling stake to Kaspi.kz, a Kazakh fintech and shopping company. The sale closed in January 2025, and Kaspi now owns about 86 percent. The ADSs still trade on Nasdaq as HEPS.

cover.theme: Constantinople on the Bosphorus (Istanbul)
cover.artwork: Contantinople - Fountain of Sweet Waters on the Asiatic Shore of the Bosphorus

fate: Bought Teads and renamed itself Teads Holding Co., 2025 (NASDAQ: TEAD)
dek: Outbrain filled the bottom of news articles with recommended links, and paid publishers for every click.
lede: Outbrain went public at $20 a share. Five years later, under a new name, its stock traded below $1. In between, it built the box of links that sits under countless news stories. Outbrain's software guessed what a reader might click next, mixing a publisher's own stories with paid ones from advertisers. Every click earned money, and Outbrain shared it with the publisher. When it filed in 2021, newsrooms were short of cash, and these links paid a real share of their bills.

sections.heading: Two Israelis and a Widget
sections.body: Yaron Galai and Ori Lahav founded Outbrain in Israel in 2006 and later based it in New York. The first product suggested related articles to keep readers on a site. Paid recommendations came next, and they became the business. Outbrain signed big publishers around the world and fought a long battle with its rival Taboola. The two agreed to merge in 2019, then called off the deal in 2020.

sections.heading: A New Name, a Lower Price
sections.body: Outbrain priced its IPO at $20 a share on July 22, 2021, and listed on Nasdaq as OB. Ad markets cooled, and the stock spent most of its public life below that price. In February 2025 Outbrain closed its purchase of Teads, a video ad company, for about $1 billion, and took the Teads name and the ticker TEAD. In August 2026 Nasdaq warned the company that its shares had closed below $1 for 30 business days in a row.

cover.theme: a family reading the newspaper (what to read next)
cover.artwork: Reading the newspaper in the family circle

tagline: From a Chennai Warehouse to Nasdaq
dek: Freshworks sold simple, low-cost help desk and sales software to businesses that found the big brands too costly.
lede: Freshworks started in a 700-square-foot warehouse in Chennai, India. Its founder, Girish Mathrubootham, had a bad customer service experience and decided to build a fresher help desk. Skeptics told him there were already 600 help desks on the market and that nobody could build a global software company from India. Freshworks priced its products low, let customers try them for free, and sold over the internet. By 2021 it sold software for support, IT, sales, and marketing to businesses around the world.

sections.heading: Six Hundred Help Desks
sections.body: Mathrubootham and Shan Krishnasamy founded the company as Freshdesk in 2010. They aimed at small and midsize businesses that the big vendors ignored. Customers could sign up online and start in minutes, with little help from a salesperson. The company later added IT service, sales, and marketing tools and renamed itself Freshworks. It moved its headquarters to San Mateo, California, while much of its team stayed in Chennai.

sections.heading: Thirty-Six Dollars a Share
sections.body: Freshworks priced its IPO at $36 a share on September 21, 2021, and began trading on Nasdaq as FRSH the next day. It was one of the first India-born software companies to list in the U.S. The shares rose on the first day, then sank in the 2022 sell-off of software stocks. Dennis Woodside became CEO in 2024, and Mathrubootham stayed on as executive chairman. Freshworks still trades on Nasdaq as FRSH.

cover.theme: spring growth (a fresh start)

fate: Acquired by Salesforce, 2025 ($25 a share, about $8B)
tagline: Going Public for the Second Time
dek: Informatica moved, cleaned, and connected a company's data so its systems and analysts could trust it.
lede: Informatica went public twice. It first listed in 1999, spent a decade and a half as a public company, and was taken private in 2015 by Permira and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board for about $5.3 billion. Six years later it came back with a new pitch. The old business sold licenses for software that moved data between systems. The new Informatica sold the same skills as a cloud subscription, just as companies raced to feed data into analytics and AI.

sections.heading: The Plumbing of Data
sections.body: Gaurav Dhillon and Diaz Nesamoney founded Informatica in 1993. Big companies kept customer, sales, and supply data in dozens of systems that did not talk to each other. Informatica's tools pulled that data together, cleaned it, and kept it in sync. The work was unglamorous and hard to rip out once installed. Under private ownership the company began moving customers from licenses to cloud subscriptions, with Amit Walia as CEO.

sections.heading: Back on the NYSE, Then Salesforce
sections.body: Informatica priced its second IPO at $29 a share in October 2021 and listed on the NYSE as INFA. Permira and CPP Investments kept control. The stock spent most of the next years below its offering price. In May 2025 Salesforce agreed to buy Informatica for $25 a share in cash, about $8 billion. The deal closed on November 18, 2025, and Informatica left the NYSE.

cover.theme: weaving silk (threads of data woven together)
cover.artwork: Weaving silk, plate 11 from the series "Silkworm Cultivation"

tagline: From Bitcoin Mines to AI Clouds
dek: IREN built renewable-powered data centers to mine bitcoin, then rented them out for AI computing.
lede: A bitcoin miner signed a deal with Microsoft worth about $9.7 billion. Four years earlier it had gone public as Iris Energy, run by two Australian brothers. Daniel and William Roberts built data centers in places with cheap, clean power, such as British Columbia, where the grid ran almost entirely on hydro. They filled them with machines that mined bitcoin. When the company filed in 2021, bitcoin was near its peak and investors wanted miners that could claim green credentials.

sections.heading: Two Brothers and Cheap Power
sections.body: Daniel and William Roberts founded the company in 2018 and serve as co-CEOs. They bought their first site in British Columbia in January 2020. The business was simple: secure power and land, build the buildings and electrical gear, and run mining machines around the clock. Owning the whole site gave them control over costs. That same infrastructure, it turned out, could house the graphics chips that AI companies were desperate to rent.

sections.heading: Renamed for a New Customer
sections.body: Iris Energy priced its IPO at $28 a share on November 16, 2021, and listed on Nasdaq. Bitcoin crashed in 2022, and the stock fell to a fraction of its offering price. The company began running GPUs for AI customers and renamed itself IREN in 2024. In November 2025 it signed a contract with Microsoft worth about $9.7 billion for AI cloud capacity in Texas. IREN delivered the first phase in August 2026 and still trades on Nasdaq as IREN.

cover.theme: cranes in an iris pond at sunrise (Iris Energy)
cover.artwork: Cranes in an Iris Pond at Sunrise

dek: Reddit gave strangers thousands of forums to swap advice, jokes, and news, ranked by the votes of other users.
lede: Reddit set aside 8 percent of its IPO shares for the people who built it for free: its users and moderators. The site was nearly 19 years old by then. It had grown from a link board started by two college friends into a sprawl of communities on everything from parenting to quitting drinking. Volunteers ran most of them. Reddit filed in February 2024, as AI companies were paying for human conversation to train their models, and Reddit had two decades of it.

sections.heading: Two Roommates and a Link Board
sections.body: Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian founded Reddit in June 2005, right after college, with backing from Y Combinator. Users posted links, and votes pushed the best ones up the page. Condé Nast bought the site in 2006. Huffman later left, then came back as CEO in 2015. Reddit's founding idea held: a real place shaped by real people, with moderators instead of editors.

sections.heading: Fifty Dollars by the Close
sections.body: Reddit priced its IPO at $34 a share on March 20, 2024, and listed on the NYSE as RDDT the next day. It opened at $47 and closed at $50.44, up 48 percent. Just before the IPO it signed a deal letting Google use its posts to train AI. In late 2024 Reddit turned its first quarterly profit, and its user numbers climbed as Google search sent more people its way. Reddit still trades on the NYSE as RDDT.

cover.theme: the Roman Forum (the town square of the internet)

dek: ServiceTitan gave plumbers, roofers, and HVAC crews one app to book jobs, dispatch techs, and get paid.
lede: ServiceTitan's founders grew up watching their fathers type invoices at the kitchen table. Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan were sons of Armenian immigrants who worked in the trades. They met on an Armenian Student Association ski trip and found they shared the same story. After engineering school, both saw their families' businesses still running on paper and shoeboxes of receipts. So they built software for plumbers, electricians, and HVAC contractors. ServiceTitan filed to go public in November 2024.

sections.heading: Built for Their Fathers
sections.body: The first customers were the founders' own parents. ServiceTitan pulled scheduling, dispatch, pricing, invoicing, and payments into one system, with an app technicians carried into each home. A plumber could show a homeowner options on a tablet and take payment on the spot. The company later added marketing and customer financing tools. It charged subscriptions and also earned money on payments that flowed through its platform.

sections.heading: Seventy-One Dollars and Up
sections.body: ServiceTitan priced its IPO at $71 a share on December 11, 2024, above its raised range, and listed on Nasdaq as TTAN. The stock opened at $101 the next day and closed up about 42 percent. The sale of 8.8 million shares raised about $625 million, one of the largest software IPOs of 2024. Mahdessian stayed on as CEO. ServiceTitan still trades on Nasdaq as TTAN.

cover.theme: a tinker with his tools (the tradesman)

dek: Chime gave everyday workers a free phone-based bank account, early paychecks, and overdraft cover without the fees.
lede: Chime is not a bank, yet two-thirds of its 8.6 million active members used it as their main account. Its partner banks held the money. Chime built the app, the debit card, and the features that big banks charged for or skipped. Paychecks could land up to two days early. SpotMe covered small overdrafts with no fee. Its members were mostly everyday workers, not the wealthy. Chime filed for its IPO in May 2025.

sections.heading: From 1debit to Chime
sections.body: Chris Britt and Ryan King incorporated the company in 2012 as 1debit. Britt had worked at Visa, and the first product was a debit card with an app. They bet that millions of Americans were tired of minimum balances and surprise fees. Chime made its money mostly from interchange, the small fee merchants pay each time someone swipes a card. It later added a credit-builder card, instant pay advances called MyPay, and free tax filing.

sections.heading: Twenty-Seven to Forty-Three
sections.body: Chime priced its IPO at $27 a share on June 11, 2025, above its expected range, and listed on Nasdaq as CHYM. The stock opened at $43 the next day and closed up about 37 percent. Britt stayed on as CEO and chair, and the two founders kept most of the voting power through a separate class of shares. Chime still trades on Nasdaq as CHYM.

cover.theme: a bell ringing in a tower (a chime)
cover.artwork: A Bell in the Tower Was Ringing the Hour, plate 4 from Edmond Picard's "Le Juré"

dek: Wealthfront let young professionals hand their savings and investments to software instead of a human adviser.
lede: In 2022 UBS agreed to buy Wealthfront for $1.4 billion, then walked away. Three years later Wealthfront went public on its own. The company had started as kaChing, a stock-picking site, before deciding software should manage money instead of people.
